#6824. Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Said About Their Friendship

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

“Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

Fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

When asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie said, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”

In November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Quickly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”

He then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion shows, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

“Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams said. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”

“It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”

The show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

“We would literally just go to set, go home, cook, work out together, and geek out over how excited we were to finally be working on this level,” he said. “If we were any less close, we probably would’ve gotten annoyed with each other really quick.”

The American actor told Vulture that they leaned into their chemistry while promoting Heated Rivalry’s first season. “If Hudson says something jokingly, like, ‘Spit in my mouth,’ I think that gives everyone else the go-ahead to get in on that too,” he said. “People are ruthless talking about our holes and our butts.”

During his discussion with Interview, Storrie added that spending time with Williams has helped ground them both during their press tour. “Hudson’s been in town, so we’ll have some quality time and come back down to ground zero,” he said. “It’s funny, because all the press and stuff is getting easier and easier and easier. You would think you would get burnt out and exhausted. Even though it’s only been three weeks of doing press for this, I’m clicking into an interesting sort of confidence and appreciation for all of this.”

Williams, meanwhile, credited Storrie for helping him keep the press tour fun during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “I have one of my best friends for life right beside me through it all, which is already a luxury that a lot of actors don’t get,” he said. “I’m sure I would’ve probably had a smaller appetite for the amount of stuff we’re doing if I didn’t have him through this. I’m an omnivert, leaning more to an extrovert, but I still get—I have ADHD, I’m unmedicated, currently, for the last while, so my social battery can just tap [out] pretty quick. At the end of the day, I’m pretty forgiving with myself if I’m talking with a reporter in a polite, more boring way. Then when I’ve had coffee, and I’ve had a nap, I let myself be chaotic. I let myself off the leash. I try to say, whatever mood I’m in, just be Canadian, don’t be mean. Whatever they get, they get.”

Timid magazine asked Williams how Storrie’s acting has helped him be a better performer. Williams responded, “He’s so incredibly present and so incredibly truthful. As an actor, it’s so much easier to think of what you should be doing or what you think would be an entertaining version of this or the most dramatic version or make sure you're hitting these lines properly or doing the scene properly or the director wants this and the script says this. But just to actually listen to the person and let what they’re saying affect you—Connor is so good at that. There’s so many moments where I am saying something and the script says he does this, and he does something so unexpectedly emotional or so unexpectedly vulnerable that even if I'm very robotic and going through a scene, he can crack me and change my trajectory in the scene. He’s a huge resource in affecting me and that makes my job way easier because I don’t have to. He makes me be present. He’s so good at that. That’s his superpower.”

Storrie, meanwhile, credited Williams for helping him understand Ilya so quickly in his Interview story. “I feel like I got the character pretty instantly,” he began. “I believed in his circumstances without almost any effort, and I just trusted Hudson so much. It’s so easy to act when you know where you’re coming from and you believe the person opposite you. I mean, I’m so gooey. I’m such a romantic. So any of the really heightened emotional moments—their love or confession or an outbreak or a fight—those are the moments that I really enjoy as an actor.”

Williams listed out all the nicknames he and Storrie have for each other during his Timid magazine interview. “He calls me Huddy, Papi, Bubba, Baby,” he said. “I call him Pookie. I used to call him Pookie a lot. Papi. Oh, Con Con. I call him that both in text form and verbally. But yeah, a lot of nicknames.”

GQ revealed that when the series wrapped, they got matching tattoos that read “SEX SELLS.”

The Canadian star revealed that he stayed at Storrie’s Los Angeles apartment when he came to the U.S. to do some press. “We were like, ‘Oh, my God, if people saw us just getting ready in the morning, giving each other big spooning hugs, just to say we’re proud of each other,’ people would be going crazy,” he told Variety. “If only one fan had access, God forbid. But yeah, we just love each other very dearly.”

The outlet asked him what creating Heated Rivalry taught him. Williams responded, “I think I had my own biases, maybe that would be too strong of a word, but my own discomfort if I expressed myself fully, physically and affectionately, both with women and men. It would feel inappropriate. I realized if you really do love someone—platonically or not—I’m such a tactile, sensory person. There are so many taboos. It’s much harder on men. I had to let that go, and I got to learn how freeing that is. That also went hand-in-hand with being myself, truly as an artist. Connor was also a great person to have at my side. I think we both opened each other up to just be freer, more fully expressive.”

During Williams’s January 2026 appearance on Andy Cohen Live, he revealed that Storrie is an “awful texter,” but they largely keep in touch with frequent video calls. “We'll Facetime each other or call each other randomly, very consistently,” he told the host. “That has sort of been my stability, especially through this. Just having my best friend who is in the same position I am.”

In a November 2025 interview with The Permanent Rain Press, Williams said he would pitch Storrie as “a beautiful little, sensitive little radical, artist boy. Who should be treated with the utmost care and hugs and friendliness because he can’t handle anything else. And that’s perfect. And that’s the way he should be treated.”

He added, “And anyone who doesn’t treat him that way should die.”

In May 2026, Williams and Storrie made their Met Gala debut. They took a bathroom selfie together, which Williams later posted to his Threads account.

The pair’s appearance at the Met Gala excited fans, with one user taking a solo shot of Williams and posting it alongside lyrics from Rihanna’s breakup song, “Woo.” (Williams has a longtime girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.) The post has since been taken down, but Williams responded and wrote, “Rpfing [real person fan fiction] gotta stop y’all.”

Moody florals feel especially right for a fall wedding, and Simkhai’s draped maxi matches the romance of a countryside estate or garden ceremony. A black-tie wedding invites a little sparkle. Jennifer Behr’s crystal-covered hoops bring the shine with a bold, rounded silhouette. Wear them with a strapless satin dress or a sharply tailored evening look, sweep your hair back, and skip the necklace to let the earrings catch everyone’s eye.

#6820. Vince Staples Is Our November 2026 Music Director

The rapper crafts an exclusive playlist for Bazaar that ranges from songs from his childhood to songs that show the vastness of what hip-hop can be

Vince Staples is known for his matter-of-fact, bluntly honest lyrics. The California-born rapper often taps into the realities of Long Beach, his hometown, meditating on urban poverty, systemic racism, and even skepticism of the music industry. This lyricism emerges from the rapper’s desire to remain authentic and has been evident throughout his career from his 2015 debut, Summertime ’06.

“Whatever your viewpoint on life is or whatever you’re experiencing at this current moment is going to translate into the music that you create, no matter what,” Staples told Bazaar in an interview this summer. “As you get older, you learn to embrace that.”

The musician, 33, did exactly that on his seventh studio album, Crybaby, an urgent, politically charged record that trades traditional beats for post-punk melodies. He confronts historical racism on songs like “Tulsa, OK” and “Cotton” while indicting the entertainment industry for continuing to incite racism against Black people in songs like “TV Guide.” Other songs tap directly into his experience, like “White Flag,” which reflects on his personal journey as an artist and entertainer.

“I want to come up with the idea that feels most organic,” he says, adding that he never listens to music when he’s in the writing process. “I don’t like to be inspired by other music,” he says. “I feel like it’s a disservice to the lives that we live every day…. Music reminds you of what you experience in your life, and it forces you to look inward.” This same instinct guided Staples as he assembled the playlist for Bazaar’s Performance issue, compiling songs that have been foundational to him as an artist and performer.

He often admires introspective songwriting. Blu’s track “Vanity,” featured on the California rapper’s album Her Favorite Colo(u)r (2011), reminds him of the personal, diaristic storytelling style that influenced his early works. “The way he tells stories, it’s the way that I really got into hip-hop music for myself,” he recalls. Today, he cites his friend Steve Lacy’s ability to capture a “good adaptation of his thoughts at the current moment” with “Nice Shoes,” the lead single from the album Oh Yeah? Staples, reflecting on how personal music is, suggests that songs “all have to mean something to us for them to even come to mind” in the first place.

Given the artist’s relationship to music, Staples chose songs that reminded him of moments in his life. One of the album’s oldest tracks is Ray Charles’s soulful “Drown in My Own Tears,” which hearkens back to his childhood. “[Ray Charles] has been ever-present in my life because growing up as a Black person in America and Southern California with older parents or older grandparents, he would be a fixture in music, whether it’s country music, soul music, R&B, music—you can put him in a lot of those different subgenres, but just as far as black music in general,” he says.

Another staple of American Black music is James Brown, but Staples decided to include the Who’s muscular 1965 cover of Brown’s “I Don’t Mind.” For him, the song offers a lesson in transformation and reinterpretation, telling Bazaar it “unearthed the idea of coverage and the ecosystem of sharing music or repurposing music.” On his new album, for instance, he samples Slick Rick’s “Children’s Story” on his song “The Big Bad Wolf.”

In this way, Staples inherently views music as an expansive medium. He recalls how recently the Beastie Boys song “Sabotage,” a buoyant mixture of rap and hardcore punk, helped him explain to a friend “the vastness of what we consider to be hip-hop music.” Ultimately, for Staples, a song’s ability to change you makes it indelible. “It’s a testament to what it meant to you in the moment you first heard it,” he says. “Having that brought back to the forefront is a cool part of the process.”

#6818. Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?

At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”

I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

We’re in the Goldilocks of jacket season. It’s been a consistent 55 to 60 degrees (knock on wood)—a temperature that doesn’t subject you to puffers and parkas, but rather transitional outerwear. And our favorite piece in this category is the novelty jacket.

Maybe you already have one. You know, that gold-buttoned, swanky blazer that you bought from the thrift store because you knew one day you would find the right occasion for it. Or maybe you’ve never had the courage to buy that fringed shacket because you didn’t think you could pull it off. Well, we’re here to tell you that you can, and that now’s the time to do it. Lately, there’s been a loud call to action for the novelty jacket on social media. TikTok influencer Tinx is one of the novelty jacket’s biggest advocates, promising that she’s going to be wearing a new one every day while the weather holds.

So listen to Tinx, and get yourself a novelty jacket. These are our 11 favorites on the market right now that will bring you endless cheer—and compliments.

This is perhaps one of the most practical options on the list. You can wear it to work, a night out, running errands during the day—it’s easily dressed up or down.

The novelty jacket that’s just begging to be taken out to a fancy dinner and then a sultry soirée. Comprised of a luxe brocade, it’s rich, luxurious, and delivering an after-dark elegance.

Not all novelty jackets are shorter or cropped. Dorothee Schumacher’s floor-dusting fringed sweater exudes timeless sophistication. It’s just as good for cozying up near the fireplace as it is for donning at a chic brunch.

Cherry LA’s brings a Western flair to contemporary clothing, and this smoking jacket is no exception. With a pair of worn-in jeans and burnished leather boots, it’s the elevated finish to a ranch-ready fit.

If you’re up for a splurge, Alice + Olivia’s jacket is ultra lavish. Whether you style it with tailored black trousers or layer it over a silky slip dress, the eye-catching jacket will glitter and gleam with opulence.

#6815. Jenny Kee and the Untold Story of Chanel’s Original Australian Debut

It's everything that anyone who loves fashion Down Under can talk about right now: when Matthieu Blazy brings his resort collection to Sydney this November, it will be the first time Chanel has ever shown in Australia.

What relatively few people know, however, is that this landmark moment will not, by a long shot, be the first time Australia has shown in Chanel.

That moment happened 44 years ago, on October 18, 1982, at the Louvre in Paris. Halfway through a Chanel show that, until then, had been dominated by powerfully pastel and friskily high-hemmed interpretations of Coco Chanel’s canonical bouclé suit, something never before seen began to appear on the models who walked out in front of a line of Chanel-branded wardrobes.

It was a print, mostly on white, but sometimes on black, composed of an apparently haphazard accumulation of shapes. Their interiors were fractured into visually immersive pools and veins of cobalt, scarlet, yellow and blue. This pattern appeared first in flashes, then took over entire dresses, as well as jackets, bags, shoes and more. And then, on one white background ruffle-detailed dress, the apparent abstraction resolved itself into something very tangible: across a model’s torso ran the unmistakable outline of Australia.

Chanel spring/summer ’83 with a Kee print showing an outline of Australia. Image credit: Getty Images.

The print was the creation of the then-35-year-old Bondi-born fashion trailblazer Jenny Kee, who is of Chinese, Italian and English heritage, and deeply Australian in sensibility. Kee has been acknowledged in the past—not least, and quite rightly, by herself—as the author of the prints Chanel used that season. In 1983, the year of Coco Chanel’s centenary, the house presented, through Vogue Australia, a Chanel suit featuring Kee’s Opal print in the lining and lapels to the National Gallery of Victoria, where it is displayed online with full and correct attribution.

Yet the story of how an Australian designer came to play a key role in a Chanel collection that, despite being largely forgotten, was one of the most significant in its entire history has, until now, never been fully told. Fashion moves fast and always faces forward; unless preserved, details will fall away as freely as loosely applied sequins from a dress in motion.

Back in 1982, I was living with my mother in the Blue Mountains, where Kee was a neighbour and close family friend. Her brush with Chanel was probably the first fashion story I ever encountered. So, to mark Blazy’s arrival in Sydney, I decided to try to piece it back together and, in the process, discovered a few details even Kee herself was unaware of. As she said when I called her at home up in the mountains this October: “Darl, I had no bloody idea!”

Unlocking the circumstances behind Kee’s cameo for Chanel takes us first to London, where, by 1968, she was living. That December, she appeared naked on the cover of Oz magazine—edited by my late uncle Richard Neville—while working with fellow Australian Vernon Lambert, the visionary vintage dealer whose stall at the Chelsea Antique Market on the King’s Road was helping to rewrite the rules of fashion. Lambert was Kee’s mentor, and when she returned to Australia in 1972, she was ready to start something new.

She opened the Flamingo Park Frock Salon in Sydney’s Strand Arcade and, together with Linda Jackson, began building a fashion language whose point of reference was Australia itself: its opals, native flowers, fauna, bushfires, rainforests and the Great Barrier Reef. “We were doing a completely Australian beauty,” she says. “We were so fresh and so completely pure and so in love with Australia. We were devoted to our country and making beauty of it.”

Chanel spring/summer’83. Image credit: Getty Images.

When Kee and Jackson took that work to Milan in 1977, it caused a sensation. Kee remembers arriving at a party thrown by the Italian stylist and publicist Nally Bellati: “Linda and I walked in and, honestly and truly, they all started jumping on the tables and clapping us, because they’d never seen anything like it,” Kee recalls.

Among those who applauded was Anna Piaggi, the Italian fashion editor who happened to be another one of Lambert’s protégées. In a 1977 issue of Vogue Italia, Piaggi dedicated a double-page spread to Kee and Jackson’s designs under the headline: ‘Fashion arrived from another hemisphere.’ “Anna was bedazzled by what Linda and I were doing back in Australia,” says Kee. The article was accompanied by a sketch of Piaggi wearing Kee’s wool designs—it was drawn by Karl Lagerfeld.

Vogue Italia 1977 featured Kee in her own designs, along with Linda Jackson. Image credit: courtesy Vogue Italia.

Piaggi and Lambert were extremely close to Lagerfeld, who was inspired by Lambert’s habit of always carrying a vintage fan and regularly drew the elaborate outfits Piaggi assembled each day. Kee was entering a tight creative orbit whose members were already constantly looking at, wearing and exchanging one another’s discoveries. In 1977, Kee and her 22-month-old daughter Grace—my oldest friend—were also on a train between Sydney and the Blue Mountains that crashed, killing 83 of their fellow passengers. During their recovery from that neardeath experience, Kee was inspired to sketch Opal and several of her other most famous designs.

Back in Milan in 1980, Kee remembers showing these designs at the home of Piaggi and Lambert, with Manolo Blahnik also present. Lambert then introduced her to Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in Milan. As Kee’s graphics became too detailed and elaborate to realise in knitwear alone, Bellotti—who had long worked with designers including Giorgio Armani and Lagerfeld—was the perfect partner for transferring those designs into print.

Jenny Kee with Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in the 1980s. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

One of those designs was Opal. Developed around the shimmering colours and fractured structures of the Australian gemstone, it became central to Kee and Jackson’s 1981 Flaming Opal collection. This was the print that eventually caught Lagerfeld’s eye one day when he was in the Rainbow Fabrics office looking for fabrics for a very important new collection.

Daniela Morera, Bellotti’s wife, remembers Lagerfeld encountering Kee’s samples through her husband. “Karl fell in love,” she says of the Opal design. Like Kee, she also suggests that Piaggi and Lambert may have helped draw Lagerfeld’s attention to her work.

Kee remembers what happened next very clearly. Bellotti called her in Australia to say Lagerfeld wanted to use the print for Chanel. She immediately agreed. “Apparently, when Karl saw Opal, that’s when he went, ‘Bingo, I want that,’” she says. “And then he proceeded to do it in 65 different ways.”

By October 1982, Chanel itself was in transition. The house had launched ready-to-wear under Philippe Guibourgé in 1978, but its owner, Alain Wertheimer, was already looking for a designer who could rejuvenate a fashion image that had become dusty and out of touch following the death of Coco Chanel in 1971 and amid the emergence of the Japanese new wave and homegrown upstarts such as Jean Paul Gaultier. Wertheimer’s eye settled on Lagerfeld and, in September 1982, Chanel announced that Lagerfeld would become its designer of couture, starting in January 1983. According to MarieLouise de Clermont-Tonnerre, then a senior Chanel communications executive, Lagerfeld ghost-designed the October 1982 collection, with Hervé Léger and Eva Campocasso—previously both assistants of Lagerfeld at Fendi and Chloé respectively—serving as its public-facing designers as his contract with Chloé wound down.

Vernon Lambert in Rome in the early 1980s with Chanel bag and shoes using Kee’s prints from spring/summer ’83. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

This subterfuge was only casually maintained. Writing in The New York Times on the day of the show, Bernadine Morris reported: “Merely a whisper of a Karl Lagerfeld connection was enough to bring out the crowds and the tension … it has been rumoured that he had something to do with the ready-to-wear presented this morning as part of the spring and summer showings here … The Lagerfeld touch seems apparent in the pearl earrings in the shape of the numbers 5 and 19, both names of Chanel perfumes. For the rest, no-one is saying just how much he did. ‘Consultant’ is as far as his friends will go.”

Back in Blackheath, Kee had no idea any of this was happening. When I tell her that the Chanel collection in which her Opal print appeared was, in effect, Lagerfeld’s covert first act for the house, she laughs. “Darl, I had no bloody idea!” Then, delighted: “I love the fact he was ghosting it. It makes it even more interesting—and it means that my print played a part in his first-ever work for Chanel.”

I also show her a picture from a misdated cache of runway images that appears to show a second Kee print, Mali Oz, on the Chanel runway in a dress and handbag worn with an Opal jacket. Kee is astonished. “I’ve never seen that before!” she says. The National Gallery of Australia records that Chanel also used Kee’s Mali Oz fabric.

Whatever the details, Kee’s role also hints at Lagerfeld’s larger creative project: keeping the codes of Chanel intact while applying startling points of difference to push them into another register. “He thought, I’ll just do something really outrageous here,” Kee says, remembering the collision of her print with “that pale pink, old-fashioned Chanel”.

The result changed Kee’s life. “It helped me enormously,” she says. “In that one year, 1982, I was showing at Chanel, and a few months earlier Princess Di was wearing my koala jumper. So those two moments really helped set me on the road. I’m eternally grateful to Chanel and Karl, to Fabio and Daniela, to Anna and Vern. One way or another, they all helped lift me up.”

The Kee Chanel connection was well reported in Australia at the time, and cemented by the Vogue Australia-facilitated Chanel x Kee donation to the NGV. Outside of Australia, however, the strongest contemporary credit to Kee was delivered by another old friend, photographer Bill Cunningham, who dedicated one of his New York Times pages in August 1984 to Kee’s designs for Chanel citing her prominently. One of his photographs was of then Chanel American president Kitty D’Alessio wearing a Kee/Lagerfeld/Chanel spring/summer ’83 jacket. The page features Kee’s Opal and Mali Oz prints on Chanel pieces.

A Chanel jacket lined with Kee’s Opal print from Chanel spring/summer ’83. Image credit: Courtesy Jenny Kee. Powerhouse Collection. Purchased 1999. Photograph Nitsa Yioupros

Nearly half a century later, Chanel is finally touching down in the country that inspired the prints in the first collection Lagerfeld created as he set the house towards its current position at the pinnacle of fashion. Kee is a huge fan of Blazy. “I love his work,” she says. “He’s really standing up to Karl and doing his own thing now.” Coming from Kee—a woman who has spent her very big life doing her very unique thing—that is high praise indeed.

This story appears in Vogue Australia’s November 2026 issue, on sale from November 2.

#6814. The “Longevity Manicure” Is the New Quiet-Luxury Treatment That Will Save Your Nail Health

Why experts love this technique for your strongest, healthiest nails ever

Nail health has quickly become central to a professional manicure. Cumulative care, safe gel removal, and prioritizing long-term strength over quick aesthetic fixes are now standard, alongside high-shine, chip-free finishes. This new philosophy stems from restorative nail treatments taking over salons, from precision dry techniques like the Russian manicure to strengthening builder gels, likely driven by the wider beauty movement toward skin-barrier protection, regenerative treatments, and customized routines.

"The future of manicures isn’t just about the latest color trends or how long your gel polish lasts, but how well we care for the nails underneath," says Krisztina van der Boom, founder of DryBy. "The longevity manicure is the answer to that. It's about beautiful nails today, without compromising the nails you'll have tomorrow."

Rather than viewing nail care as temporary color, this manicure takes a skin-first approach, treating the nail plate and surrounding skin as just as important as the polish itself.

“Think skincare versus makeup; a traditional manicure is the makeup, the beautiful, glossy finish, while a longevity manicure is about everything underneath,” van der Boom explains. “It's all about looking after the natural nail."

Where a conventional gel appointment might focus more on buffing and thick gel overlays to mask imperfections, a longevity manicure uses tailored, restorative techniques. Examples include keratin treatments to rebuild weakened nails, LED red-light therapy to boost collagen and cellular renewal in the hands, integrating hand care into your routine, and microexfoliation techniques that clean the cuticle without damaging the surrounding delicate tissue.

To understand how a longevity manicure works, consider the full life cycle of a nail appointment. "We think of a manicure in four stages: preparation, application, maintenance, and removal," van der Boom says. "Traditionally, most of the attention goes into the first two—achieving that perfect, glossy, long-lasting finish. But what happens afterward matters just as much."

The core philosophy is to eliminate harsh mechanical buffing and aggressive chemical soak-offs. "Some of the most avoidable nail damage happens not when a manicure is applied, but in how it's worn and removed. That's why we place so much importance on thoughtful preparation, precision techniques, responsible maintenance, and gentle removal."

To do this, salons are drawing inspiration from advanced skin health technologies and incorporating high-tech tools and barrier-strengthening formulas into the treatment steps.

"It's about bringing the same thoughtful, preventative approach to our hands and nails that we've come to expect from facial skincare," notes van der Boom.

Whether your nails are naturally brittle, damaged from years of harsh gel removals, or simply need a healthier routine, this approach suits all nail types and needs. "The longevity manicure is designed as an ongoing ritual rather than a one-off treatment," van der Boom says. “With consistent, thoughtful care, the aim is to preserve the integrity of your natural nails, minimize avoidable damage, and support the skin of your hands over time.”

She believes this is all about prevention rather than correction. "You can disguise unhealthy nails with a beautiful finish, but there's nothing chicer than beautifully groomed, healthy nails even when they're completely bare."

Cuticle Hydration: Apply cuticle oil daily to support skin elasticity and keep the nail plate from drying out and becoming prone to chipping.

Protect the Skin Barrier: Treat your hands with the same care you give your face. Use moisture-rich hand creams formulated with ceramides or hyaluronic acid, and always apply broad-spectrum sunscreen to the backs of your hands to protect against UV damage and premature aging.

Change Your Removal Technique: Avoid peeling, scraping, or forcing off gel polish, which can strip keratin layers from the surface of your nail.

Try a Strengthening Treatment: Add repair treatments to your manicure routine, such as keratin strengtheners or at-home red-light therapy devices, for stronger, shinier nails.

#6812. Better American Sunscreens Are Here—But We’re Still Way Behind the Best

Anyone who’s applied sunscreen only to be left with a chalky white cast, a greasy finish knows American sun care has long been a frustrating experience. The US is decades behind European and Asian counterparts, which have long been blessed with sunscreens that are lighter, more luxurious, and easier to wear every day. For skincare obsessives (this writer included) trips abroad are also opportunities to stock up on superior sunscreens they can’t find at home.

The root of the problem is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration classifies sunscreen as a drug rather than a cosmetic. Because of that distinction, more time and testing is required to get new sunscreens on the shelves, dramatically reducing innovation in American sun protection. But for the first time since the ‘90s, we’ve had some movement on that front. In June of this year, the FDA approved a new sunscreen filter called bemotrizinol—also known as Tinosorb S or BEMT—after years of lobbying in the states by dermatologists, skincare brands, and Congress members. It’s a meaningful step toward better sun care, but the US is still lagging behind.

Bemotrizinol is prized for its ability to provide both UVA and UVB protection while remaining stable in sunlight. That’s a significant advantage over some existing US-approved filters, which offer protection against one type of UV radiation more effectively than the other. BEMT also has the potential to make sunscreen more pleasant to wear: “And because it’s a large, oil-loving molecule, it mostly stays on the surface of your skin instead of soaking in, and it blends into lightweight, non-greasy formulas with no white cast,” says Dr. Joel Spitz, co-founder, chief medical officer, and board-certified dermatologist at Honeydew, a virtual dermatology platform.

Bemotrizinol might be new for the US market, but it’s already been used in sunscreen formulations abroad for 20 years, Spitz says. That long track record helps explain why consumers in the US have spent years coveting the more cosmetically elegant formulas available in countries like South Korea and France. While most consumers would love if major brands like Neutrogena, La Roche-Posay, or Beauty of Joseon brought their European or Asian formulations to the US, those SPFs still contain filters that the FDA hasn’t approved. As a result, many brands are developing entirely new BEMT-centric formulas for use stateside.

Australian label Ultra Violette was the first brand to release a BEMT sunscreen in the US with its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in August 2026. Neutrogena debuted its Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 in September. Earlier this month French drugstore staple La Roche-Posay put its Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 up for sale online. Don’t mistake the relatively quick arrival of these products after the FDA’s approval for ease in which brands can develop new formulations. According to Emanuella Louis, La Roche-Posay’s public relations manager, the brand had been working on its new formula for more than two years.

That long lead time reflects the way sunscreen development works: Brands can research and test formulas in anticipation of regulatory changes, then move a product forward when a particular filter gets the green light. Louis says La Roche-Posay has access to filters the FDA may be considering for approval and is “actively working, playing, testing on what possibly those formulas would be.” When a filter is approved, she explains, a formula already in the testing pipeline can be moved up.

Some brands are still tinkering with BEMT formulas for the US. Round Lab, one of South Korea’s most popular sunscreen manufacturers, has sold a version of its SPF in the US since 2024, and is hard at work on a new version of those formulas that contains bemotrizinol.

“Bemotrizinol’s approval in the US is a meaningful change, but it does not mean a Korean formula can simply be brought to the US market as is,” says Koochul Kwon, Round Lab’s chief technology officer. Beyond incorporating the newly approved filter, brands must ensure the ingredients keep the UV filters stably dissolved and working alongside other components, including moisturizing ingredients. The finished product must then meet US requirements for SPF and broad-spectrum testing, product stability, and labeling. With those considerations in mind, Kwon expects Round Lab to release its own bemotrizinol sunscreen sometime in 2027.

A sunscreen is only as useful as a person’s willingness to wear it consistently. Bemotrizinol’s ability to protect against UV damage is important, but its potential to make formulas lighter, less greasy, and more comfortable could be just as consequential to get people to implement it in their everyday skincare routines.

“One of the strengths of Korean sun care is how naturally it has built sun protection into the everyday skincare experience,” Kwon says. “For people to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it when needed, the way it feels matters as much as how well it protects.”

But better filters alone won’t transform American sun care. The real breakthrough will be sunscreens that people actually enjoy wearing—and, as a result, are more likely to apply generously and reapply throughout the day, a key step to ensuring its effectiveness.

Charlotte Palermino, cofounder and chief brand officer of skincare brand Dieux, has been an advocate for easier sunscreen filter approvals ever since she tried her first Japanese sunscreen, Biore UV, a decade ago. She realized sunscreen could stave off skin issues after her dermatologist told her that her hyperpigmentation had been the result of failing to use sun protection. In the years since she has publicly pushed for regulatory reform. She’s hesitant to put an estimated release date on Dieux’s upcoming BEMT-centric sunscreen, simply because the brand is dialed in to ensure its able to deliver a quality, wearable product.

“We’ve gone through this with [Dieux’s] SkinMercy, which is an OTC colloidal oatmeal cream, but for sunscreen, the stability of your sunscreen is so fucking important,” she says. “If my sunscreen separates or if it’s not at that stated SPF 50, if that degrades at all with broad spectrum protection, I would be mortified.”

Palerimo cites brands like Korea’s Beauty of Joseon, which is more popular in the US than in its home country, as evidence that Americans have long been on the hunt for better sunscreen. And though BEMT is a step forward, we still have a way to go. Board-certified dermatologist Jane Yoo has been lobbying Congress to get new sunscreen filters approved for the US and is tracking the FDA’s progress in making those approvals. Currently there are seven other filters—bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane, octyl triazone, amiloxate, diethylhexyl butamido triazone iscotrizinol, ecamsule, and enzacamene—under the agency’s Time and Extent Application (TEA) pipeline. Those filters are part of the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act meant to speed up the process of determining if ingredients are Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective, or GRASE. But here we are 12 years later, and we’re still waiting for their approval.

“A good analogy is we’ve been making sunscreens with both of our hands tied behind our backs,” Palermino says. “We’ve now had one hand released. I would like both hands released.”

#6811. The Easiest Exercise for Longevity, According to Science

A few months ago, I had never so much as lifted a barbell—let alone thought about exercises for longevity. However, during a stay at Buchinger Wilhelmi Clinic, I attended a life-changing lecture by Felipe Isidro, a professor of physical education and CEO of Physical Exercise & Health Consulting. That was the day everything changed.

“Who here works out?” Isidro asked. “When I say ‘work out,’ I don’t mean normal physical activities like walking, climbing stairs, and carrying shopping bags. I mean ‘exercise,’ which is movement that is both planned and scheduled. I ask, because 7 out of 10 people don’t: That’s 70% of the population.”

Of course, any physical activity is better than none. “But you don’t get the same benefits as with exercise,” Isidro explained. “The ideal, instead, is to combine both—to move more on a daily basis and to set aside specific time for training. In a society that invites us to move less and less with cars, elevators, and escalators, the objective should be to exercise—and, especially, to do strength training.”

Up until then, I had never thought of the true importance of exercise: I’d only thought of it as a means to an end—to lose weight and, ideally, to look better in my clothes. Although it is true that exercise can help on both accounts, Isidro allowed me to see that neither of those are as important as keeping the body’s muscles and mitochondria healthy for as long as possible. “The mitochondria are like little batteries that produce the energy that impact vitality,” Isidro explained. “When the mitochondria work well, we feel strong; when they deteriorate, we feel fatigued. It’s also difficult to burn fat, even when we diet. Fat not only accumulates under the skin but also in organs, viscera, and even in the muscle itself.”

Here, there is no miracle pill—the only “medicine” proven to improve mitochondrial function is exercise, and especially strength training. Just as a cell phone battery lasts for hours when it’s new but loses its ability to hold a charge, the same thing happens with mitochondria—as we age, we may wake up with energy but feel exhausted by mid-morning. Thus, we must keep our mitochondria as healthy as possible.

Within the muscle there are slow twitch fibers and fast twitch fibers— slow twitch fibers are responsible for prolonged efforts such as walking; fast twitch fibers are essential for power and speed.

As we age, fast twitch fibers are the first to decline. “Walking improves endurance, but it doesn’t stop the loss of fast twitch fibers. If you don’t train strength, you become sluggish. We see it in older people, who end up walking in short steps because they have lost those fibers. Strength training is the only way to keep them,” Isidro points out. “We gain muscle until the age of 25, maintain it until the age of 35 and, from then on, we start to lose it slowly, accelerating from the age of 50, and even more at the age of 65. There are cases of people in their 70s who maintain the strength of someone sedentary in their 40s or 50s thanks to daily training, proving that this habit can subtract up to 20 years from biological age.”

After all, what you don’t use, you lose. That goes for muscle—but also for bones, the respiratory system, and the pelvic floor. Regular exercise also improves the non-REM phase (deep sleep in which the eyes do not move), and that also decreases with age. Having longer non-REM phases is related to gradual and healthy aging. “Strength training is an investment in health for the future,” Isidro says. “It reduces anxiety and it makes us feel better at all levels. In reality, a healthy body is a perfect body.”

While water is essential for our hydration, too much of it can cause us to drown. Strength training is similar: The proper dosage is key. It’s not about doing it in excess; it’s about doing it right. The right dose, says Isidro, means few repetitions, lots of recovery time, and, above all, not looking to fatigue: “Many people think that, if they don’t get tired, they haven’t trained properly. It’s actually just the opposite. In strength, we’re not looking to exhaust ourselves, we’re looking for quality.” To that end, here are seven points to keep in mind in order to strength train properly, no matter your age or fitness level.

The minimum for adaptation is two days a week, although the ideal scenario would be to progress to three or four with breaks in between—one day on, one day off. You should also do strength before endurance; if you do both on the same day, it’s best to finish with cardio.

If you’re new to working out, it’s best to focus on the legs. They are the largest reservoir of muscle mass in the body and also the quickest to deteriorate. In addition, the legs contain a lot of fast twitch fibers, so training them is vital.

Do reps at a high intensity (quickly) to work the fast twitch fibers. It is recommended to do a few repetitions—half or less of the maximum you can do—to avoid fatigue. “The key is speed and intensity, because that’s what activates the fast fibers through the nervous system,” says Isidro.

Give yourself plenty of time to rest between sets. At minimum, rest time should be one minute, but two or three minutes between exercises is even better. “You’re fully recovered when you can speak and sing, not just utter and grunt monosyllables,” says Isidro.

“It is essential that the exercise be non-exhausting or fatiguing. When you fatigue, you’re working the slow twitch fibers and continuing to lose fast twitch fibers,” says Isidro. “It’s better to do a few exercises well and repeat them a couple of times. Stop before fatigue sets in.”

Start with short workout sessions that last 5 to 15 minutes. Do them in a circuit format, alternating exercises with breaks. “We all have 10 minutes a day if we prioritize. Forget your previous experience—many of us think that exercise should be tiring and painful to work. If we do less, we enjoy it more and see the benefits, creating a positive ripple effect.”

Working the respiratory muscles is also essential, because it improves recovery and endurance. Take long, full breaths, breathing into the diaphragm.

According to Isidro, the best time to exercise is in the morning: “This stimulates the sympathetic system early, which makes it easier for the parasympathetic system to be stimulated in the evening, improving sleep.” If possible, exercise outdoors, because contact with nature and socialization have a direct effect on health.

You don’t need a full gym to get the benefits. Working out with your own body weight can be really effective. “The important thing is that the exercises are adapted to your fitness level so that you can repeat and maintain them over time,” Isidro says. “And if you can do them in a group or with friends, even better. Socializing motivates, engages, and, as studies show, lengthens life.”

There are several simple tests that can be done at home in order to check our current strength level and to show us where we may need to improve. “The important thing about these tests is not only to know where we are, but also to measure how we are progressing,” notes Isidro. “Sometimes the change is perceived in how we feel, but other times we need objective data, and these are very simple tools that allow us to tangibly see how strength training is helping us improve.” Below, some of those tests.

One useful test is to stand up and sit down five times as fast as possible using just your legs—all you need is a chair and a stopwatch. This test measures the strength of the legs, which is where we have the most muscle and, at the same time, where we usually lose muscle first.

This one combines strength and balance. It involves standing on the non-dominant leg and lifting the other leg. The goal is to maintain posture without using the arms. In people under 50 years of age, it is done with eyes closed, and in older people, with eyes open to prevent falls. The ideal is to balance for at least 45 seconds.

The six-minute endurance test involves walking as fast as possible for six minutes. Walking less than 500 meters indicates poor cardiorespiratory fitness; walking between 500 and 700 meters is acceptable; walking more than 700 is excellent.

Shawn G. Anthony, MD, an orthopedic sports medicine surgeon and associate system chief of sports medicine at Mount Sinai, says that almost every form of movement will help with longevity and has some value. But you shouldn’t rely on just one type of exercise to do everything. “There is no single longevity exercise,” Anthony says. “The goal is to build cardiovascular fitness and strength while preserving the ability to move well and remain active over time.”

He goes on to explain that the strongest evidence for longevity is combining aerobic exercise with resistance training. Think brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming, or sports with free weights, resistance bands, or body weight. With that in mind, here are some other exercises to consider.

Walking is one of the easiest exercises you can incorporate to daily life and is backed up by science. “It is accessible, low impact, and easy to sustain, and meaningful health benefits occur well below 10,000 steps per day,” Anthony explains. “There is also good evidence that walking after a meal can reduce the rise in blood glucose that follows eating, so even a brief post-meal walk can be a useful way to incorporate more movement into the day and improve metabolic health.”

He says that weighted walking can help. And while trendy walking exercises such as tai chi walking and lymphatic walking come with limited research in regards to longevity, anything that gets you moving is beneficial.

Picking up a new sport like tennis isn’t easy in the sense that you’ll get the hang of it in one (or even several) tries. But if you’re not trying to be the next Serena and just doing it for fun, it can be a form of exercise you look forward to. Anthony adds that sports can be especially useful because you train a lot of things at once, and one of the best examples is tennis. “It combines aerobic conditioning with bursts of higher-intensity movement, changes of direction, coordination, reaction time, and a social component,” he says. “Studies of racket sports have reported favorable associations with longevity.”

Yes, these workouts are hard. But finding a workout that you like and want to stick to will make it easy for you to meet your longevity goals. Anthony says that trendy workouts such as Pilates, HIIT, and Zone 2 training can be useful as long as the underlying training makes sense. You want to identify your fitness goals and find an exercise that will help you meet them safely and consistently. “If a trendy workout motivates someone to exercise regularly, that has real value,” he says. “What matters more than the label is whether the workout contributes to a well-rounded and sustainable exercise program.”

Anthony says to avoid anything that will repeatedly cause joint pain, tendon problems, or overuse injuries. “That is not a successful longevity strategy,” he says. “The goal is to increase physical capacity without repeatedly exceeding what the body can recover from.”

He also says that our fitness and strength are built up over time in our 20s, 30s, 40s, and 50s. So while it would be ideal to not wait until later in adulthood to begin thinking about longevity, starting now is still better than later (or never).

And just remember that the foundation of longevity remains regular aerobic exercise, resistance training, and daily movement. Whatever will get you those three will be the best workout for you. “Longevity requires durability,” he says. “Ultimately, the goal is to preserve enough physical capacity to keep running, skiing, playing tennis, traveling, and doing activities that matter to you 20 or 30 years from now.”

In August, Grande spoke to fans at her Chicago show about her decision to take a break. “It’s a plan that I had quietly made a long time ago, and it’s a decision that was made from a thoughtful and empowered place,” she explained. “And I want you to know that many things can be true at the same time. Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Between gift shopping, family gatherings, and holiday parties, the season can quickly fill every moment of your schedule. An everything shower offers a chance to slow down and indulge in a little self-care, transforming an everyday rinse into a more immersive beauty ritual. Think of it as a moment to reconnect with yourself, recharge, and savor a little calm amid the holiday rush.

The right combination of sensorial fragrances and thoughtfully formulated products from Ulta Beauty can elevate an everything shower into a spa-worthy ritual. From skin-nourishing essentials to indulgent finishing touches, these picks will help you create a routine that feels uniquely your own.

An exfoliating body scrub helps buff away dead skin cells, leaving skin feeling smoother and softer. Tree Hut’s sugar-based formulas pair gentle exfoliation with shea butter and hydrating oils, all wrapped in an inviting fragrance. The fresh, citrusy fragrance, with notes of grapefruit, lime, mandarin, and cypress, adds a sensory finishing touch. The set also includes a matching body wash and mood oil, so you can carry the scent through your routine.

Complete your ritual with a final touch of fragrance. The Sol de Janeiro Cheirosa Anywhere Jelly Perfume Balm & Mist Gift Set pairs perfume mists with solid balms designed to last up to 10 hours. Choose Cheirosa 62, a warm gourmand blend of pistachio, almond, and vanilla, or Cheirosa 68, a brighter, more floral composition featuring pink dragonfruit, jasmine, and sun musk. Either way, you’ll carry a little of that just-stepped-out-of-the-spa feeling with you long after your shower.

#6808. 30 Gifts for Dads Who Swear They Don't Want Anything 2026

Your old man is funny about gifts, ain't he? That guy will wear the same jacket for 20 years, spend a small fortune on something you've never heard of, and insist he doesn't need a thing. More often than not, finding the best gifts for dads involves putting your thinking cap on to mentally trawl through all of the very practical things they already own, along with the stuff that they’d just never use. Fortunately, we've got a few good dads on the GQ staff. Opinionated dads. Handsome dads. Great dads. And they've actually got some ideas.

Still no dice? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

Simple, generously proportioned, and blessed with a great collar, this checked shirt from Japanese label Frizmworks gets all the little things right. And the price? Legendary.

It's a good idea to pay closer attention to what's been happening at Filson lately. The brand's been digging into its archives and finding fresh ways to offer up its outdoorsmen roots, as evidenced by this Tacoma jacket, an old-school silhouette recast in a handsome denim.

There's a reason a Burberry check scarf costs what it does. The pattern is destined to outlast every passing trend and come back into fashion again and again. And the cashmere? Every bit as luxurious as he'd hope.

A Shaggy Dog for the shaggy ol' dog, y'know. J.Press's sweater is the real deal, made from Shetland wool that's hand-brushed to achieve its signature fuzzy texture. And yes, it's still made in Scotland, where the wool comes from. Tradition is tradition.

There's always a good reason for another pair of work boots, so why not make 'em Western? These meet the safety standards for commercial construction but look handsome as hell doing it.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

Of all the tech you could get him this year, a portable cassette player is probably the last thing he'd expect. This one comes from the nostalgia peddlers at Retrospekt. And if he doesn't appreciate the format, he'll at least appreciate the transparent casing that puts the inner circuitry on display.

Five generations in, JBL still hasn't found a reason to make the Go any bigger. And why would it? The pint-sized speaker continues to deliver outsized sound, with the latest iteration adding 10 hours of battery life and USB-C wired audio support. Still the one to beat in its size class.

Nocs Provisions is the first name in cool binoculars, and now it's got a lo-fi digital camera to match. It's a fun little shooter in its own right, but I love that you can take photos straight through a pair of binoculars or a monocular.

String 'em up or stake 'em in the ground—BioLite's solar-powered site lights make illuminating a campsite (or a backyard, balcony, or any outdoor area) a cinch. If he's a camper, he'll be a happy one.

Twelve South is known for its AirFly Bluetooth dongle for flights, and now it's coming for your car. The new AirFly Drive is a clever little device that does away with the cords, letting him connect to Apple CarPlay or Android Auto wirelessly.

I've reached the point where I trust Anker with just about anything that plugs into a wall. This nifty universal charger uses GaN technology to power up to four devices at once, with interchangeable plugs for the US, UK, and EU. Australia, regrettably, remains off the itinerary.

I'm of the mind that you can't have too many fragrances, and of the three versions of Bleu de Chanel, the original EDT is the one I recommend most. It's the brightest and most citrus-forward of the lot, before settling into something warmer and woodier.

Byredo's new body mists offer a more casual way to wear scent, with a lighter touch and a shorter lifespan than your typical cologne. Mojave Ghost leans the most masculine to my nose, though there's nothing gendered about smelling good.

What a great form factor for a shaver. Panasonic's ARC5 Palm packs five Japanese stainless-steel blades and the power of a full-size electric razor into a handsome little device that fit in the palm of his hand.

A hangnail is a small indignity, but an indignity nonetheless, especially when you're a thousand miles from home. German grooming specialists Mühle have been at it since 1945, and this handsome travel manicure set comes equipped with a nail clipper, scissors, tweezers, and file.

Vermont-based Ursa Major comes up a lot in our grooming coverage, and that's no accident. This set brings together a few of our favorites, including its vitamin C serum, night cream, and face wash. A very solid skincare routine, all in one box.

This beef tallow balm from Sky High Farm, the upstate New York agricultural project with a fashion-world following, is as good as anything for soothing and restoring dry skin.

ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

No man in his right mind would turn down a pair of L.L.Bean's Wicked Goods, which is practically its own category of slipper. Sometimes the obvious choice is the right one.

I've been meaning to take up sewing for years, but my excuse has always been a lack of space. Then I spotted this mini sewing machine at the MoMA Design Store, and suddenly that excuse isn't so convincing.

It's always better when you make it yourself, and that's certainly true of shibori. This beginner-friendly kit comes with bandanas, tenugui cloths, indigo dye, rubber gloves, and easy-to-follow instructions. Might as well throw a few white tees into the mix while he's at it.

Now that's one helluva coffee mug. Made from stainless steel with double-wall construction to keep it cool to the touch, this industrial number from Copenhagen-based design studio Service Projects comes with a generously proportioned saucer that does double duty as a serving tray.

Before there was John Wilson, there was Phaidon's photographic ode to the world's most ubiquitous building material. Give him a nudge and a wink and tell him it's a “solid” gift. He'll appreciate that.

He should absolutely wear these sunnies from Satisfy and Oakley while running. But does he have to? Not in the slightest.

You might think running requires little more than a pair of sneakers, but you'd be surprised. This vest from Lululemon has pockets aplenty for all the little things he needs to bring along, without weighing him down.

It wouldn't be the holidays without a little tension. Therabody's new massage gun is made for the face, combining gentle percussion with heat to help relieve tightness around the jaw, temples, and cheeks.

A few minutes of cold therapy can work wonders on a puffy, sleep-deprived face. Quiet Hours' facial ice roller makes the ritual dead simple: chill it, roll it across the skin, and let the cold do its thing.

Electrolytes have gotten awfully sophisticated lately. Freaks of Nature's zero-sugar powder goes beyond hydration, with a formula designed to support gut health and the skin barrier, too.

Google's new Fitbit Edge splits the difference between its screenless fitness bands and full-fledged smartwatches, adding a bright OLED display to a slim, handsome tracker. There's built-in GPS, heart-rate and sleep tracking, and up to seven days of battery life.
