#6807. Why I’m Wearing Nothing But Pajamas

Last March, the 20th to be exact, I decided I was never going to wear anything but pajamas again, day and night. That was the day my life changed forever. That was the day my husband, Tad, died.

Tad was the only thing I never wanted to return or take back. I’m impossible to please, impossible to buy a present for, but he never stopped trying. I had no doubt about him. We met nearly 40 years ago, when I interviewed him on January 27, 1987, at three o’clock in the afternoon. He sat on a sofa, a large, overstuffed pale-gray one, in his writing studio in New York. A year and a half later, I was sitting on that same sofa and his writing studio had become our apartment. After we married, we did everything together. Worked together, played together—​our work was our play—traveled together. That never stopped, until it did.

I suddenly had four children, from my age (then mid-30s) down to four years old, plus four ready-made grandchildren and two new sobriquets—belle-mère and GrandDodie. (This was Tad’s way of easing me into early onset grandmotherhood and keeping that awful word stepmother from floating into my life.) Happily, none of the dear ones have ever called me the evil S-word, exceptfor one time on our way out to Quogue on Long Island on a summer weekend. Trying to keep cool on a hot Friday night, I’d tied my long dark hair in a knot at the top of my head. “Ooooohhhh,” Tad’s five-year-old daughter, Sarah, screeched from the back seat of our tiny Fiat convertible, where she was squished comfortably on her rocking horse. “The wicked stepmother!” There it was, out in the open.

But I stray. Pajamas. Or is it pyjamas? I like the word spelled the way the Brits do it, but feel it’s worthy of two spellings, like doughnut and donut. Either is better than the humiliating nicknames—pj’s, jammies, or jam-jams.

Pajamas—I’m going to live in them, go everywhere in them, never wear anything else. If Julian Schnabel can do it, why can’t I? Pajamas are for wearing inside, but when I feel up to going out again, I’ll wear them outside too. One night, I got a glimpse of my oldest stepdaughter, Trippy, wearing a pair in navy with white piping. I like that look. I filed the thought away. But the notion to live in pajamas hit me over the head when Tad’s niece Torrie drove me up to our house in Newport a week after Tad died. As soon as we arrived, in the middle of the afternoon, Torrie changed into the most delicious, crisp pair of navy-trimmed white-poplin Matouks. That was it. It was pajamas forever for me.

I might have mentioned my pajama game plan to my Vogue editor, because a few days later, a box from Petite Plume arrived containing the perfect pair of tailored striped ones, blue and white, a long pant and a long-sleeve top, 100 percent cotton. Chloe, my six-foot-tall editor, is more of a nightgown person and says, “Pajamas are often not made for tall people. You end up with the pant leg an awkward length.” But I don’t feel sorry for Chloe—I’m envious of her glorious monumentality (I’m five feet two when I can stand up straight), and, anyway, she gets the best nightgowns from Salter House in Brooklyn, spun from the finest cotton in all of Western Christendom.

My new pajamas are size extra-extra small and they fit just right, which means with a very loose and baggy ankle-​length pant. Webster’s defines pajamas as “worn for sleeping or lounging, typically consisting of a jacket or top and matching trousers.” The word dates back to the 19th century, derived from the Hindi term (also pājāma), which in turn comes from the Persian words pā for “leg” and jāma for “garment.” The pajama pant has long been worn throughout Asia as everyday wear, well before they became the sleeping-and-lounging uniform for every law-abiding Westerner.

I have no interest in lounging (loathe the word) and I’ll never wear them to bed. And it’s definitely not cool to wear the pajama top—pajama bottom or no pajama bottom. Pajama tops are like anchovies—they get pushed to the side of the plate. No one wants to wear just the top, except for maybe Ryan Gosling, who topped off a pair of crisp white pants with a white-piped pajama shirt at the Cannes Film Festival in 2011.

But bottoms are the tops for me, and for almost everyone I know. I’ve lived in my striped Petite Plume bottoms since the day they arrived last April. And not long ago, I found myself watching Doris Day in the 1957 movie The Pajama Game, where she worked in the Sleeptite Pajama Factory. “Wear Sleeptite at all social functions,” the workers sang. “Dresses are fine but Sleeptite’s divine. Sleeptite has everything—grace, style, and comfort.” I’m with Doris Day on this one.

WEDDING BELLE Dodie and Tad on the Day they were married.

During this mourning period, a few close friends have been visiting me for lunch and dinner, and I haven’t gone out. One day, the artist Jamian Juliano-Villani dropped by with Kat Herriman, a young writer friend of mine. Jamian said she likes her pajamas to be “versatile, so if you need to leave the house, you don’t look like a crazy person.” She wears two things on rotation—a Matouk robe and pajamas an art dealer gave her by the Copenhagen brand Tekla, which she wears outside. “They’re very, very cool. If you throw on a pair of sunglasses, you look great. They’re not cheap but they’re worth it.” She’s one of the few people I know who likes a matching set. “You feel more together. Go to bed, wake up….”

She does. I tell Jamian that I don’t know anybody who sleeps in their pajamas. Everyone I spoke to who wears them takes them off before going to bed—to sleep in the nude. (Not I.)

And not my friend Ruth Ganesh, who brought a herd of 100 life-size elephant sculptures made from the Lantana camara weed in Southern India to America to raise awareness for wildlife conservation. She wears Indian cotton pajamas, made in Jaipur using block technique. “They make the most beautiful multicolored ones, with flowers and patterns all over them, that give me the happiest dreams,” she tells me. “It’s a rite of passage when English people visitIndia to go pajama shopping in Anokhi. We stuff our suitcases full of them.”

Funny, Cecily Brown had told me that one of her dealers and a dear friend, Stefania Bortolami, gives her artist friends pajamas from Rome for Christmas. Seems pajamas-​as-​Christmas-​presents are a thing with art dealers and their artists. John Currin tells me that his London dealer, Sadie Coles, sends him ones from Turnbull & Asser for Christmas. The artist Diamond Stingily comes by with Pucci, her artist friend Martine Syms’s best-in-show Pomeranian, and my ears perk up when she tells me that the only place to get pajamas is a store called Schostal in Rome. “All the artists go there,” she says. Turns out artists know about the place because of Gavin Brown, whose Roman gallery is in Sant’Andrea de Scaphis, a ninth-​century deconsecrated church. Gavin and his wife, artist Hope Atherton, have introduced legions to the brand. Schostal pajamas are made of the finest materials, sewn with a sky-high thread count that makes them as soft as a baby mole’s skin and slightly see-through. They come in solids and stripes in mouthwatering colors.

I have to have a pair. However, I’m hopeless when it comes to ordering anything online, even FreshDirect. Then, Hope herself drops by for afternoon tea one Monday in June—and before I know it, a delicious pair of lemon Schostals with red-and-white pinstripes are winging their way to me from Rome. They’re not cheap—nearly $300—thanks to Trump’s tariffs.

The whole idea of wearing pajamas is to trick myself into feeling better. When I tell my friend and favorite dermatologist Joel Kassimir that I’ve decided to live in pajamas from now on, he says, “Like Peter Marino’s leathers, Julian Schnabel’s pajamas, and Vinny ‘Chin’ Gigante’s bathrobe, it is a uniform, and it works.”

The artist Rachel Feinstein brings me the best sashimi lunch from Sugarfish by Sushi Nozawa and we talk pajamas. She loves hers. “They’re by Dôen, a company that Flora (my 17-year-old daughter) is into, and she’s gotten me into them. It’s not really my style. They’re very Laura Ashley, actually—new Gen Z Laura Ashley. Made out of incredibly thin fine cotton. But I love them. They have a blue delft-like pattern, and the minute I’m home, I put them on. I don’t like silk—too cloying and hot.” No silk for me either. Or satin: too 1930s starlet boudoir—Carole Lombard, Claudette Colbert, Lauren Bacall, or Katharine Hepburn in Bringing Up Baby.

I can’t possibly make a decision about pajamas without talking to Vogue’s head of fashion, Virginia Smith. She’s running to catch a flight to Los Angeles when I reach her by phone, just in time for her to tell me about For Restless Sleepers, Olivia von Halle, and what she calls “the classics”—Charvet, Brooks Brothers, and Ralph Lauren. She also tells me about Grace Coddington wearing Michael Kors blue pajamas to the 2015 Met Gala—and that she herself wore Erdem mint pj’s to the 2024 Met Gala, “Sleeping Beauties.”

Last night I saw a woman on Park Avenue in matching pajamas walking her dog.

A few very close artist friends of Tad’s and mine have been keeping me afloat—or vertical, to use Tad’s word—throughout these difficult days, weeks, months without him. In the last 5 or 10 years of Tad’s life, whenever anyone asked him how he was doing, his answer was “I’m still vertical.”

Pajamas make me feel safe—and vertical—even though you wear them in a horizontal position. Pajamas are my safety net.

One mid-June sunny evening, Maurizio Cattelan and Anna Weyant come for dinner. Over the 30 years Tad and I have known Maurizio, every time he’d come for dinner, he’d surprise us with a wildly original present, each one topping the one before in outrageousness: ​a blowfish ceiling lamp; a human-size package of Oscar Mayer wieners; a Gucci box—open the cover and out pops a two-dimensional cutout of Tad and me. This time, he brings the tennis ball Billie Jean King signed for him the day before—he did a photo shoot with her for his magazine Toiletpaper. He mumbles something about the shoot and why she signed the tennis ball, but I don’t get it.

In advance of my birthday, which is the next day, Anna Weyant brings a present too—but hers is in a traditional white box tied up with a very pretty exaggeratedly wide vanilla grosgrain ribbon. It looks just like one of her hyperrealistic paintings. Inside is the perfect gift for me—the navy blue with white trim Eberjeys I’ve been dreaming about. “You can return them if you don’t like them,” she says. “No, I don’t want to return these,” I say with delight. I’m in pajama heaven.

“Will you wear sleepers?” Maurizio asks me.

After he repeats the word three times—“sleepers, sleepers, sleepers”—I finally get it. Slippers to go with my Eberjeys.

June 17: It’s my birthday, and I’m happily (and stylishly) wearing my new Eberjeys. They fit just right, make me feel safe, at home, sleek, well-dressed. These are going-out-in-the-world pajamas. They’re not 100 percent cotton but rather 95 percent Tencel Modal, a proud member of the rayon family, descended from the noble beech tree. Tencel promises all the benefits of cotton—super soft, durable, and a friend of the environment.

At three o’clock in the afternoon, Cecily Brown, Rachel Feinstein, Anna Weyant, and Kat Herriman surprise me with a pajama party. One by one they arrive and immediately change into their pj’s. Rachel didn’t have time to go home to get hers, but Cecily happens to have an extra pair in her bag—a fetching solid peach with navy trim. Rachel wears the top and bottom. She looks perfect, but nobody else dares.

The conversation roams all over the place, from what Cecily did the night she turned 30 to a book about witches and witchcraft called Abject Eroticism in Northern Renaissance Art.

I go to the Mark Hotel for dinner with my friend Peter Gelb, general manager of the Metropolitan Opera, in my navy blue Eberjeys with pearls. All I need are open-toe little satin bedroom slippers to complete my outfit. Nobody notices I’m wearing pajamas, not even Peter. But I know, and I know how much I need them. I need them forever. Or at least for now.

#6806. Inez and Vinoodh Mark 40 Years With a CFDA Lifetime Achievement Award

The celebrated photography duo and couple will be honored at the annual ceremony.

This evening, celebrated photography duo Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin will be given the Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award at the CFDA Fashion Awards. The pair, who are married, have been working together for 40 years, creating ad campaigns for brands like Gucci, Chanel, and Saint Laurent and shooting for major magazines.

“We didn’t know it was possible for [the Geoffrey Beene award to be given for] photography because it was always designers until now,” Matadin tells ELLE. “We’re just so happy that the CFDA is recognizing photography as such an integral part of the industry we all work in. The fact is that we as photographers translate a designer’s vision into an image or a film, so their designs live on in another world, in another way, in other media.”

This year also saw “Can Love Be a Photograph,” a museum retrospective of their work at the Kunstmuseum Den Haag in the Netherlands. Below, Van Lamsweerde and Matadin spoke with ELLE about the award, working together as spouses, and how digitalization is changing how we connect.

Inez van Lamsweerde: What was so unbelievable about that experience of choosing 200 works to reflect on our 40 years of working together was that now there’s a new baseline. Now this is from where we keep going, keep growing, keep having new ideas.

Vinoodh Matadin: At one point we said it’s not a retrospective, it’s a futurespective.

IVL: In most of the works in the exhibition it feels like there’s an element in this work that we could explore more, that asks for more new work to be made. It’s incredibly energizing and exciting to see that ideas from the mid-’90s can still be developed more.

VM: We realized when we did this exhibition that our work is almost timeless because it deals with the real and the unreal.

IVL: What’s so exciting every time is to step into someone’s world and hear about their influences, their inspiration, who they want to talk to, who they want to relate to, and what part of our work represents that for them. Then together, we form the ideas for a campaign. It always starts somewhere and then it ends somewhere completely different because as you go along together and work with the models or stylists, there’s new input all the time.

IVL: There is a series we made called “Thank You Thighmaster.” It’s large-scale photographs of a model shot nude in the studio that we then combined with faces of mannequin dolls from the ’70s. We took away all the orifices to show a hermetically closed person that still has all these feelings inside of her, but no way to communicate, because computers are the way we now are in contact with each other, and physicality is less and less important.

IVL: The title of the exhibition and the book that goes with it is “Can Love Be a Photograph?” To us, it’s not a question, it’s a statement. The exchange that we have with the person that’s sitting in front of our lens and then the viewer’s relationship to what they see on the photo is actually the most important thing. It’s this triangle of relationships, of emotion, of trust, of reflecting back on yourself that really drives everything for us. The bottom line of that is we love people. It’s just the most wonderful life to learn from everybody every day.

VM: The sad part of all this digitalization is that it was invented to connect us all. Now, we’re all disconnected while we’re all connected. No one can communicate with each other, and we don’t know what’s the real and what is the unreal anymore, and what is the truth. The only thing that we still have left is human contact and being in the now.

IVL: If you’re both rigid, it doesn’t work. You have to give and take one or the other way. I think a lot of people say to us like, “Oh my God, I could never work with my spouse.” We’re just constantly thinking, How could you not? For us, this is our way of living, and we’ve now also been together and worked together longer than we weren’t together.

VM: We still have the feeling we just started.

IVL: We still feel like young photographers.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6805. 11 Best Men's Dress Shirts 2026, According to GQ Editors

Even if your closet is ninety percent fleece, the best men's dress shirts are non-negotiables. At some point, you’ll face an occasion that requires one—a laid-back wedding, a high-stakes job interview, a weirdly formal middle-school piano recital. But the right dress shirt won’t just save you in a pinch or help you sneak past upper management at your new corporate gig. (Especially if said corporate gig is working at GQ.)

Because the superlative versions of the style aren’t simply dress shirts—or, at least, not exclusively dress shirts. Buy one equipped with the right fit, details, and fabrics, and even the most formal of the bunch can kick it in less stuffy environments without eliciting snickers. We’re on-the-record fans of throwing one on with a groovy tie and crisp trousers, but toss a dress shirt over a graphic tee and baggy shorts, and suddenly, your otherwise schlubby fit looks exponentially more considered—and exponentially more stylish.

For starters, polos aren’t dress shirts just because they have a collar. We know, we know—finding the line between casual shirts and formal shirts is hard. Then there’s fabric, little details like cuffs, plackets, and color. And on top of all that, “the perfect fit” is so subjective. Take a deetp breath. We’ve got you. We’ve done the dirty work, buttoned more buttons than we thought was possible, aggregated a heap of our favorites, and wore ‘em every which way possible to determine, once and for all, the absolute best dress shirts for men.

We’ve wholeheartedly recommended J.Crew’s Bowery dress shirts for a long time. But it was up until just recently that the revered preppy label quietly released a new button-up that we had to do some internal reckoning. The Slim Portuguese cotton Oxford dress shirt doesn’t enjoy the distinction of being named after a New York City street (e.g. the Ludlow suit, or the 770 jeans). But don’t let the straight-forward, flavorless nomenclature fool you. Let’s start with the obvious: the fabric. It’s an all-cotton Oxford cloth woven exclusively for J.Crew by the respected Portuguese mill, Solemos. It’s smooth and luxurious with an elegant drape. Plus, the thicker yarns of an Oxford cloth makes it versatile enough for less formal occasions when you want to wear it with a pair of jeans, untucked, even.

It gets better from there. The shirt is a tastefully trimmed down to a silhouette that’s not skin-tight nor 2010s #menswear slim, but svelte enough to look clean without a blazer. But the real star of the show is that 10-out-of-10 collar. Most of J.Crew’s shirts are designed with wimpier collars that are likely, for better or worse, a product of those aforementioned #menswear times. This newcomer, however, extends it enough to a more classic size that bridges the blazer-collar gap so it sits neatly below a jacket lapel. That larger collar means it’s more proportional when paired with a tie.

We’re not a part of J.Crew’s internal meetings, but if anyone there is reading this, we think this needs to be expanded into more fabrics, colorways, and silhouettes—perhaps, it should even be dubbed with a new name.

If it comes as any surprise that Uniqlo sells one of the best bang-for-your-buck dress shirts on the market, you’re likely new to GQ Recommends—and the Japanese retailer’s assortment of eminently affordable men’s clothing staples. Unlike its Calvin Klein counterpart, Uniqlo’s riff on the genre isn’t available with the added benefit of Prime shipping, but what you get instead is a dress shirt that’s worth exponentially more than what you pay for.

You might only go to Uniqlo for the basics—tees, underwear, socks, maybe a hoodie. So I'd understand if you thought dress shirts were too refined a category for Uniqlo to be any good. But every I time I encounter a dress shirt from the Japanese retailer, I'm reminded of just how surprisingly solid its fits and construction are. Unlike most of its price-conscious competition, Uniqlo’s dress shirt is made from 100% long-staple cotton with absolutely zero stretch involved. While you might think of a little elastane as a good thing, generally speaking, it tends to mean that corners were cut. Plus, if a dress shirt fits well, you won't need any stretch.

The fabric is treated for wrinkle resistance, which is great if you're the kind of guy who has a “clothes chair”. But there's a funny sort of sheen that comes with wrinkle-resistant shirts that can be off-putting. That said, the details redeem it completely: no sloppy stitching, exposed seams, or wimpy collars here. Perhaps most crucially, the slim fit isn’t so svelte that you’ll look like you got dressed in 2010.

Both our overall pick and budget pick are solid options no matter your budget or snobbery. But if you're ready to graduate or just feeling like skipping ahead to the finer things, Todd Snyder's line of in-house shirting is where we'd point you. A great dress shirt starts with great fabric and Mr. Snyder's collection is full of top-notch poplins, twills, and broadcloths sourced from Thomas Mason, a revered mill that's been around since 1796 and have been the go-to for grail shirtmakers like Turnbull & Asser, not to mention the Royal family.

In the hands of American menswear nobility, the fabrics are given that distinct yet trend-averse Todd Snyder flavor. It's cut with a tastefully slim silhouette that's not Slimane-skinny, but not what your dad thinks of as skinny, either. The back features comfy side pleats, which are sewn into a split yoke (a fairly uncommon, but appreciated detail for the menswear nerds). Fine stitching and single-needle construction throughout, the shirt is built with a ton of delectable details for stylishly discerning, but what we love most is the extended collar. It's a detail that feels refreshing but also recalls shirts from the 1930s, arguably a golden age for tailoring in the States.

This beauty will run you a bit over $200, which ain't nothing. But that's a resonable sum compared to the heritage shirtmakers whose reputations have been built on shirting alone. Often, their shirts can cost you as much as your car's mortgage. That said, Todd Snyder's will get you like, 90% of the way there for a third of the price.

Got a last-minute invite to a swanky event and need a dress shirt ASAP? Not to fear, Amazon is here (and there, and pretty much everywhere). Calvin Klein’s no-frills slim fit shirt is cut from high-quality cotton that’s just a tad more stretchy than our overall pick, and comes equipped with plenty of next-gen specs its counterparts eschew—including moisture-wicking properties to keep you cool and a non-iron coating to keep it looking crisp. (You’re short on time, right?) Mercifully, the added spandex offers a little give without making the shirt look too shiny.

Throw it over your finest chinos or the dress pants you impulsively splurged on or wear it with jeans on a relaxed Friday in the office. Even if you bought it at the eleventh hour, it won’t take long for it to supplant the pricier competition.

When you’re rolling with the movers and shakers of the world, you need a dress shirt that can keep up. And that’s exactly what the vaunted Parisian chemise-makers at Charvet specialize in, to the delight of royalty both literal (countless French kings) and cultural (Sofia Coppola is a well-known fan). This breezy cotton number is no exception: It’s cut on the looser side and features an extremely classy double cuff for when you're ready to break out the cufflinks you inherited from your old man. Even with the tres formale flourishes, though, we wouldn't shy away from rocking it in a more casual context. When you slip on this sucker, you don’t need to meet with the boss—you are the boss.

“Charvet does not fuck around,” Grossman says bluntly. There’s no shortage of reasons why it remains the first name in old-world dress shirts—and its centuries of pedigree barely cracks the top five. Sure, the brand has outfitted kings, presidents, and titans of industry in equal number, but its core value proposition comes down to one exceedingly simple principle: uncompromising quality. Every dress shirt is still made by hand in Charvet’s wood-paneled Parisian townhouse, which is worth the cost of a flight to visit, Grossman notes.

If you’re not quite ready to drop half a grand on a dress shirt your grandkids will fight over, he also recommends a more wallet-friendly hack: These days, Charvet’s shirts are all over the vintage market, and “you can reliably score one for a lot less than retail”.

Proper Cloth’s been an open secret to menswear heads for years thanks to its surprisingly granular made-to-order service which offers a wide range of custom options from fabric to design details to sizing. Beyond the near-bespoke service, Proper Cloth’s quality will turn the heads of the keen-eyed tailoring nerds. 80s two-ply pinpoint fabric made from American Supima cotton, split yoke construction, and a handsome semi spread collar all come together for one of the best dress shirts you can get for the price.

One of the most compelling arguments we’ve seen in favor of dressing up right now comes straight from Paris, where Husbands outfits its worldly clientele in exquisite dress shirts exactly like this, a masterclass in retro ‘70s swagger so good it clinched a spot in GQ’s inaugural All-Stars class. It looks rad unbuttoned to the navel, and even groovier with a hefty foulard tie.

One of the best things about a cutaway collar? It gives you more room for a declaratively large tie knot.

The J.Crew pick up top is incredible. But it's slim. This Ludlow dress shirt has all the same reliability, but is also cut to a fuller shape.

Given the brand’s stellar reputation in the tailoring place, it shouldn’t come as a shock that Sid Mashburn hawks a grip of bang-up dress shirts, too. This bengal stripe number is a tried-and-true riff on a traditional office-ready pattern, but the spread collar and Goldilocks cut imbue it with Mahsburn’s signature Southern charm—and yank it firmly into 2025.

While this nicely-priced shirt does also come in white, it's also a good reminder that dress shirts can still have some edge, too.

As with any garment, “good” is subjective—but as a general rule of thumb, it comes down to three crucial factors: fabric, construction, and fit. Men’s dress shirts are no different. Michael Hill, Creative Director of Drake’s says, “Versatility is important. Customers need to understand fabric and context. For instance, Oxford cotton is going to be more versatile than poplin, which is typically a bit more formal.” The fabric will help dictate the occasion (or the other way around?). There are so many at your disposal from herringbone to end-on-end to pinpoint, not to mention stripes to plaids. So if you’re not sure, ask the sales staff.

Hill also emphasizes that fit is essential to a good dress shirt and to pay attention to the details like “The way the collar sits on your neck and against the body of the shirt. Does it stay tucked in throughout the day? How do the cuffs sit against the wrist?”

He goes on to give this absolute, “Great dress shirts are never made from synthetic or stretch fabrics.” The majority of good dress shirts eschew synthetic materials in favor of natural long-staple cotton, woven tightly for extra durability. Cotton, of course, is not a prerequisite—but almost every single great dress shirt we’ve swaddled our torsos in has been made from some riff on the fabric, from poplin to pinpoint Oxford cloth.

Other reliable indicators of quality shirts? Telltale details like French or felled seams, which are sleeker and more durable; mother of pearl buttons; and a denser or finer stitch count, usually commensurate with the amount of craftsmanship involved. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth also notes to look out for less common details like reinforced shirt tail gussets, a split yoke, tight and straight stitching, and emphasizes the importance of buttons. “Are the buttons shanked so they won’t come loose? Are the buttons a durable enough material that can withstand your cleaners repeatedly?” These small details reveal whether a shirtmaker is paying close attention.

One unique difference between dress shirts and other garments comes down to the collar. Skerritt says the collar “often has the largest impact on how the shirt makes you look.” That’s because it frames your face and interacts with directly with your suit jacket and its lapels—no small job for a garment. While Skerritt advises to look for fusing (the way that the collar is attached or glued to its interlining) that’s crisp, and a collar that stands up well around the neck, ultimately it “should look natural and effortless. The end result should be [that] you like how it makes you feel in the way that you like to dress.”

As any menswear wonk will tell you, dress shirts boast no shortage of nuances. So in the name of brevity (and general wonk-avoidance), we compiled a handy-dandy glossary to the terms you’ll encounter most often. As a rule of thumb, the less adornment a dress shirt has, the more formal it is.

Like all of menswear, collars are susceptible to the whims of the trend cycle, swelling and shrinking with any given era’s silhouettes du jour. Collar sizes are prone to change, too (see: the massive collars of the power-suited ‘80s; the ultra-shrunken collars of the indie-sleaze 2010s). These are the three you should know.

Cuffs are the small pieces of additional fabric at the end of the shirt sleeve; they're often constructed with stiffer linings to give them structure and thoroughly cover your wrists. These are the two you should know.

Plackets are the strip of fabric that runs down the front of the shirt, designed to be fastened with buttons, snaps, or zippers. (When it comes to dress shirts, you’ll almost always encounter the former.) These are the three you should know.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6804. All the Stars at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards

From Hailey Bieber to Elle Fanning to Pamela Anderson

Every fall, the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) brings together designers, editors, and the biggest names in entertainment to celebrate another year of American fashion. At a dinner held at New York City’s storied Natural History Museum, underneath a 94-foot-long model of a blue whale, new faces and tenured creatives alike are honored for their contributions to the industry—with awards such as the Emerging Designer of the Year and the American Accessory Designer of the Year handed out throughout the evening.

This year, the event was hosted by Keke Palmer, with presenters including the likes of Demi Moore, Naomi Osaka, Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, and Cole Escola. Ralph Lauren took home the American Menswear Designer of the Year award (for the third time!), Rachel Scott of Diotima was awarded American Womenswear Designer of the Year (for the second time), and Ana Khouri was recognized with the aforementioned accessory designer accolade. Colleen Allen won the coveted Emerging Designer trophy, in a stacked lineup of nominees that included Lii’s Zane Li and Emily Dawn Long, among others.

In addition to the winners announced last night, several powerhouses were also spotlighted. Anthony Vaccarello, who recently announced his departure from Saint Laurent after a decade as creative director, was recognized as the International Designer of the Year, joined by YSL muses Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, Rosé, and Anja Rubik. Tory Burch received the Positive Change Award, Linda Fargo accepted the Founder’s Award in honor of Eleanor Lambert, and Gap Inc., under the direction of Zac Posen, took home the Innovation Award.

The Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award went to photographers Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin, Eva Chen accepted the Media Award in honor of Eugenia Sheppard, and the Isabel Toledo Board of Directors’ Tribute was awarded to Susan Cianciolo. Lastly, the Fashion Icon Award—previously presented to everyone from A$AP Rocky to Zendaya to Naomi Campbell—recognized architect Peter Marino.

Ahead, see all of the guests at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards.

#6803. Jennifer Lopez’s ‘Frosted Pearl’ Nails Are This Season’s Dreamiest Manicure Trend: How to Try Them Now

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Between fashion week appearances and making a return to music, Jennifer Lopez has become a major beauty muse for fall 2026. A few weeks ago, her cozy, “chai latte” nails—courtesy of her longtime manicurist Tom Bachik—served as our top inspiration for new-season manicures. Now? The duo has added “frosted pearl” to the list.

In an Instagram post yesterday, Lopez sported a sheer base with a soft, luminous sheen; the result felt like a fresh take on classic chrome. According to pro nail artist Jessica White, the new trend features a reflective “glaze”—which Hailey Bieber famously popularized—but in a subtler way. “Rather than an intense, mirror-like chrome, it catches the light gently, giving the nails a pearlescent finish.”

Lopez’s natural blush-toned base color is essential to the frosted pearl effect, says White. “A sheer milky white or soft nude creates a delicate pearl effect, whereas a pinker base gives a warmer finish.”

With the colder seasons in full swing, understated, minimalist nail trends are to be expected; those who typically refrain from bold colors and elaborate nail art will often turn to traditional nudes, creamy neutrals, and your-nails-but-better manicures.

But White considers frosted pearl to be the best modern alternative. “There’s something about the subtle shimmer that feels a little more elevated and luxurious for the coming months,” she notes.

“For minimalists who want to introduce something a little different, it still feels clean, understated, and incredibly wearable, just with an added touch of luminosity.”

For the pearl finish, White explains that “chrome powder is the professional technique, but you can find chrome-like nail polishes, which are perfect for at-home.” Opt for one with a pink base. Sealing everything with a quality top coat will extend the life of your manicure and enhance the glossy shine.

#6802. Brittany Howard and Anna-Maria Babcock’s Tennessee Wedding Was a Celebration of Their Mexican and Southern Roots

Given their day jobs, musician Brittany Howard and record executive and artist Anna-Maria Babcock’s meet-cute feels entirely appropriate: they first crossed paths at a concert. “We met at a friend’s album release show on October 10, 2023, at The Blue Room in Nashville,” Anna-Maria explains. Brittany, who is best known as the lead singer and guitarist of Alabama Shakes, was helping out at the merch table after the show. “I walked up to the table and a mutual friend introduced us by putting our hands in each other’s while asking, ‘Have y’all met yet?’ It was love at first sight for the both of us,” says Anna-Maria. A few days later, the two went on their first real date and fell in love over pizza rolls and mocktails at Brittany’s home. “The first date that never ended!” Anna-Maria jokes.

Just over a year later, Anna-Maria proposed on November 15, 2024, at Smith Lake in Alabama. After an extensive tour year, she encouraged Brittany to come with her on a fishing trip. “Little did I know, this was more than a fishing trip,” says Brittany. “On the first night of our stay, under the last full supermoon of the year, Anna-Maria got on one knee in a freshly made wood-fired hot tub. After the proposal, I said, ‘yes!’” Despite spending hours preparing the hot tub, the couple jumped out to share the news with their friends and family. “All those hours to prepare the hot tub, just to get out after five minutes! It’s okay though,” says Brittany. “We got all of our life together to make another fire.” Adds Anna-Maria, “Brittany followed up with a double proposal (the gay way) during our trip to Portugal for my birthday just a few months later! I also said yes to forever!”

Anna-Maria and Brittany spent the next two years planning their perfect wedding celebration. The big day arrived on October 24, 2026, at the Southall Farm & Inn in Franklin, Tennessee. The couple describes planning as both “so much fun” and “a lot of work.” “We had a hand in every single design aspect of the night; we wanted the space to feel like us,” says Anna-Maria. Alongside planner Carly Pickett, the brides lent their handwriting to save-the-dates, made an ofrenda to honor ancestors, and hand-selected planters from home to fill with florals. Says Anna-Maria, “We wanted our people to feel like they knew exactly whose wedding they were at—one that was very Black, very Mexican, and very queer!”

The couple also wanted to feel their cultures reflected through their fashion choices for the wedding weekend. “We wanted to feel gender affirmed, beautiful, sexy, and ourselves,” says Anna-Maria. “We were not interested in traditional wedding wear, so designing our own garments and sourcing from small women-owned, Black-owned, Indigenous-owned, and queer-owned brands was extremely important to us.” She adds that wearing family heirlooms was also an important part of their wardrobe curation. “We wanted our ancestors to be honored in this space,” says Anna-Maria.

For her wedding look, Brittany worked with stylist Courtney Mays to craft a custom gown with a detailed bodice and dramatic off-the-shoulder cape. Later in the evening, she changed into a bright red ensemble with diaphanous flowing fabric designed alongside Loulette Bride. Anna-Maria found a halter Danielle Frankel dress at Nashville bridal salon The Dress Theory. To walk down the aisle, she paired it with a veil from queer-owned brand Tanner Fletcher.

When Brittany changed into her red reception look, Anna-Maria changed into a textured, red dress of her own that was designed alongside Mays. The brides also created a mood board for their wedding party and even helped style some looks for them. “We wanted our wedding party to be more concerned with having fun, letting loose, and connecting with others—not with whether or not they liked the outfits we picked out for them that they will never wear again,” says Anna-Maria.

The weekend kicked off with an intimate sunset dinner overlooking the Tennessee hills. The rehearsal dinner was hosted by Anna-Maria’s parents, Sylvia and Randy Babcock. “We ate delicious Mexican food, danced to cumbia, and cried hysterically as our wedding party, parents, and grandmas expressed their love for us,” recalls Anna-Maria. “The feeling of watching your blood family and chosen family fall in love with each other was nothing short of magical and healing.”

The ceremony took place the next day in a meadow along a creek. Guests were surrounded by nature and gathered amongst florals that lined the aisle. “We walked to everyone’s smiling, expectant faces under a beautiful fall sunset while the mariachi band played a rendition of ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face,’” describes Brittany. The couple walked towards one another on the arms of their parents. “When we got to the altar, we then encouraged our two-year-old nephew, who was the ring bearer, to come meet us up there! Holding a wooden fish ring box—the one Anna-Maria gifted me when she proposed—in one hand and picking his nose with the other, he joyfully ran up to us while stopping to smell the flowers halfway down the aisle,” she recalls. “A perfect reminder of what’s important in life. Always stop to smell the flowers.”

Anna-Maria’s Tía Pinky read a poem written by the bride’s late grandfather, Roberto. “His words reminded us of why we are here and why it’s important to not waste time with the ones we love,” says Brittany. Remembers Anna-Maria, “I was so giddy and my cheeks hurt from smiling so much. I felt so excited and humbled watching our family grow right before my eyes. I felt proud of myself for never giving up on love. Little us would be so proud.” Brittany emphasizes that she felt “full of pride” throughout the ceremony and as if the moment was “magical and sacred.” This magic was made complete as a rainbow appeared in the sky once the brides kissed. “We think that was a little sign from the ancestors that we were all right where we were supposed to be,” says Anna-Maria.

The mariachi band led the way towards the reception, followed by the newlyweds and their community as “Isn’t She Lovely” played. “We danced and sang our way around the lake to cocktail hour where the sun finally went down over the hill in a blaze of pinks, reds, purples and oranges,” recalls Brittany. “The moon was so bright it would stop us in our tracks.” Cocktail hour followed with reunions, hugs, and tears of joy. “We drank and danced to cumbia before walking over to the ofrenda to pay our respects to our loved ones who couldn’t physically be there with us,” says Anna-Maria. “We could feel their spirit throughout the entire night.”

The reception moved indoors for a dinner full of Mexican and Southern cuisine, along with a night full of music. “Lloyd Buchanan, who plays with my touring bands, led an incredible band during reception where he played our first dance song, ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face’ by Roberta Flack in a hauntingly beautiful rendition,” says Brittany. “This song also happens to be Anna-Maria’s grandparents Maria and Roberto’s wedding song. Anna-Maria and I both took turns dancing to the end of the song with her 86-year-old grandmother.” She recalls, “There wasn’t a dry eye in the room.” The newlyweds then danced with their fathers and also did a special dance with their moms to “I Say A Little Prayer” by Aretha Franklin before welcoming all their guests onto the floor.

Special performances went on throughout the evening. “I come from a long line of family drummers, and my Uncle Scott and little brother Robert graced the stage, playing drums to Sinatra’s ‘Fly Me To The Moon’ and Bobby Caldwell’s ‘What You Won’t Do For Love’ respectively,” says Anna-Maria. “The very first time I saw live music, it was at an underground jazz club in DC where my uncle would play with his big band. When Uncle Scott was up there playing at the reception, I was instantly transported back to that club when I was a little girl.”

The after-party was held at Dottie’s, a speakeasy on the grounds of the property. The couple’s friend, DJ T1BG, spun until 2 a.m. “The room was vibrant with belly laughs, dirty dancing, wigs, bologna sandwiches, hot dogs, and deep conversations around the fire pit,” says Anna-Maria. “Our feet were aching—with Brittany nursing my blisters at 4 a.m.—but our hearts were exploding with love.” Adds Brittany, “We were so moved seeing our family and friends from thousands of miles away dancing together and making their own relationships. It’s the very thing we wanted our wedding to embody: communion.”

While the brides share they are truly excited to settle into their married lives with each other and enjoy the simplicity and joy of being newlyweds, they also emphasize how grateful they are to share their love today: “Getting married in the South as Black and brown lesbians feels extra heavy in today’s political climate. We live in a country where we have a Supreme Court justice who wants to ban interracial marriage. We live in a state where LGBTQIA+ rights are under attack, and the local government is working with ICE to tear families apart. We aren’t going anywhere. This is our home and we are here to stay. We are here to dig in deeper—into love and into our beautifully diverse and queer community. We believe love always wins, and it certainly felt like that at our wedding. While we were the first gay couple to get married at this venue in Franklin, Tennessee, we certainly won’t be the last!”

We started the most perfect weekend with our rehearsal dinner at golden hour overlooking the rolling hills of central Tennessee. Nothing beats Mexican food, our favorite people, cumbia music, and lots of happy tears. —Anna-Maria

We loved working with our wedding planner Carly Pickett on all paper goods! Carly also happens to be a close friend and an incredible visual artist, so working on these designs with her was so fun! We came up with our own custom gay quail lovers logo and custom icons to represent us as a couple. A lot of love went into these so that hopefully our guests could frame and display them in their homes to forever remember the special weekend we shared together. —Anna-Maria

My mom, dad, tías, and sister planned and decorated our beautiful rehearsal dinner. My mom has always been the party planner of the family—always making everyone feel so special and celebrated. The smells of the tortillas cooking, the floral arrangements made by my mom and sister Caroline, and the way the custom-made “Anna-Maria & Brittany” papel picado looked blowing in the breeze made us feel right at home. —Anna-Maria

The tablescape of our dreams! My mamá is so talented. —Anna-Maria

#6801. Duchess Meghan and Prince Harry Have Reportedly Moved Into a New Home

They have been living in the Cotswolds since late August, according to an insider source

A few months after Duchess Meghan and Prince Harry made their surprise move across the pond, it seems they’ve finally found a more permanent residence.

According to a new report from The Daily Mail, the pair have been living with their two children—Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5—in a friend’s house in the Cotswolds since they arrived to the United Kingdom in late August. The friend is allegedly a wealthy businessman who Harry became acquainted with through their mutual military charity work.

Originally, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were “living in the main house,” but now, they’ve “moved to a property on the estate,” per an insider source. Further details about the residence remain under wraps, though.

Meghan and Harry shocked the world when they revealed at the end of the summer that they would be returning to the U.K. for an extended period of time, six years after they stepped down from their senior positions as royals and moved their family to Montecito, California. (Currently, the pair are still holding on to their $14 million mansion in the starry West Coast neighborhood.)

The move precedes Harry’s 2027 Invictus Games, which are set to take place in Birmingham, England, and which may have partly inspired the move. Meanwhile, Meghan has already been busy at work too, teaming up with Malala Yousafzai for a project tied to International Day of the Girl, and joining Junior MasterChef Australia as a guest host.

In a recent interview with GQ, Harry opened up about why he and Meghan decided to move their family back to the U.K., saying: “Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn’t know how important it was to me.”

He added: “I think that having been [in the U.S.] for six years now and only being able to go back to the U.K. for short periods of time, to actually have my whole family there with me, the place that I grew up, wanting to be able to show my kids where I grew up and have them have the experiences to some extent that I had—the good rather than necessarily the bad—provided real, proper, serious thinking as to, ‘This is an opportunity, let’s do it now.’”

#6800. Nobody Wants to Have a Baby Boy Anymore

It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, and a new ritual was born.

Nearly 20 years later, we all know the drill. If it isn’t a cake, it’s a balloon or a cannon. Friends and family gather. Someone counts down; something explodes in blue or pink; the parents-to-be hug; a grandparent enters the frame looking thrilled and slightly confused. And, of course, there’s a camera rolling, meaning my daughter could have in theory earned her first “like” long before she drew her first breath.

For the first time in a century, nearly less than half of parents are circumcising their newborns. New dad Kevin Lincoln investigates how America’s favorite elective surgery became as debated as childhood vaccines—and considers his own decision.

The gender reveal has evolved from a modest party trick into a full-blown genre of internet spectacle, complete with its own newborn industrial complex. Private ultrasound companies now sell “gender-reveal experiences,” with rooms that glow pink or blue and teddy bears containing recordings of an unborn baby’s heartbeat. Online, the reveals have become more elaborate: smoke bombs, pyrotechnics (one of which started a wildfire in South California in 2020), choreographed dances, skydivers and, in one particularly memorable case, a Louisiana alligator called Sally biting through a blue jelly watermelon.

But the spectacle has moved on. A new kind of gender-reveal video is becoming a genre of its own, one in which a particular reaction is the main event. A recent compilation racked up 33 million views and three million likes on TikTok. Expecting couples do not scream with delight when the color appears. They scream in horror. They collapse and cry. The reason is nearly always the same: it’s blue. They’re having a boy.

What looks like internet absurdity may actually point to something much bigger. Last year, The Economist published data showing that in mostly higher-income countries, the centuries-old preference for sons is starting to reverse. And in some countries, the data shows that opinion has fully flipped: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Portugal and the Czech Republic are showing evidence of a preference for girls.

In the US, the same trend appears among adoptive parents. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, prospective parents were willing to pay an average $16,000 more for a girl than a boy. Among couples having IVF in the US—where, unlike the UK, sex selection is legal— leading clinics have reported that 75–80% of patients want a girl.

This is a big demographic plot twist. On one hand, it’s what progress looks like. For most of human history, boys have been the prize. They inherited the family name and property. They were expected to earn money and carry the family line into the future. Girls, in turn, were generally expected to marry out or care for relatives.

In the worst cases, the preference for sons has had lethal consequences. In China, where a one-child policy enforced by the government lasted 35 years, and in India, sex-selective abortion and the killing or abandonment of female babies has led to generations with far more boys than girls. Misogynist discrimination has been so pervasive that in 1990, the Nobel Prize–winning economist Amartya Sen estimated that more than 100 million women were “missing” from world history. (Researchers have since questioned the precise figure and methodology, but the point still stands.)

But there is another, stranger side to the reversal. You don’t have to spend long reading the 20,000-plus comments beneath a viral gender-reveal video to realize that some of this isn’t simply about girls finally being valued properly. There is a growing and increasingly open distaste for boys—a sense that they are inherently problematic, undesirable by default.

Having a son, in certain corners of modern parenthood, has become unfashionable. A curious society might ask itself why this is—and where it might lead.

Ruth Whippman is the mother of three boys. She grew up in England but now lives in America, in what she describes as a “progressive area of the country [with] very progressive school districts”. As she writes in her 2024 book, BoyMom, friends and neighbors kept saying versions of the same thing: “I hope for your sake this one is a girl.”

“We were a year into the [first] Trump presidency,” she tells me. “There were incels on the news. There was just this huge backlash against toxic masculinity. So it wasn’t even just a sense of, ‘Oh, boys, their clothes aren’t as nice; you don’t get to play Barbies.’ It was this sense that boys are actively toxic and harmful.”

My son and I were calling to each other across a great distance, a distance that I was aware might never close.

When Whippman’s first son was due, she had the standard worries about raising a child of the opposite sex. Would they have enough in common? Would she know how to navigate experiences she hadn’t had? As a lifelong feminist, she tells me, the additional sense of cultural disapproval made everything worse. “It was really horrible, because nobody likes to be pitied,” she says. “Nobody likes to think that their children are second best. But I think it played into something in me as well, if I’m totally honest. I had my own fears and feelings about [having boys], and hearing everybody else’s reaction just made it much worse.”

Nearly a decade on from #MeToo, with Donald Trump back in the White House and male chauvinism metastasizing across the internet, it’s unusual to hear the word “masculinity” without the word “toxic” prefacing it. So parents can end up feeling—even if they’re guilty about it—that having a son is more complicated than it was for previous generations.

“When you hear about boys at the moment, at best, they’re this underachieving lunk who won’t go to college, is doing badly at school and will fail to launch,” says Whippman. “And at worst, he’s deep in the manosphere, commanding his AI girlfriend to let him choke her, or whatever. It gets to this wider consumerisation of parenthood. [The idea that] girls are better consumer products, in a way—which is a terrible, terrible way to talk about human beings.”

I’d be lying if I said it hadn’t crossed my mind, when I discovered I was having a daughter, that if I could raise her to be a confident, secure, kick-ass girl, I’d win the approval of the types of circle I move in. “Girl dads” who let daughters paint their nails are the subject of endless kind TikTok videos.

Parents of boys, not so much. Whippman, who has heard more and more fathers say they would prefer daughters, recognizes the problem. “Parenting a son is almost seen as a harm reduction project, rather than anything empowering,” she says. “That’s really at odds with our modern parenting culture, which is about encouraging [our kids] to reach for the stars and be happy and access all the world has to offer.”

And like everything else in 2026, the random, happy event of your unborn child’s sex can somehow thrust you into the us-versus-them culture war. “In the States and in the UK, there’s a sense that if you are on the progressive left, you are on the side of girls and women… any time you’re defending boys and men, it has this sniff of something right-wing, or being a bad actor,” says Whippman. “That’s a really hard thing to hold as a progressive, feminist parent of a son.”

There are other theories for why parents in Western countries, in particular, are increasingly downbeat about having boys. Millennials are having fewer children than any generation in history, and we’re doing it later in life. In other words, by the time it happens, we’re already exhausted. And boys are often perceived as more work, especially when they’re little: more physical, and harder to keep occupied and under control.

Lara Miller has been a midwife for more than 20 years. She uses social media to demystify pregnancy and childbirth. She thinks there is some truth to the idea that older parents may be wary of boys. “When you see older people having babies, they tend to be more controlling about everything to do with it,” she says. “I say this without judgment—I was an older mum myself—but you become used to doing things your own way and to your own routines.”

Of course, it would be silly to assume every girl will be content quietly coloring in while every boy spends his childhood trailing dog shit through the house. But according to Alex Trippier, a kids’ club leader who runs the social media account Be A Happier Parent, there can be real differences in behavior. “You get testosterone surges around age two, which I really see with the kids that I look after in my groups,” he says. “All of a sudden the boys come in and they’re going crazy. Parents who are on the quieter side can be overwhelmed by the sheer energy. Some people insist this is all nonsense, and [boys being more boisterous] is completely socialized. I think it’s a mixture of both. You’ve got that developmental layer going on, and you’ve got all the socialization on top of it.”

Trippier, who has two boys and a girl, thinks culture has shifted. Parents have always worried about teenage girls. But now, they have a whole new list of concerns for boys: porn, gaming addiction, exam results, algorithms. “There are all these fears we have for our sons, this kind of moral anxiety about the impossibility of raising good men,” he says.

In 2024, Zach Baron documented his long journey to fatherhood via IVF in GQ. Now, he reports on the mind-altering chaos (and occasional brilliance) of life with two walking, talking young boys.

Miller, who had similar feelings when she was pregnant but is now the happy mother of two sons, thinks there’s another factor: Schools aren’t always very good at accommodating boys. “We have changed as a society and we’re not as accepting of boys,” she says. “Boys don’t tend to fit the school model. You get worse reports. [Our school] gives the boys set days to be allowed to kick a football. Well, you don’t remember that at school, do you?”

She recalls being summoned by a headmaster after her son made a gun sign with his fingers. “The girls do better at school,” she says. “They’ve read 20 books; my boys have only read two. The teacher’s gone, ‘Well, if you buy a football magazine, do you think they’d read that?’ You’re like, ‘Oh, fuck off. Just fuck off.’”

There’s something else unusual about today’s parents, beyond grappling with the manosphere and Parkrun injuries. We’re the most psychologically literate generation to have ever lived. If we haven’t done therapy ourselves, we’re at least sufficiently fluent in the language of therapy to take a stab at self-reflection (or, as Boomer parents might call it, self-absorption). We know about childhood trauma. We know about attachment styles. We know that our parents’ behavior has consequences. We know that our childhoods don’t simply disappear when we become adults. It gives us an enormous number of things to worry about.

One of the most interesting conversations I’ve had on this subject is with a colleague who is expecting a son. He’s delighted now, but initially, the prospect of having a boy unnerved him—as it did me, before I knew the sex of my baby. We both agreed this probably came from remembering difficult experiences with our own fathers, and being afraid of repeating them. For me, it may have gone a step further. The idea of having a son scared me because I had a pretty broken relationship with myself.

Dr. Chrissy Jayarajah is a psychiatrist and the author of the world’s only academic paper on “gender disappointment.” She’s quick to point out that the term is not a clinical diagnosis, but what you might call a “known phenomenon” (particularly on TikTok, where thousands of videos are tagged with it).

“Something I always say is that becoming a parent will undoubtedly make you reflect on the way that you were parented,” she says. “Whether it was a good relationship, a bad relationship, an indifferent relationship or a non-existent relationship—they all play a part. An absent father is still very present in your mind. We are more psychologically minded and reflective compared with, maybe, the generation before. But I also think we don’t know what to do with that reflection.”

This can manifest in different ways, explains Jayarajah. “Working predominantly with mothers, I would say they fall into two camps,” she says. “They either want to emulate exactly how their mother was, from recreating those childhood memories, making those family favorite meals on a Sunday, and so on. Or they’re: ‘Oh my God, I’m turning into my mother.’”

That can produce powerful feelings about your baby’s sex. “We see that with women who have experienced abuse of some kind,” says Jayarajah. “Some absolutely do not want to have a girl, because they don’t want their daughter to experience what they went through. On the other hand, I have had women who say, ‘No, I definitely want a girl. I don’t want to have a son,’ because a son [would remind] them of the perpetrator.”

The sex of your baby, in other words, can become a vessel for all sorts of fears that existed long before the baby did. Then, there’s the demographic problem. There just aren’t enough babies. A rapid collapse in birth rates and fertility is playing out across the world. In 1990, global fertility was about 3.3 children per woman. Today it is around 2.2 to 2.3. More than half the countries in the world are already below “replacement level.”

The consequences will be huge. Labor shortages. Pressure on pensions. Rising social and healthcare costs. Less of the innovation and forward momentum traditionally associated with younger populations. In that context, favoring one sex over the other seems beyond counterproductive.

Maybe we are retreating into old, narrow assumptions. “We’ve never thought about gender more as a society than we do at this present day,” says Jayarajah. “Ideas about gender are in our face all day long. There was no such thing as a gender reveal party 20 years ago, let alone putting it online. What’s happening, in my opinion, is gender essentialism. This sexist idea of what it means to be a man, what it means to be a woman, is playing out in what we expect for our children.”

The following week, I saw this in action. I took my 19-month-old daughter to a soft-play morning, where she likes to roll around on the multicolored shapes and go down the slide on my lap. A few minutes after we arrived, I heard a scream. “Aaaargh!”

At one end of the ball pit, a little boy was staring at his own reflection in a mirror. “Aaaargh!” he went again, hammering his fists against the perspex and making the entire frame shake. A few feet away, my daughter watched him quietly. I made a mental note to keep them as far apart as possible.

The boy’s parents were nearby, deep in conversation. They seemed oblivious, or perhaps simply immune, to their son’s King Kong routine. A dozen judgmental thoughts zipped through my head. Why aren’t you keeping a closer eye on him? What kind of irresponsible shit are you pulling at home for him to do this? If he harms her, I swear to God…

I took a sip of my coffee, scrolled through my phone, then turned around, ready to rescue my sweet, innocent little girl. The boy who had been screaming a moment ago was now shyly handing her a dumper truck with a missing wheel. She closed her eyes, grinned, and took it with both hands.

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “For Centuries, Everyone Wanted Boys. Now, Not So Much”

#6798. Hailey! Demi! Keke! An Exclusive Behind-the-Scenes Look at the 2026 CFDA Awards

The biggest and brightest names in American fashion all came together last night for the 45th annual CFDA Awards, which are often referred to as the Oscars of Fashion. Taking place at New York’s Natural History Museum, the night celebrates both the unique contributions of American designers throughout the previous year and honors those who have made an indelible mark on the industry throughout their illustrious careers.

“Continue to share important stories and do work that means so much to you,” said CFDA chairman Thom Browne at the ceremony. “Work that you couldn’t imagine doing anything else, because the true marker of success is being able to do something you love always at the highest level. And never sacrifice the true creativity and quality of what you do.”

Awards were presented to Ralph Lauren, Rachel Scott of Diotima, the jewelry designer Ana Khouri, and Colleen Allen. Fashion world luminaries were also honored, including Tory Burch, Linda Fargo, Peter Marino, Susan Cianciolo, and Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin.

The night welcomed a retinue of A-listers to help celebrate, proving that fashion now touches every part of culture, from entertainment to tech to sports. Bold-faced names included the night’s host, Keke Palmer; presenters Zoe Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, Rosé, Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, Naomi Osaka, Demi Moore, and Cole Escola; and celebrity attendees Gracie Abrams, Megan Thee Stallion, Travis Scott, PinkPantheress, and many more.

“Anthony is not only an extraordinary designer, but also an extraordinary human being,” said Zoe Kravitz while presenting Anthony Vaccarello with his honor for International Designer of the Year. “He has this rare ability to make you feel completely understood, and that is reflected in everything he creates.”

“Anthony doesn't just design clothes,” added Rosé. “He creates an attitude, a sense of freedom and confidence that is distinctly his own.”

Donatella Versace, who attended with Vaccarello, had this to say about the honor. “I love what Anthony has built at Saint Laurent over the last decade and cannot wait to see what he does next. New chapters are always inspiring.”

From the red carpet to the seated dinner to the ceremony and even behind-the-scenes, there were buzzy, celeb-filled such as this. To capture all the glitz and glamour, we sent photographer Hunter Abrams to bring you an exclusive look at all the action. Take a look below.

#6797. Pamela Anderson, 59, Pairs a Classic Red Manicure With a “Bombshell Bob”

The actress makes a case for minimal makeup and statement curls on the red carpet

In 2023, Pamela Anderson famously vowed to wear less makeup on red carpets. Since then, the actress has attended countless events makeup-free—but she has never left her hair behind. In fact, Anderson, known for her iconic long blond hair, makes her hairstyle the centerpiece, as she did last night at the 2026 Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) Fashion Awards.

Anderson walked the CFDA Fashion Awards red carpet in her typical minimalist makeup look, but with “bombshell curls” inspired by old Hollywood. In a black halter dress with feather detailing, accessorized with a just-bitten berry lip, Anderson wore a coiffed bob with old Hollywood pin curls. Because the curls fell away from her face, they showcased her glowing, fresh skin.

Anderson’s retro hair wasn’t the only statement look last night. She wore fall’s boldest nail trend—a bright, cherry-red almond manicure—contrasting with her satin black-and-white polka-dot clutch. With no shortage of buzzy new nail trends swirling around the internet, like “chili pepper nails” and “vanilla nails,” Anderson proves that sometimes the best shade for your manicure is classic red.

Lately, Anderson has given a master class in the many ways to style bobs. Just a few weeks ago, while at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles, Anderson wore a head full of curls with subtle bangs and lots of volume.

In an interview with Anderson last year, she shared her hair philosophy—why she never sticks to one style. “I think people associate me with big blond hair, but if I look at my whole life, I’ve always been one to change up the way that I look,” Anderson told Bazaar. “Your hair is another way to express yourself, and I’ve never been shy.”

She continued: “I guess I’m genetically blessed, but I’ve always had very thick, healthy hair. I do like to cut it and to style it differently. It’s freeing. I am a big lover of change; that’s what keeps us young and excited.”

#6793. Inside Sophie Bille Brahe’s Danish Seaside Home, Where Every Object Tells a Story

It’s almost dusk in Copenhagen when jewelry designer Sophie Bille Brahe tells me over the phone that she’s about to take a quick dip in the ocean before dinner. It’s a small ritual tied to the reason she chose her five-bedroom, three-bathroom seaside home, 20 minutes north of the city center, in the first place. Designed by Danish architect Ib Lunding in 1929, the house sits on one of three small streets of similar homes in what Danes call the “flower neighborhood,” each one a slight variation on the next. For Bille Brahe, it’s this setting—and the sensory elements that come with it—that were non-negotiable. “I open up my window and I can see trees. I can smell the sea,” she says. “For me, that’s very important to have in my life every day.”

The space is a respite for the designer, who views the home as a collection of memories and a backdrop for her bustling family life, kids, and border collie included. It’s also where her namesake fine jewelry line begins. In fact, Bille Brahe often develops her designs within the home’s walls before she ever takes them to the workshop. “I sometimes catch these sensations, these small ideas, and make them a little bit more stable by doing drawings of them here at home. And then, when I have an idea of what I want to do, I’m ready to go to the workshop and start,” she explains. In those beginning stages, she works alone. “I need to be able to make really ugly things or really great things,” she says. “I need a bubble around me.”

That bubble is her workspace, an all-white room anchored by an 1870s Swedish fireplace Bille Brahe had installed when she moved in. “It has gold detailing, and it’s so beautiful,” she says. “A fireplace has a way of gathering family and speaks to a house built with love.” Nearby sits her desk, which belonged to her father’s best friend. “It’s basically where everything I make starts,” she says. “I’d loved it since I was a kid.”

Pulled up to the desk is a chair that visitors to her New York showroom may recognize: a curved stainless-steel design by Mats Theselius reupholstered in Sahco zebra fabric. The same seating appears in the showroom, a throughline between her personal and professional worlds. Marc Chagall’s Soleil Couchant, a Le Klint lamp, a neon work by Gun Gordillo, and a collection of seashells share the desk with her sketches and notes. The room opens onto the dining room, centered on a Børge Mogensen Øresund table surrounded by Gio Ponti chairs and a bouquet of sunflowers resting on it.

Of course, Bille Brahe furnished her boutiques with intention. In Copenhagen, she sought out one-of-a-kind Danish furniture and even began making her own vases in Murano. In New York, she tracked down a rare Poul Kjærholm table, square with a gray leather top instead of the round marble version many Danes grew up eating breakfast at. At home, she followed a similar rule and took her time, layering pieces slowly and making sure each one felt collected and had a story connected. “It took me many years to find a sofa, because every time I bought one I’d almost have a panic attack about the idea of buying something new, something everybody could have,” she says. “Everything I have in my home I’ve inherited, borrowed, or a friend made for me. If something doesn’t have a story, it doesn’t belong.”

Her jewel-toned Svenskt Tenn sofa is piled with pillows, each one a gift from a Swedish friend who came to visit. Beside it sits a slim side table, part drink trolley, stacked with books, a seashell, and a lamp she inherited from her grandfather. Most of the lighting in the house is inherited, except the Noguchi lanterns, which she brings back one at a time from trips to Japan. Another Japan find, the Nextmaruni Armless Chair by the architect duo SANAA (known as the Rabbit Chair for its ear-like back), sits beneath a pink painting by Danish artist Tal R.

Above all, though, it is a family house at its core. “It never feels like it’s an empty house,” she says. “I absolutely love my life with kids.” That’s particularly evident in the kitchen, where the day begins with coffee, breakfast for the kids, and, when the weather allows, the garden door thrown open. “It’s not a big house, so the kitchen needs to be efficient,” she says. “I cook a lot, so it ends up being a kitchen that can manage a lot of food without a lot of space.” Despite its small footprint, the room is warm, with kids’ art hung above the seating, embroidered tablecloths dressing the table, and an airy pendant overhead.

The same energy carries into the hallway, with its rounded window (a signature of the neighborhood’s houses) and walls in a blush pink by Farrow & Ball, the same color as the hallway in her previous home. When she moved, she changed everything else but kept the pink. “I normally don’t like colors on walls,” she says. “But I felt this was bringing something I used to love into the new house.”

Outside on the terrace, that pull toward nature continues. Every plant on the deck is one she’s had for 15 years or more, from a pomegranate tree she’s carried from home to home to the pink nerines called the “autumn flower,” and she has a story for each of them. According to Bille Brahe, there’s no need for more than this. If the trees are close enough to smell and the sea near enough to hear, she’s set and then some. “I’m not a person who needs a lot. I just need something close and clear, and if I have that, I can do what I need to do.”

#6791. What Exactly Was Barry Keoghan’s Skin-Lifting Treatment?

Even during his busy filming schedule for the upcoming quartet of Beatles biopics, Barry Keoghan manages to find time for self-care. Just last week, an Instagram video by skincare practitioner Nilam Holmes showed him undergoing his second XERF treatment at her UK-based clinic Dermaspa. The non-invasive treatment uses radio frequency to support collagen production and improve skin firmness without risking any fat loss on the face. According to its website, results last around 12 to 18 months, with pricing around $6,000 for two sessions (or about $3,300 for one).

“Barry is filming a big project at the moment with a very intense schedule, so he hasn’t been able to get in much and he can’t have any downtime,” Holmes tells GQ, referring to the recovery period more invasive procedures require. “That’s why I chose XERF for him. It gives a firmer rested look to his face without interrupting his work.”

According to Holmes, XERF is popular because people say it offers a “non-surgical facelift,” but she says the results are not that dramatic. The best candidates for XERF are people who want “subtle, natural-looking results” and have “mild laxity,” which is skin that’s only slightly loose or saggy.

She tells us that Keoghan has been a client of hers for “a while now” and that she’ll tailor his treatments based on what his skin needs. For example, if he’s feeling tired from filming, she might do some RF skin tightening—another form of radio frequency for addressing sagging skin—or lymphatic drainage. If his face is “being troubled from makeup” she’ll do a mild laser with a deep-cleaning HydraFacial. She says Keoghan manages to come in every four to six weeks for appointments during which she’ll offer Skinpen Microneedling—a treatment that reduces the appearance of fine lines, acne scars, and uneven skin texture.

“Once a year we’ll do a more intensive skin-tightening treatment such as Ultraformer III HIFU"— a non-invasive ultrasound device for skin tightening—“or Morpheus8”—a tool that combines microneedling with radio frequency—“which do involve some downtime,” she adds.

Keoghan has been pretty tight-lipped about those Beatles biopics he’s starring in. But in recent years, the 34-year-old Oscar-nominated actor has been open about other aspects of his life like growing up in foster care—which resonated with him while he was making the movie Lemonade—and being bullied online for his appearance. In an interview with SiriusXM in March this year, Keoghan talked about the “abuse” he receives online about his looks and how it makes him “not want to go outside.”

In Holmes’ Instagram post, Keoghan voices over: “I feel better about myself; I look better.” From Holmes’ perspective, the actor’s trips to her clinic are simply about taking caring of his skin.

“Looking after your skin isn’t about changing who you are—it’s part of looking after yourself, in the same way people look after their health, fitness and well-being,” Holmes says. “When it comes from that place, it’s a really positive thing.”

She says a lot of her clients want to enhance their features. In the past, she says it used to be mostly younger women. Nowadays, she’s seeing “more inquiries from young men with the rise of ‘looksmaxxing.’”
