#6788. The Best Exercises for Lymphatic Drainage, Courtesy of a Detox Expert

We are a world obsessed with the lymphatic system right now and the best exercise for lymphatic drainage. Google searches for lymphatic drainage have gone up by 60% across America year over year, while on TikTok there are more than 79 million views of the term and growing.

Lymphatic drainage massage (and other techniques like dry body brushing) can help reduce water retention, puffiness, and inflammation by flushing out toxins and excess liquids. Celebrities love it, but is it accessible to the rest of us?

The easy answer—happily!—is yes. And celebrity lymphatic specialist Rebecca Faria (known as @DetoxbyRebecca on Instagram) is leading the charge. Based in Beverly Hills, Faria specializes in Brazilian lymphatic drainage (a rhythmic massage that combines pressure and long strokes) and has a roster of A-list clients who swear by her techniques (including Jennifer Aniston, Hailey Bieber, Ariana Grande, and Anne Hathaway). While a treatment with one of Faria’s team starts at $350, she has shared some of her favorite (easy) exercises that are designed to stimulate your lymphatic system at home. And they’re free.

Done while either lying down, seated, or standing, knee hugs aren’t just good to get the lymphatic system going but help release back tension. Hug one knee into your chest and hold for 20 seconds, then do the other side.

Lie on your back and place the soles of your feet together, letting your knees fall out in a butterfly formation. This stretch is also a fantastic way to stretch your hips as well as release your pelvic floor.

While lying down, hold your legs straight up, then lift one as you lower the other. These are called flutter kicks–do 20 of them. (Incidentally, these are also great for your core, a muscle group that has long-term benefits to help with bloating.)

These aren’t just for your Pilates class. Remain lying down. With one leg on the floor, lift the other leg and move in a circular motion 20 times. Repeat on the other leg.

No bike needed. With your legs in a tabletop position, straighten one leg, then the other, 20 times.

Another Pilates movement to try out. Lying on your left-hand side and keeping the legs relatively straight, circle your right leg 20 times. Do the same on the other leg.

Stand with your feet flat on the floor, then raise up onto your toes, lifting your heels off the ground. Do this 20 times. This is also a favorite movement of Jesse Inchauspé (a.k.a. the Glucose Goddess) to help with balancing blood sugar.

#6787. Peptides Are About to Flood the Market. And Bro Science Is Coming for Us All

This past February, Health and Human Services secretary and MAHA Final Boss Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made it known during an interview with Joe Rogan that he intended to direct the FDA to lessen restrictions on a handful of peptides that had previously been banned under the Biden administration. The peptides in question, which included influencer favorites BPC-157 and TB-500 (collectively dubbed the “Wolverine stack” for their reported regenerative properties) had been placed on the FDA’s “do not compound” list, effectively barring pharmacies from providing them to patients, for reasons including serious safety concerns and a general lack of comprehensive human trials. No new research had emerged to prompt RFK Jr.’s announcement. Rather, the HHS head, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, believed the drugs should never have been banned in the first place—a decision that, in his view, was responsible for the subsequent explosion of a thriving black market for peptides online. So, for the past eight months, healthcare professionals have been waiting with baited breath for the other shoe to drop.

And then this past Wednesday hit with a thud.

In a seemingly unilateral decision—one that flies in the face of FDA scientists who warned earlier this year of the potential, largely unknown implications of effectively releasing scantily researched injectables into the wild—RFK announced that patients (or anyone with a prescription) would now have access to six of these previously outlawed peptides through a loophole-like policy called “enforcement discretion.”

Internet-famous peptides like BPC-157 and TB-500 might be the future, but right now they’re a shot in the dark.

To explain exactly what that means, I called up Edgar J. Asebey, a life sciences regulatory and transactional attorney at the law firm Frier Levitt. “I always tell people I speak three languages: English, Spanish, and FDA,” he says. “Enforcement discretion means that the FDA will not enforce a certain regulation. And in this case, it's the prohibition against compounding these six peptides. That's what it boils down to.”

Enforcement discretion is typically considered a break-in-case-of-emergency avenue for freeing up availability of certain drugs when warranted, Asebey says. “For example, when the GLP-1s were in shortage, pharmacies could lawfully compound exact copies of Ozempic and Wegovy.” In other words, the six peptides in question—BPC-157, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, KPV, and Epitalon—are still categorically unapproved by the FDA for human use, but Kennedy is going to allow pharmacies to dispense them as if they were, until further notice.

While this may seem outrageous, not everybody is outraged. For one, obviously, peptides are big business. (Market research firm Grand View Research valued the global peptide industry at over 140 billion in 2025, with North America accounting for more than 60% of that revenue.) Aside from that, however, one of Kennedy’s stated motivations is to reduce people’s incentive to procure peptides from regulation-skirting med spas and the dark corners of the internet, where substances like BPC-157 can be ordered to your door with the same ease as buying paper towels on Amazon. Since July, the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies (ASOP Global) has tracked nearly 21,000 peptide listings across more than 300 websites, including upwards of 8,800 listings for BPC-157 alone. As you might imagine, quality and safety present serious concerns to anyone choosing to go that route—that is, beyond the potential risks of using these peptides even in their purest forms—hence the burgeoning cottage industry of peptide purity trackers and testing services.

“My view is simple,” says Meena Verma, MD, MPH, a board-certified internist and nephrologist, and founder of Blue Coast Longevity in Newport Beach, CA. “People are already using these peptides, and there is an urgent need for harm reduction. Allowing licensed pharmacies to compound them under physician guidance means patients can now have an accountable channel with assurance of safety.”

But how this policy change plays out may not be quite that simple. Whereas purveyors of these six peptides—whether operating online or in person—were previously identifiable as unlawful simply by virtue of offering the unapproved drugs, Kennedy's mandate to usher these peptides into the broader health marketplace muddies the waters, making it harder for consumers to tell which providers are legit. "The online market is already flush with illegal actors who now can more easily hide amongst the masses with limited risk of getting caught,” reads a statement that ASOP Global released within hours of Kennedy’s announcement on Wednesday. “Without enhanced and consistent new enforcement of the market, today’s policy will allow criminals to hide amongst the newly compliant.”

Kennedy’s plan notes that compounding pharmacies will be subject to specific safety criteria, like requiring that the peptides are manufactured in an FDA-registered facility, but as The New York Times has pointed out, “the step basically only requires a manufacturer to notify the agency of its address.”

When you consider the scale of the peptide market alongside the reality of what the FDA is actually capable of policing with its post-DOGE workforce—following the laying off of 3,500 workers—it begs the question of whether the criteria laid out in Kennedy’s plan will even matter at all.

"For one, if you're going to have guardrails, you're going to need to enforce them,” says Leigh Verbois, PhD, ASOP's global board chair and the former director of the FDA’s Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response. “There needs to be resources to actually take action, full stop. And two, the organizations that are intended to utilize those guardrails may not even look at them. There are too many [compounding pharmacies] to be able to enforce against."

But I’d argue there’s something far more dangerous, and more consequential, than the possibility that this latest decision might inadvertently feed the back-alley peptide market rather than curtail it. After all, not everyone is out there looking for peptides. (I know I’m certainly not.) But we all need to go to the doctor at some point—something that could now conceivably land you on the receiving end of a prescription for a drug that has never even been researched in a human being.

“To classify this as safe would just be irresponsible,” says Motisola Lewis, MD, an Internal Medicine physician and the founder of Lewis Medical NY. “If you have a cancer patient—say, a woman who just had breast cancer—and she wants to fix her knee that just got injured, and she ends up getting an injection of BPC-157. This is known to promote tissue growth. This is known to promote vascularization. We don't know what effect it has on a patient who has had cancer. Does it promote cancer growth? We don't know.”

Peptides are blurring the line between supplements and prescription drugs.

The inescapable irony here is that not long ago it was the MAHA movement that was encouraging people to be skeptical of mainstream medical providers, to do your own research before just allowing your doctor to jab you with a COVID-19 vaccine. And now, by injecting these six potentially harmful peptides into mainstream medicine, where they will be readily available to physicians with varying degrees of familiarity with the substances themselves and the politics surrounding them, the administration has gone ahead and given the rest of us a very real reason to do our own research. Sure, this only applies to peptides at the moment, but a precedent has been set. And you can no longer afford not to pay attention. None of us can.

“When patients walk into their physician's office, or talk to a telehealth provider, they have an assumption that there will be a positive outcome—that the patient is seeking and that the physician is intending to meet,” says Dr. Verbois. “But without any of the quality, safety, or efficacy, it's completely the wild, wild west. If anyone in my family, in need of a drug for treatment, were to ask me if they should go down a path of utilizing a peptide of this sort, my response to them would be, ‘Never. Instead, seek out a treatment for that disease that's been shown to be safe and effective. These have not been, and you are putting yourself in harm's way.’”

#6784. Inside Francesca Allen’s New Publication, Hair

Last year, Francesca Allen brought Plaukai (Lithuanian for “hair”) to PhotoVogue Festival’s Women by Women, taking us into the world of a traditional long-hair competition in Lithuania. Now, she returns to the subject, continuing her exploration of the many ways women define themselves through hair.

For her new publication, Hair, Allen travelled to Las Vegas, where women from around the world gathered to compete for the inaugural title of Miss Rapunzel. She followed the contestants beyond the competition itself, from hotel rooms to casino floors and, finally, the stage where their hair is measured. Her photographs capture the curious rituals and unexpected intimacies of a pageant devoted entirely to hair.

Designed by Adam Ridgeway, Hair features a text by Claire Marie Healy and will be released as a limited edition in Paris on 12 November, during Paris Photo.

Francesca Allen’s practice spans photography and film, often centering on intimate depictions of girlhood and the complexities of coming of age. Her work has appeared in publications including AnOther, Dazed, i-D, M Le Monde, Vogue and ZEITmagazin, and has been exhibited at institutions such as the Grand Palais in Paris, BOZAR in Brussels, Somerset House and The Photographers’ Gallery in London. She is also the author of I’d Like to Get to Know You (2022) and Aya (2018). She lives and works in London.

#6783. Demi Moore Wears a Gown Made of Jeans to the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards

Zac Posen transformed classic denim waistbands into sculptural eveningwear.

There’s no denim without Demi. At tonight’s 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City, Demi Moore stepped out in a tongue-in-cheek GapStudio look that redefined the meaning of denim-on-denim.

Designed by Zac Posen, Moore’s custom gown centered on a series of indigo denim waistbands stitched one atop another to form a corseted shape. The bodice featured a halter neckline with folded-over ends, while the low-waisted maxi skirt had a long slit and a slight train.

Moore completed the look with suede pumps, diamond drop earrings, and, of course, a fully denim handbag created by the brand’s executive director of accessories, Reed Krakoff.

Later in the evening, the actress presented the Innovation Award to Richard Dickson and Zac Posen on behalf of Gap Inc. Dickson and Posen, naturally, both wore denim too.

While sculptural and evening-ready, Moore’s gown put a distinctly American spin on the evening’s “American Black Tie” theme. Plus, denim is woven into the fabric of American style—and Gap’s DNA, too.

“Denim is at the heart of Gap’s identity, and I wanted to explore its function in an entirely new way for my dear friend Demi,” Posen said in a statement. “By deconstructing the familiar details of a classic jean and reimagining them through the lens of elevated eveningwear, we created something sculptural, unexpected, and distinctly GapStudio.”

#6782. Reckoning With Borat, 20 Years Later

Last month, I sat in a packed-to-the-gills movie theater to experience the latest release from a controversial comedian whose work regularly blurs the line between docu-reality and narrative fiction. I am, of course, referring to Ali G: Who Iz I?—the cinematic return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s once-and-still-somewhat-beloved durag-doffing titular character.

Before the film was unceremoniously dumped on Prime Video last week, I managed to snag a ticket to the only New York City screening that wasn’t totally sold-out, booking a seat—last row, tucked in an alcove of the theater—with the intention of isolated note-taking and (gasp!) the occasional phone-glance should the movie prove tedious. The recliners next to me were eventually claimed by a gentleman decked in a very Ali G-esque skull cap and wraparounds, who unleashed a deafening “BOOYAKASHA!” after Nicole Kidman’s AMC intro.

Cohen’s brand of confrontational cringe comedy continues to attract a level of interest, thanks in part to a certain mustached-and-mankini’d Kazakh journalist. The cultural explosion that was Borat! Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (has any movie title so padded the word count?) turns 20 years old this week, and it remains a curious artifact of the 2000s: impossibly dated and slightly better than you might remember, even as its creator’s talent has slowly and unmistakably eroded.

If you were just old enough to purchase a ticket to an R-rated movie in 2006, Borat felt like a truly out-of-nowhere phenomenon in terms of mass impact. But the character, armed with little more than a shabby suit and an aggressive cheer, emerged from Cohen’s cult favorite Da Ali G Show, which ran for one season on BBC’s Channel 4 in 2000 before making the leap to HBO in 2003. Alongside Ali G and the gay Austrian fashion correspondent Brüno, Borat Sagdiyev was just one of the many personalities Cohen regularly deployed in the thorny thickets of gotcha-mentary, trading in culturally oblivious and antisemitic observations supposedly inherited from his Kazakh homeland, often to the shock and dismay of his unsuspecting subjects.

These fool-me-once hijinks weren’t necessarily groundbreaking, even for HBO’s then-provocative late-night programming. Several years prior, The Chris Rock Show engaged in similar man-on-the-street shenanigans (once, he polled residents of NYC’s notoriously hate-crime-prone Howard Beach region about renaming a street after Tupac Shakur). But segments in which Ali G addressed Buzz Aldrin as Buzz Lightyear, or the one where Borat led a bar full of Arizonans in a rousing chorus of “Throw the Jew Down the Well,” were practically reverse-engineered for virality in the internet’s pre-social-media infancy, and the appeal of Cohen’s approach—how far will he go, and will ordinary folk follow him?—was easy to understand, regardless of the visceral discomfort it may have generated.

Straying from the sketch-based format of Da Ali G Show, Borat embraced a loose narrative structure, with its titular inquirer setting out for America to make a documentary on the country’s social peccadilloes with the intent of eventually romancing Pamela Anderson. If you want to get highfalutin about it, the plot itself situates Borat within the legacy of films about Europeans attempting to understand America—a small-but-fascinating subgenre that includes Paul Verhoeven’s fairytale-cum-nightmare Showgirls, the post-hippie pessimism of Michaelangelo Antonioni’s Zabriskie Point, and Kristoffer Borgli’s social-mores rom-dramedy The Drama.

Don’t get it twisted, though: Borat was and still is best enjoyed as a showcase of physical comedy and inflammatory non sequiturs. It’s no less funny in 2026 to watch a grown man wash his face in a toilet bowl, or gesture toward a tortoise while sincerely asking, “What type of dog is this?” The scene in which an etiquette coach attempts to guide Borat through the intricacies of comic timing is itself an excellent study in comic timing; the notorious full-frontal hotel chase sequence between Borat and his producer Azamat (portrayed by steadily-working character actor Ken Davitian) is a marvel for its sheer escalation alone. This stuff killed in a massive Northern New Jersey movie theater when I was 19, and it still kills from the confines of my couch 20 years on.

Unlike much of Cohen’s subsequent work, Borat is not an explicitly political film. Nonetheless, a good deal of its “GREAT SUCCESS!”—$262 million in box receipts off an $18 million budget, with a Best Actor Golden Globe for Cohen himself—is undoubtedly owed to a different sort of comic timing. The film came out in the throes of George W. Bush’s second presidential term, with the US mired in two wars abroad and a hell of its own making. Americans were thirsty for easy targets to shoulder the blame and, if possible, provide some cheap laughs in the process.

Their thirst was quenched in the form of Borat’s many unsuspecting subjects. Some of this was low-hanging fruit: Borat telling a group of feminists to smile more, or acting like a literal bull in a china shop amidst Confederate memorabilia. But the film’s more sensational material depicted rough corners of the American psyche long hidden in plain sight. Most memorably, Borat encounters a group of rowdy frat boys who huff about white pride and express dismay at the abolishment of slavery before engaging in a viewing of Anderson’s infamous leaked sex tape with ex-husband Tommy Lee.

Not everyone was displeased at their portrayal, though. Joe and Miriam Behar, the Jewish couple who offered Borat and Azamat room and board, were good-natured in a 2006 interview with the Boston Globe. For her part, Miriam shrugged off Borat’s naked antisemitism. “To me it's an anti-Muslim movie, not anti-Jewish, because Kazakhstan is mostly Muslim,” she offered.

Behar’s observation underlines the casual bigotry that otherwise stains Borat. The film’s portrayal of Kazakh culture is undoubtedly offensive, and provoked mixed reactions from the country’s government for years to come. For what it’s worth, Cohen pushes back—intentionally or not—on anti-Muslim sentiments during the film’s rodeo sequence, in which Borat tells a particularly racist attendee that he is indeed “not Muslim.”

But given the post-9/11 climate into which Borat was launched, the implications of a foreign correspondent from a majority-Muslim country espousing antisemitic and misogynistic viewpoints are crystal-clear, and Cohen himself seems too smart to sincerely profess a lack of awareness as to how this might be received. It doesn’t help that his subsequent projects resulted in exponential escalations of offense: 2012’s more narratively-focused The Dictator spared no quarter when it came to stereotypes of Arab culture, while the astoundingly homophobic Brüno, from 2009, was loaded with gags about anal sex and resulted in an out-of-court settlement with a Palestinian grocer who was falsely credited as a former terrorist in the film itself.

After 2016’s box-office bomb Grimsby, which is most notable for the allegations of on-set sexual harassment co-star Rebel Wilson later brought toward Cohen, his work went in a more explicitly political direction. There was his 2018 docu-satire series Who Is America?—two episodes of which featured writing and directing contributions from Nathan Fielder—and 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a second-verse-same-as-the-first sequel which earned several Oscar nominations and brought a truly bizarre “October surprise” to that year’s presidential election involving actress Maria Bakalova, Rudy Giuliani, and the former New York City Mayor’s pants zipper.

Both of those films were more explicitly message-y than they were riotously funny. Cohen’s latest, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is neither, carrying the all-too-familiar stink of a comedian insisting that their capacity to offend amounts to protected speech. At 55, Cohen is clearly not as willing to submit himself to the ragdoll physics he once deployed; in its place is an often-sullen-looking Ali G, his dreads now gray, weighing the merits of cultural appropriation and sparring with a DEI coordinator about the origins of the durag. The entire affair is belabored and depressing.

It made me think of the Who Is America? character Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, a send-up of Rachel Dolezal-flavored liberals in the form of a Berkeley professor who dons dashikis and keffiyehs. Early in the film, he rages against Ali G’s culturally appropriative ways to a majority-Black community meeting in Oakland. “We don’t care!,” shouts one participant. In hindsight, it’s as much an expression of exhaustion with the dictates of capital-D discourse as it is a referendum on Cohen’s confrontational method, which now yields far less interesting insights about the national psyche than it did when Borat arrived on American soil in 2006.

#6781. “Who Knew Zorro Was So Important?”—Catherine Zeta-Jones Looks Back at Her Life In Movies in Bazaar’s “Building Character” Series

The Welsh actress reveals the secrets of some of her biggest roles, from Cabaret to Wednesday.

Since the 1990s, Catherine Zeta-Jones has played a bevvy of strong women on screen who hold their own space—weapons and all—against powerful men. For Harper’s Bazaar’s latest installment of the video series Building Character, the Welsh actress looks back at her storied career, beginning with her first-ever television role as Mariette in The Darling Buds of May, a British comedy drama that ran on the ITV Network in England from 1991 to 1993.

It was another small project she embarked upon after moving to America, a Titanic TV series (no, really) that aired on CBS, that would go on to change her life. Apparently Steven Spielberg caught one of those early episodes “on a Sunday night, as if he had nothing else to do in his life,” as she explains it, and was so taken with the young actress he made sure that Martin Campbell, who directed 1998’s The Mask of Zorro, would cast her in his film. Within one week, she was taking riding and fencing lessons in preparation of the movie, which she starred in opposite Antonio Banderas. As if that wasn’t enough, “My husband [Michael Douglas] saw me in it and fell in love with me so...” she laughs. “Who knew Zorro was so important?”

In the full video above, she talks about starring in Zorro and Chicago, finally feeling cool during the filming of Ocean’s Eleven, and how her mother reacted after she was cast in Entrapment.

#6780. Discover the Best Dresses for Every November Occasion

All products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something.

No matter the occasion or season, there are always plenty of opportunities to wear a dress and, of course, an overwhelming number of options from which to pick. We’ve put together an edit of the best dresses of the month; check back every two weeks for a new selection of styles, handpicked by Vogue.

November is here, calling for wardrobe reshuffles and a fresh look at the fall trends defining the season. Based on this month’s standout finds, the key elements are texture, color, and fabric. Art Deco influence appeared throughout the runway—there’s no better time than now to embrace the trend with drop-waist styles that fit the bill, as seen at Kallmeyer and Fforme. Cummerbunds, usually known for tuxedo dressing, have now found a feminine place, notably at Róhe. It’s also the season for autumnal textures in wool, velvet, jacquard, and knits—try a jacquard number from Tory Burch for an evening occasion, or pick up a sweater dress from Laura Manoogian to wear throughout the winter. And for all fall weddings and holiday festivities on the horizon, there are simply too many good options—from Maria McManus to Khaite—that will make you the best-dressed guest.

Whether you’re shopping for new essentials, vacation, or a destination wedding, these are November’s best dresses.

Cooler temperatures are no reason to retire color. Consider this your invitation to embrace it. Fforme’s elegant take on the evening dress features a dropped waist, mock neckline, and sleeveless silhouette—all in a rich berry hue.

What’s a fall wardrobe without a knit dress? This under-$300 find from Banana Republic makes for a go-to in any wardrobe. Style it with knee-high boots for effortless cold-weather dressing.

Tory Burch sent this printed dress—in a trompe l’oeil pattern resembling tiger stripes—down the runway in two iterations: a delicate pastel jacquard and a rich purple version. With a fitted bodice that cascades into a handkerchief hemline, it’s a romantic silhouette that needs little extra to feel styled. A close-cut jacket and patent pumps should do the trick.

A knit dress is always a good idea. Simkhai’s ribbed iteration, accented with a delicate white trim, makes a subtle yet striking statement. Add a knee-high boot, a sweeping opera coat, and a chic clutch.

A dress that’ll get you multiple double-takes. This red maxi with a built-in cummerbund reimagines traditional black tie dress codes for a feminine-meets-masculine twist.

ICYMI: Jacquard is having a moment. This black V-neck dress, accented with a cummerbund sash, brings a polished edge to evening dressing. Even better? It’s under $300.

Conner Ives can do no wrong. Spaghetti straps, delicate pleats, and a vibrant color story—the dress is composed of four different printed vintage scarves—make this a vacation must-have, whether you’re spending Thanksgiving in Nayarita or St. Barths.

The shift is a forever classic and Posse’s silk-satin take is minimalist in the best way. Bring that less is more ethos to accessorizing with a simple pouch and drop earrings.

Emily Dawn Long—a CFDA 2026 runner-up—has a knack for intuiting what we want to wear before we do. This bright color-blocked midi is just one recent example.

Consider this sleeveless, funnel-neck knit dress a blank canvas for styling. Layer it over or under a long-sleeve knit (for extra warmth), throw on a sweeping shearling coat, then finish with flat boots. The possibilities are endless for cold-weather dressing.

You know the LBD, you (we hope) love the LBD. Play with proportions to give it a fresh look: a long duster coat, statement brooch, and polished loafers toughen up its feminine spirit.

Why yes, it’s Kallmeyer’s fall collection opening look: a creamy drop-waist style made from a silk charmeuse with caped armholes and a high funnel-neck. Follow the fall show’s styling notes and pair it with patent leather knee-highs–a pulled-back bun and minimal jewelry give the dress its well-deserved moment.

Maria McManus first introduced this dress in an off-white shade; this rich eggplant hue makes for a wonderful autumnal option.

Khaite’s chiffon maxi strikes the perfect balance between delicate and wearable. Give it heft by styling with a leather coat, tights, and strappy sandals.

Weddings or galas on the horizon? This strapless satin gown—as seen on supermodel Karlie Kloss, who wore it earlier this year for Taylor Swift’s wedding—works for either occasion.

Minimal, elegant, and endlessly versatile, this long-sleeve satin number is the kind of wardrobe staple that moves easily from desk job to after-hours plans. Dress it up with pumps or keep things understated with a flat—it looks sophisticated however your style it.

Kallmeyer’s Ivette dress is easily one of the season’s most talked-about dresses. With Art Deco influences leading the trend conversation, its embellished design feels especially on-trend.

Feathers, feathers, and more feathers! Whether you’re dressing for a special occasion or are a bride-to-be, this Loulou de Saison dress is designed to make an entrance. The drop-waist silhouette, adorned with feather embellishments around the hips, delivers just the right amount of drama. More is more!

Print enthusiasts, look no further than this floral maxidress from Banana Republic. Rendered in a rich persimmon print, the silhouette skims the body before flaring into a sweeping skirt. A romantic take on fall florals.

J.Crew’s cult-favorite rollneck sweater has officially entered its dress era. Just in time for sweater weather, its simple silhouette makes a strong case for becoming your new go-to. Style it with hosiery and loafers, then tie a colorful knit around your for an extra layer.

ICYMI: Purple is the color to own this season, and this violet maxi from Zara features an alluring open-back silhouette. Not quite ready to bare it all? Layer a lightweight top underneath, either in a neutral hue or a contrasting pop of color.

Caftans can be worn year-round—you just have to pick one in a more fall-friendly fabric. Taller Marmo’s long-sleeve is cut from double satin, with adjustable buttons that allows you to wear it in more ways than one—off-the-shoulder, single-shoulder, or or with a boat neckline.

Velvet chartreuse has never looked better, courtesy of Reformation x Alexa Chung, whose recent collaboration delivered one of the finest evening dresses of the month. Pair it with a satin bag and kitten heels.

This Staud dress creates the illusion of separates: A fitted black silhouette contrasts with a white draped skirt. A study that proves that opposites really do attract.

Meryll Rogge’s debut collection for Marni has officially dropped. The color-block mini is cut from one of the collection’s most memorable prints: a playful floral print that captures the house’s signature eccentricity. Pair with loafers and a long necklace.

For a quiet statement, consider this tea-length dress from Merlette, crafted from a rich butter yellow satin with ruched sleeves. On chillier days, add a faux-fur coat on top.

Altuzarra’s flutter-sleeve dress balances romance and structure, with delicate draping that creates soft movement. Save this for a special occasion.

Straight from the runway, this sleeveless knit turtleneck is a master class in sculptural dressing, crafted from a stretch rib that contours the body and falls to a handkerchief hem.

Who needs a necklace when the dress is the jewelry? Brandon Maxwell turns a V-neck dress into a work of art, with a beaded neckline that moves like fringe. An elegant, embellished option for an evening affair.

No dress roundup is complete without a little black dress. This off-the-shoulder option from Fforme is cut from a thick scuba fabric for a sculpted look. Complete the idea with strappy sandals and an embellished evening bag.

This Tory Burch runway dress was an editor favorite. Cut from jacquard in a slate blue and cherry-check motif, the color combination creates an optical illusion of a rich purple hue (one of this season’s trending hues). Two versatile details make it especially wearable: Both the necktie and belt are removable. Complete the look with fall boots.

To celebrate Vogue’s book club selection Sense and Sensibility, Vogue collaborated on a limited-edition nightgown inspired by Jane Austen's heroines. A nightgown that isn't exclusive to home can be styled with a trench and equestrian-inspired boots for an effortlessly romantic look.

Simon Miller's take on the slip dress is both elegant and flattering. This dress works season after season; it's the kind of piece that always makes an entrance, whether paired with boots or sleek mules.

CJR is known for its bold use of color, and this dress is no exception. Inspired by the work of Ettore Sottsass, the graphic polo maxi makes for a statement for any occasion. Dress it up with pumps or style it with flat boots for the weekend.

For upcoming weddings or formal events, look to this artful Tove dress. Playful yet sophisticated, the halter-neck silhouette is elevated by sculptural detailing. Finish off with strappy sandals for a polished finish.

For a minidress to wear this fall, opt for Khaite's Scarla dress. The modern skater silhouette, cut from delicate silk chiffon, feels romantic yet contemporary, making it an especially chic option for a bride-to-be.

Call it the ultimate party dress. The holiday season may still be a little off, but it’s never too early to plan your party wardrobe. This embellished Posse mini will make you the best-dressed guest.

Zara has collaborated with filmmaker Luca Guadagnino and production designer Stefano Baisi on a collection spanning from ready-to-wear to homeware. This scarf-draped dress strikes the perfect balance of elegance and ease.

Minimal yet statement-making, this Magda Butrym gray dress has an off-the-shoulder neckline and a fitted silhouette. A tonal floral appliqué adds a feminine, sculptural finish. Pair it with kitten heels and a clutch for an elegant evening look.

When your wardrobe is craving a dose of color, look to yellow. This H&M Studio dress is cut from a lightweight fabric with romantic ruffle detailing, making it an effortless choice for a warm-weather holiday or a destination wedding.

For a fall dress, look to this minidress inspired by the ’60s. Cut from a wool blend, this double-breasted dress is an ideal layering piece. Style it with a colorful turtleneck or button-down and add tights and boots for a milder fall day, or pair it with loafers.

Alaïa's approach to construction is like no other, creating some of the most flattering silhouettes around. Cut from velvet, this tank dress makes for an understated yet impactful evening option—a minimalist statement.

Maygel Coronel’s dress proves that simplicity can still make an impact. The elongated drop waist, fluid draping, and bubble hem give the silhouette a fresh modern feel.

A fall wardrobe essential, this long-sleeve satin dress is a versatile piece that works from nine to nine. Polished enough for the office and elegant enough for an evening, it transitions seamlessly from day to night.

A black dress is a timeless choice, and this Altuzarra option interprets the style for modern wardrobes with draping and an asymmetric knotted waist. A chic choice for fall weddings: Just add a kitten heel and a clutch.

A little lace, or in this case a lot, goes a long way. This runway favorite from Khaite strikes the perfect balance between romantic and edgy. Ground it with sleek black shoes.

Violet! Purple! Amethyst! However you choose to call them, deep shades of purple are having a serious moment. Style with something red—a clutch or heels, or even a bold lip—for contrast.

Toteme makes the kind of dresses you’ll want to wear on repeat—and this draped maxi is one of them. New in for the season (we’ve written about it in cream, red, and butter yellow), this rich olive hue feels just right for fall.

Casual meets sophisticated in this fresh-off-the-runway Prada mini, featuring a drawstring waist and cultural motifs at the hem. Wear it over pants for an unexpected look.

Cut from a thick satin, Róhe’s sculptural one-shoulder dress contours the body just so, and needs little in the way of styling to feel complete; simply finish with a tassel clutch and kitten heels. Also available as a top, it’s equally chic styled as a full ensemble for an important event.

Color is all everyone can talk about this season—and chartreuse is one of the It hues. This Taller Marmo dress with an integrated cape makes for a striking wedding guest option.

A knit dress streamlines getting ready on a cold, rainy day, and this colorful knit intarsia style by Celine–as seen in the Vogue Shopping print guide to fall–is one worth investing in. Wear it with loafers on a crisp fall day, then switch to knee-high boots for the winter.

The kind of dress Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy might have worn. This simple boatneck style from Zara is minimal yet endlessly versatile.

Tory Burch knows her way around a shirtdress, and this style–straight off the fall runway–comes with a removable necktie, allowing you to switch up the look depending on the occasion.

From weddings to galas, look to this Fforme drop waist dress in blue sapphire hue. Pair with strappy sandals and a sleek pouch bag.

&Other Stories’s pleated mock neck dress is an effortless style that can easily be transformed for any occasion. Pair it with blazers and loafers for the office or dress it up with pumps for evening events.

For a lace dress that’s feminine but not overly sweet, look no further than Maria McManus’s black satin midi. Style it with a button-down or cardigan knotted at the waist, then add an unexpected pop of color with either your shoes or your bag.

A rich blue hue and draped silhouette give this dress a modern take on the 1920s drop-waist silhouette. Dress it up with heels for evening or ground it with loafers for an uptown-meets-downtown approach.

The nightie was a summer favorite, and for fall, Dôen gives it a polished update in a maxi silhouette with silk and lace trimmings. The result is a romantic yet refined style that works just as well at the office as it does for cocktails.

The LBD for minimalists comes courtesy of Toteme, who’ve crafted a short sleeve style from a bonded scuba crepe with darted seams for a subtly sculptural silhouette. Pair with tights and patent heels.

Khaite’s new fall collection has arrived, and this layered maxi, crafted from a sheer silk organza, is a standout. An elegant bustle detail at the back adds unexpected drama.

You’re not imaging it: Purple is one of the season’s standout shades and Toteme’s scarf dress is one of our favorite renditions. Finish with contrasting red or lemon hues for a jaunty color story.

Florals aren’t just reserved for spring. Ulla Johnson’s long-sleeve turtleneck dress makes the print feel autumnal. Pair with boots for this transitional period.

Kallmeyer’s Nala dress has Vogue bride written all over it. Keep the finishing touches pared-back with drop earrings and sleek white shoes.

Straight from Proenza Schouler’s fall runway is this artfully printed dress that’s great for any number of September occasions on your calendar. Pair it with kitten heels and a leather jacket for dinner out with friends, or with boots on cooler days.

Alaïa knows how to celebrate the female form, and this maxi from Pieter Mulier’s final collection for the house does just that. Crafted from ultra-soft merino, it’s also available in a zesty chartreuse, and classic black.

Not your typical minimalist ’90s slip. This olive-green version gets a romantic update with intricate lace trimming.

Whether you’re heading somewhere warm this month or simply leaning into fall’s version of artful bohemian dressing, a caftan always delivers. Easy and elegant, all you need is a long pendant and some chunky bangles to style it out.

COS reimagines the gather dress with a twisted detail at the front for asymmetric like draping. A no-brainer 9-5 option that needs minimal styling.

#6778. A Look Inside the 2026 Dia Art Foundation Fall Gala

Attendees included Sofia Coppola, Marion Cotillard, and Matthieu Blazy

Last night marked a busy evening in the world of fashion. In New York City, the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards were hosted at the American Museum of Natural History, while in Los Angeles, a party was held to celebrate a new book documenting photographer Richard Avedon’s work in Harper’s Bazaar. But that wasn’t all—even more members of the fashion and art worlds united for the Dia Art Foundation’s annual fall gala in NYC.

The event acted as a celebration of two creatives—artist Roni Horn and British film director Steve McQueen—as well as a fundraiser for the arts. Guests gathered at the Dia Chelsea museum before migrating to a cocktail party and dinner where the honorees were toasted.

Some of the starry names in attendance included director Sofia Coppola and Oscar-winning actor Marion Cotillard. This is the first year that the gala has been sponsored by Chanel, after the French fashion house announced its partnership with the non-profit organization back in May. So, this naturally meant that Chanel’s current creative director, Matthieu Blazy, was also present (and he has been teaming up with the organization for years, even since he was at the helm of Bottega Veneta). In 2027, Chanel will sponsor the Dia Beacon gallery’s annual Spring Benefit luncheon, too.

Remarks were shared by the chairman of the Dia Foundation’s board of trustees, Nathalie de Gunzburg; the Dia director, Jessica Morgan; as well as by Matthew Barney, who paid tribute to Horn. Proceeds from the evening will go towards the foundation’s restoration projects, while also contributing to art-related lectures, commissions, educational programs, and more.

Ahead, see all the stars who attended the Dia Art Foundation’s 2026 fall gala.

#6777. The Fall Denim Trend Giving Barrel Jeans a New Shape

These are the most flattering, effortless styles to shop now.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Cocooning proportions were rife on the fall/winter 2026 runways. From billowing dresses at Stella McCartney and Jil Sander to long, rounded sweater vests at Chanel and expressive, cloud-shaped trousers at Chloé, the message was clear: eye-catching silhouettes are in.

When it comes to denim, the cocoon silhouette thrives. Not quite as dramatic as barrel-leg styles and occasionally featuring gentle pleating, the subtle banana-inspired shape is made to flatter the female form. Sitting snugly on the hips and gently blossoming out, they taper only slightly at the bottoms, allowing plenty of space for the wearer to move freely.

Horseshoe-shaped jeans first gained popularity on Alaïa’s spring/summer 2025 runway for their ability to add interest to an otherwise minimalist look—and the cocoon silhouette moves the trend on, offering a subtle tweak to the runway-inspired style.

In terms of styling, they are ideal for autumn days. Throw them on with a V-neck cashmere knit and a pair of pumps, and what would have been a simple ensemble is transformed by the directional curvature of the denim. For evening, watch them do all the heavy lifting, turning a cami top and kitten heels into a dinner-ready outfit.

It comes as no surprise that Japanese high-street stalwart Muji, known for its refined homeware and wardrobe solutions, has created a perfect pair of cocoon jeans. The lightweight denim features a slightly curved leg shape and the kapok-blend fabric feels soft to wear, while keeping the structure of classic denim.

As for a slightly more substantial take, Topshop’s pair features a front pleat detail that helps to create a sculpted, dimensional shape through the leg. The oversized proportions and gently tapered ankle create an effortlessly cool look, while the mid-rise waist and oversized, sculptural leg give them an edge that will swiftly upgrade your outfits.

If you’re ready to level up your denim drawer, you really can’t go wrong with either pair. Shop them below.

#6776. Jude Bellingham Stripped to His Skivvies for Calvin Klein’s Latest Campaign

Last week, Calvin Klein dropped a hint of their next underwear campaign star via Instagram. The clip featured a guy gliding his fingers from his boxers up to his chest. Very suggestive. Very sexy. Instagram, obviously, went wild. A teaser of a teaser, you might say.

Now, the New York label has revealed all. The model in question? Jude Bellingham.

Shot by Oliver Hadlee Pearch on a hot Madrid day, the campaign features Bellingham posing against a clean white background—all the better to keep the focus squarely on the England international. In the exclusive photo above (don’t say we don’t spoil you), Bellingham is sporting CK’s Icon Cotton Stretch Boxer Slim.

Bellingham wears the rest of the Icon Cotton Stretch collection (and nothing else) throughout the campaign, which includes the new Stretch Shine Trunk with a shiny Infinity Bond logo waistband, the Boxer Brief, Low Rise Trunk and Hip Brief. In one shot, he’s pictured doing his goal celebration, which means the image may pop into your head the next time he scores on the pitch.

Maybe it’s obvious from the campaign, but the 23-year-old took to the role of model very naturally. He attributes his ease in front of the camera to the underwear.

“I really enjoyed working on this campaign,” Bellingham says via email. “I liked the idea of ‘the icon underneath’—that confidence starts with feeling comfortable in yourself. Calvin Klein is such an iconic brand, so it was great to bring that idea to life in my own way.”

Over the years, CK has linked up with its fair share of footballers. In 2023, the label shot Liverpool captain Virgil Van Dijk. That same year, Tottenham’s Son Heung-Min stripped to his skivvies as well. And at the end of 2025, it was Bellingham’s Real Madrid and England teammate Trent Alexander-Arnold’s turn. Maybe Bellingham went to him for advice—not that it looks like he needed it. Clearly, the guy knows how to nail the shot.

This story originally appeared on British GQ.

#6775. Maura Higgins Seemingly Responds to Harsh Fan Feedback After Her “Toughest” Week on ‘DWTS’

“Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay. I’m only human,” she wrote, in part.

Maura Higgins is opening up after tackling her Disney Night choreography as Tinker Bell on Dancing With the Stars. The Love Island alum got candid in a lengthy statement she penned alongside a carousel of behind-the-scenes photos from Monday night’s episode after fans criticized her performance in Team Slaytopia’s group number.

“This week was definitely one of the toughest I’ve had so far. I was really unwell, running on very little energy and trying to learn two dances, but I gave it absolutely everything I had,” she started her message, adding that she had no previous dance experience before joining DWTS.“I wanted to challenge myself, step outside my comfort zone and give something completely new my absolute best & that’s exactly what I’m trying to do every single week. I’m learning, I’m making mistakes, I’m pushing myself and I’m growing along the way!! Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay,” she continued, adding, “I’m only human.”She insisted she wasn’t sharing the message for “sympathy or to make excuses, but simply to share a little of the reality behind the scenes.”

The Traitors star uplifted her pro partner and “biggest support throughout this journey,” Mark Ballas, before seemingly addressing harsh feedback from viewers who criticized her “low energy” performances in both of her numbers this week.

“Genuinely what is up with maura tonight…she was the clear weak link of that team dance,” one person wrote, while another added, “i'm going to be very honest with you i genuinely think maura did by far the worst of any celebrity tonight and the judges were just distracted by how good of a show mark is able to put on that they didn't notice lol.”

Per her message, Maura seems to be focusing on those who continue to uplift and support her throughout the competition.

“To everyone who continues to support me, encourage me and cheer me on, please know how much it means,” she wrote toward the end of her statement. “You genuinely give me the strength to keep going, especially on the harder days. Your kindness never goes unnoticed.”

She then closed her post by expressing how “grateful” she is to still be in the running for the iconic Mirrorball trophy.

Based on that alone, I tink she’ll be just fine either way!

#6774. I Went on a Cowboy Road Trip Through the American West—and Finally Learned to Disconnect

It’s dusk in Montana, and I am sitting on a porch, huckleberry lemonade in hand, watching the sun set behind the Big Sky mountains. To my left, a string of horses are grazing peacefully in a meadow; to my right, a coterie of children are throwing footballs and making s’mores on a campfire as the distant twang of bluegrass ripples through the air. It is unquestionably idyllic. I, a born-and-bred Londoner, am momentarily situated within a pastoral fantasy of the American West: the sort of scene that I didn’t believe existed outside of Ralph Lauren billboards. It turns out it does: at Lone Mountain Ranch.

Lone Mountain is the first stop on my weeks-long quest to immerse myself in the cowboy lifestyle: a role (or at least an aesthetic) that has, in recent years, infiltrated seemingly every demographic. As much as there is the libertarian agitprop of Taylor Sheridan’s Yellowstone cinematic universe, there are the coastal cowgirls who populate Ethel Cain and Chappell Roan shows; the enduring Cowboy Carter fandom; the obsession with Bella Hadid’s (ex-)boyfriend. No matter your inclinations, in 2026, the back-to-basics, willfully offline lifestyle of the American cowboy appears to maintain its long-standing allure—and, as fashion takes August off, I’m committed to spending the month figuring out why.

So, I fly from London to Bozeman—to an airport which more closely resembles a giant log cabin than a transport terminal—and find myself swept towards what I have determined is a soft entry into the rough-and-ready lifestyle. Lone Mountain, just over an hour’s drive away, is a dude ranch that comprises a series of beautifully bedecked, individual cabins scattered across its vast property. (While it is not my first time in a cabin on a ranch, it is certainly the first time that it’s incorporated a freestanding bathtub with three types of locally-sourced salts, Frette bathrobes, and a Dyson hairdryer.)

The ranch, first established in 1915, was initially conceived as a one-stop-shop for the complete cowboy experience—and, a century on, has only enhanced its original mission, offering everything from trail rides through its astonishingly beautiful 148 acres to a weekly, on-site rodeo; archery lessons in its forests to fly-fishing in its creeks. Turn up ill-equipped, and they have a cozy outpost stocked with essentials from Lucchese boots and Schaefer jackets to Stetson hats to complete your transformation.

Then, there is the Horn and Cantle restaurant, where we eat bison short rib and elk meatballs the size of baseballs (“cowboy portions”) beneath a mountain lion resting on the rafters. Or, for those seeking something that speaks to the affluent rancher demographic that now populates Big Sky, the on-site, leather-lined members’ club, The Auric Room (where Taylor and Travis are known to hang out), where we are served caviar and fancy Big Macs by the most charming hosts imaginable, alongside people pairing Birkins with their cowboy boots.

But home comforts aside (and there are infinite examples of glorious Western hospitality on offer here: flasks of coffee and cream arrive silently on our porch before we wake up, and chocolate cowboy hats have appeared on our pillows when we return home), perhaps the best bit about Lone Mountain is its proximity to Yellowstone, the national park through which it offers guided tours. We really lucked out when we were assigned Randy: a Montana native and former wildfire fighter who, at the beginning of our day together, beamingly tells us “everybody wants to be a cowboy now… but Yellowstone is the last wild place in America.” As we drive through the park with him, he explains everything from the evolution of its geothermal landscape—Yellowstone contains more than half of the world’s active geysers—to the shifts in its biodiversity since wolves were reintroduced to the ecosystem; the politics around Big Sky’s land ownership since Bill Gates and Oprah moved in, and it became the “Hamptons of Montana” to the lifecycles of the hundreds upon hundreds of bison we see rutting across its plains.

In fact, we are so sold on the glory of nature that when my travel companion and I leave what feels like our three-day honeymoon at Lone Mountain Ranch, we evolve our plans so that we can almost immediately return to the park. We are two city-dwelling fashion editors—not exactly outdoors aficionados—but Randy has fully convinced us that we need to see the other half of Yellowstone (the park is divided into two main loops, and a day is only really enough to visit one). On the recommendation of a friend who spent her childhood summers there, we drive over to Chico Hot Springs—a resort with far fewer frills than Lone Mountain, but which is simply great nonetheless—which comprises a series of rooms, lodges and cabins built around two geothermally-heated pools. Backing onto the bar, and staying open until 11 p.m., the pools remain filled with men wearing their cowboy hats in the pool and reading Bibles on loungers late into the night, who will happily explain the rules of shuffleboard, or their complicated feelings about the division between church and state. We are delighted; we extend our stay.

Despite the fact that, without Randy leading the way, we get a flat tire moments before arriving back in the park, our second trip to Yellowstone is as good as the first (not least because we now come equipped with his understanding of the landscape). Endless hours spent in a remote mechanics shop, and an extensive (albeit picturesque) trip to trade our rental, mean that we arrive at sunset—just in time to see the Grand Prismatic Spring (the largest hot spring in America, and the third largest in the world) transform into what appears to be a celestial body, its vivid rainbow basin just so unspeakably beautiful in the fading evening light that I burst into tears. We stay through the evening, until the park is pitch black and near-empty, to watch Old Faithful—apparently a particularly notable geyser—erupt with clouds of steam and columns of boiling water that we illuminate with torchlight. I’m under a week into my new life, and it appears I am fully invested in the wonder of the West. I hardly even bother blow-drying my hair on the wall-mounted hairdryer when I get back to Chico. (I do miss the Dyson, but I decide I can simply tuck it under my Stetson.)

The following days’ itineraries revolve around, essentially, the most American activities we can conceive of: I download Tinder and match with a cowboy who offers to take us rafting down the Gallatin River, which we enjoy thoroughly; we drive over to Cody, in Wyoming, to stay in the Irma, a hotel founded by Buffalo Bill, and learn to shoot a Civil War-era Gatling gun at the local range. We pick up recommendations for restaurants as we go (Follow Yer Nose BBQ and The Old Saloon in Emigrant are both great shouts; the latter plays a constantly rotating stream of live rodeo and old The Price Is Right episodes), and sit in bars swagged with America 250 flags waiting for locals to illuminate us on local activities. (And they do: one night, we meet the world’s best cattle auctioneer—as awarded in North Dakota last year—and he invites us to an auction where we learn the difference between a steer and a heifer.)

We go to the nightly Cody rodeo, and to the assorted museums (many of which are Buffalo Bill themed, or feature an astonishing amount of artillery). We scour thrift stores and leave the Irma to stay above a barn on a llama farm in the town of Pinedale (town slogan: “we have all the civilization you need”), where we discover that llamas are used to pack the bodies of elk on hunts and I spend immeasurable stretches of time silently watching the animals gallivant towards the endless horizon. We begin to feel immersed in our new lives, where our phone signal is intermittent, but our new hobbies—and friends—are plentiful. When I ask a man in a bar what he makes of the tourists who are starting to infiltrate his world, and why he thinks that might be, he tells me simply that, out here, people just want to have a conversation with you and don’t care what your job is. I realize that nobody has asked me anything about work in weeks, and that my constantly frenetic nervous system has begun to still.

Then we make our way to our final destination: Hyattville (population: 75), then Paintrock Canyon Ranch, to camp for a week on 80,000 acres that promise no phone signal or electricity, but plentiful horseriding. It is only my second time camping—and the first was with Haider Ackermann, in the most luxurious set-up imaginable, so it doesn’t quite feel like it counts—and I am slightly apprehensive about the lack of amenities. But as soon as we see our tents, pitched amidst a meadow and beside a babbling creek, I am sold on my new home. Then, when I unzip to see a wooden dresser and a king-size bed with linen so soft that every single person comments on it at breakfast the following morning, I never want to sleep anywhere else again.

The first evening, we settle into our new surrounds: at dinner around a giant picnic table upon which platters of fire-cooked steak and vegetables appear, we meet the nine fellow guests with whom we’ll be spending the following days, and who range in riding experience from complete novices to one woman who lives across the valley with ten horses. As the sun sets, we collectively descend to the campfire with our blueberry pie and thick cream to begin to discuss our respective lives, and what brought us to remote Wyoming. Without phones, laptops, or televisions to return to, we all stay talking long into the night, like teenagers on a school trip.

The next morning, we awaken to coffee, fruit, and yogurt served in our communal lounge tent before sitting down for another delicious meal somehow magic-ed from the “kitchen tent” and going to meet our horses at the nearby stables. What unfolds is a series of days that we came to collectively refer to as adult summer camp, where we spend our mornings riding for endless hours in groups of two or three through some of the most beautiful landscapes I’ve ever seen—across sandstone hills striped in infinite shades of red, only punctuated by silvery-grey sagebrush, or between the dramatic crags of limestone cliffs. I learn to canter within vast expanses of unpopulated, untouched wilderness beneath infinite skies, where the only things that appear on the horizon are occasional clusters of cattle, or packs of horses roaming the terrain.

When we return to camp in the afternoons, we all gather to learn ranch skills like roping or leatherwork from the wranglers (I make a terrible roper, as well as a terrible leatherwork coaster; others fare better). By the third day, we’ve all formed a sort of utopian collective where, afterwards, we grab armfuls of beers and freshly-brewed iced tea and make our way down to the swimming hole to sunbathe, skim stones, and discuss who’d be best suited to which role if a freak avalanche were to trap us all in camp together forever (we unanimously nominate Sarah, a divorce lawyer from Utah, our president). There are no clocks; no phones. It’s, to put it bluntly, paradise.

My companion and I spend our days riding with Grace, the daughter of Duke Phillips III: a third-generation cattle worker who started Ranchlands in the late ’90s with the belief that ranching is “the greatest alternative to large-scale conservation.” At drinks one evening, he joins us—his remarkably good handlebar mustache and low-tipped cowboy hat presenting the perfect picture of a Wyoming rancher—to explain, in few words, that nobody understands the land like those who work in harmony with it. He explains that, at Ranchlands, they breed their cattle in alignment with a program that I become disproportionately fascinated by, which works to evolve cows that are best suited to the natural environment so that they require minimal human intervention to thrive—and they can, in turn, improve the ecosystem through regenerative grazing (my learnings from the cattle auction really begin to pay off here). When he and Grace begin to discuss their apprenticeship program, which recruits young people from both urban and rural environments to consider land as “a multi-dimensional resource” while training them across hospitality, management, marketing and conservation before they join one of their four ranches, I become somewhat convinced that ranching can save the world.

“Everyone in this world is deeply connected to land—whether it’s a ranch, or their garden,” reflects Grace as we sit by the creek one day, eating our (consistently delicious) packed lunches as our horses doze under the trees. “And today, to provide an open space where people can breathe feels more important than ever.” Over the weeks, I’ve quizzed everyone I’ve met about what it is about the American West that has taken such a hold on the world; why the image of a cowboy still appears so remarkably cool; how a nation’s mythology can appeal even while the nation itself appears in abject crisis. Nobody had quite been able to put a finger on it until Grace.

These weeks, these open spaces have given me the opportunity to catch my breath: to lounge on porches and watch the sunset, to silently watch the stars outside my tent, to spend long days phoneless and horseback, to sit in excited darkness waiting for a geyser to erupt. I don’t even have a garden back in London, but I am connected to something here—and she’s spot on: right now, it feels more important than ever.

#6773. All the Highlights From Lagos Fashion Week 2026

The 16th edition of Lagos Fashion Week celebrated sustainable circularity and local talent.

The spring/summer 2027 fashion month may have come to a close in the major cities, but it’s just getting started everywhere else. Over the course of this past weekend, designers and industry insiders came together in Lagos, Nigeria, for the 16th edition of Lagos Fashion Week. Workshops, panels, and presentations focused on sustainability and local talent, alongside a strong lineup of emerging designers and Nigerian household names. Above all else, the designers demonstrated a commitment to craft and heritage. As Aisha Ayensu, the designer behind Christie Brown, said during a panel discussion on day one: “It is necessary to build a sustainable relationship with African artisans, because the success of any African fashion brand relies on the craft people.”

Global favorite Orange Culture (which has shown internationally at New York and London Fashion Weeks) kicked off the season in the city. Curious about the other moments that happened during Lagos Fashion Week? Read on for some of the designers to know from the new season.

Founded in 2015 by Segun Aladejana, Sevon Dejana puts an emphasis on high-drama evening wear with a sculptural, artistic nod. Think: gowns covered in explosive florals and feathers, but sculpted in an unusual way, with a modernist take on traditional haute couture shapes. The label is for the bold, and there is certainly no lack of embellishment or color, as was the case for the new collection presented on the runway for the new season.

Hertunba puts an emphasis on African craft with experimental, sculptural silhouettes. Founder Florentina Agu started taking dressmaking classes at the age of 13, and officially started her line in 2020. The brand makes a point of employing (and training) local women to sew and weave and also reduces waste. 90 percent of Hertunba’s excess materials are repurposed into handcrafted interior décor like rugs and throw pillows, or are pieced together into new, wearable pieces.

Designed between Lagos and London, PiiLLz and PoiZn takes a slow fashion approach to maximalism. Designer Ifeoma Umenyiora creates pieces that embrace stripes, sequins, and feathers, always with a focal point on color. The label maintains its local craft by offering bespoke tailored gowns and other pieces, all made on-site in its atelier in Lagos.

Launched as a sustainable, gender-neutral line by Adedamola Adebayo, most of Bornstar Nigeria’s pieces are made of fabric that is manufactured locally in Nigeria. The brand’s relaxed tailoring is a colorful new take on Nigerian style. Details like intricate beadwork, crochet, and tassels accent the streamlined, tailored separates, and accessories, like chunky bags, are also strong.

Founded in 2021 by designer Adedayo Ilori, Dimeji Ilori upcycles old pieces to create new garments that are collaged, cut, bleached, and transformed into new tactile wonders. Texture is definitely at the center of the aesthetic. Think: a fluffy hat and matching trims or dresses fully embellished with cowrie shells, as shown above.

#6772. Louisa Jacobson’s Suited Streetwear Couldn’t Be More Different From Her Gilded Age Character’s Style

From corsets to bustles to floor-length skirts, the womenswear of the Gilded Age was known for many things. But Louisa Jacobson’s frayed raw hems and buckled collars were certainly not in the ladies’ 1880s style guides.

While doing press in New York City for the fourth season of her smash HBO historical drama The Gilded Age, Jacobson showed us a bit of her own street style... and it was a far cry from the looks that her character, Marian Brook, has donned on the very same streets.

Leaning instead into a bit of menswear, rather than the pastel gowns we’ve come to expect from her on-screen alter-ego, the actor experimented with suiting and modernized tailoring, thanks to the help of her stylist, Edward Bowleg III.

Last Monday, Jacobson turned to Mel Usine for a light-gray set from the label’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. Composed of a frayed, collarless jacket and matching inside-out skirt, the ensemble offered an unfinished, deconstructed look you’d have never seen during the 1883 Metropolitan Opera House opening.

It was layered over a black-trimmed white tank with a skinny red tie wrapped around her waist, and paired with peep-toe heels.

The next day, the actor pushed things even further, wearing a black-on-black monochrome look from Commission’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. This one was all about the buckle accents, with a zip-up blazer topped with a belted collar and little capri leggings trimmed with the same detail. In between was a pleated skirt, and for shoes, Jacobson wore pointed-toe pumps over calf-high socks.

Later in the day, Jacobson was a proper Calvin Klein girl—seen in Hudson Square wearing a dark-clay satin blazer and matching trousers with a heather-gray jacket over both. Her little nude ballet flats featured a contrasting reflective strap, and she grabbed a shoulder bag before heading out for an afternoon of press.

In an age of constant method dressing, it appears Jacobson is doing things her way.

#6771. Why El Clasico Is the Best Grudge Match in All of Sports

Last Saturday, before the biggest grudge match in international soccer, Spanish police officers decked out in riot gear surrounded my Barcelona hotel. Blue lights bounced from the sun-stained stone of the alley as kids scrambled away in the distance. In the skirmish, one had lost a single ASICS sneaker that sat idly in the road until, sometime between night and the light of day, someone snatched it up for themselves. You often hear of the way heated football rivalries and cup finals bring out a kind of mob mentality among fans. The match, however, wasn’t set to kick off for another 24 hours.

Three days prior I’d landed in Barcelona to attend FC Barcelona versus Real Madrid, better known as El Clásico, for which Tyler the Creator’s GOLF brand had partnered with Spotify on Barcelona’s gameday kits. If you care about football in the slightest you know about El Clásico, though it’s worth knowing about even if you don’t.

Since 1902—the year of Real Madrid’s founding, and three years after that of FC Barcelona—the two biggest football clubs in Spain have clashed in a rivalry match dubbed El Clásico (the face-off now happens twice a season, plus various tournament play that varies in schedule year to year). Before last week’s installment, the match had been played 264 times over 122 years. In most high-stakes football rivalries, one club holds a historical edge: Arsenal has a handy 20 to 30 wins over Tottenham Hotspur in the North London Derby, depending on when you start keeping track, while Manchester United edges out Liverpool in total wins. But heading into the first El Clásico of the 2026-27 La Liga season, Barcelona and Real Madrid stood deadlocked with 106 wins each.

American sports rivalries are often the result of proximity, with most pitting divisional neighbors and crosstown rivals against one another, with the exception of teams that share a bitter history of championship bouts (like the Lakers and the Celtics). But if we’re being honest, not even Yankees-Red Sox holds a candle to El Clásico. Apart from both competing in the upper echelon of La Liga’s clubs, FC Barcelona and Real Madrid’s rivalry has stewed in over a century of political turmoil between the Catalan capital and the city that houses the Spanish throne. During the 20th century as Spain looked to enforce a uniform identity across the nation, Catalonia sought to maintain its independence from the crown and, crucially, its right to speak Catalan rather than Spanish. Francisco Franco’s dictatorship brought more enmity, as Madrid became the proxy club for a centralized Spain while Barcelona came to represent Catalonia’s Republican Left. During the Franco years, when both the language and the flag of Catalan were banned, Barcelona’s Camp Nou stadium became a safe haven for the free expression of Catalan identity. Meanwhile, Franco’s foreign minister Fernando Maria de Castiella declared Real Madrid “the best embassy we’ve ever had.” The wounds of that era have hardly subsided: while the war may be over, as recently as 2017 the Catalan people voted on whether or not they’d remain a part of Spain (the vote was declared illegal by the Spanish government, and there was police intervention at polling stations).

Today, the clubs are recognized as polar opposites in every sense, from politics to style of play: Real Madrid stands for conservatism and a unified Spain, while Barcelona remains the club of the rebellious Left. Madrid takes an Evil Empire approach to roster construction, buying up the most exciting free agents on the market for record-breaking fees. (This century alone they’ve rostered Cristiano Ronaldo, David Beckham, and Zinedine Zidane, and the club currently boasts a striker line that includes Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, and Vinicius Jr.) Barcelona, on the other hand, has the most acclaimed and successful youth academy in all of football. The school, La Masia, has promoted a singular theory of football for decades, prioritizing position play and a dominant possession game perfected by FC Barcelona veterans like Lionel Messi, Xavi, Pep Guardiola, and Andrés Iniesta. When Spain won the World Cup this summer, they did so with eight former students of La Masia on the pitch (one of whom, Marc Cucarella, currently plays for Real Madrid).

To this day, the rivalry is characterized by an unmistakable hostility. In my four days in Barcelona, I didn’t see one person wearing Real Madrid’s crest, though the souvenir shops lining La Rambla were well-stocked with the club’s bootleg gear. At one point, I walked past a wall scrawled with graffiti: “SPANISH GO HOME.” When we finally got to the match, most Madrid fans were sequestered to a supporter section in the upper deck surrounded by protective plexiglass.

“This is the biggest match in club football,” explained Joel Jaggar, a British transplant who’s lived in Barcelona for a decade. Jaggar runs Real Vintage Football, a rare jersey boutique in El Raval (just outside of the city’s Gothic Quarter) that was unsurprisingly overwhelmed with visitors all weekend. He’d stocked up on at least a hundred Messi jerseys, all of which were gone by the time they closed on Friday. “A lot of people come to Barcelona specifically for this game,” he shared. “Big fans, sure, but also people who want to experience the game for the sake of the experience.” Globally, he argued, the word “Barcelona” is as closely associated with the club as it is the city. “You can’t say the same for Madrid,” he quipped.

Jaggar and I met the morning after a swell of student-organized protests regarding the city’s cost-of-living crisis boiled over into vandalism and looting near the neighborhood that houses his store. There was even suspicion El Clásico would have to be postponed or cancelled altogether. Come morning though, those anxieties had faded–as is so often the case, football continued uninterrupted.

Even with capacity capped at around 62,000 during ongoing renovations, Camp Nou is something to behold. Ahead of kickoff, supporters lifted color-coordinated pieces of poster nestled into each seat,forming a massive, stadium-wide tifo in the colors of the club and, in our section, the Catalonian flag. Fireworks exploded, and El Clásico began.

But much of the match’s first half was mired in tension, as Barcelona dominated possession but failed to score. The crowd finally began to pop when Madrid nabbed their first goal, then properly exploded when Barca tied it up in the second half. When Mbappé scored his second goal of the evening at ‘87 minutes after a beautiful assist from Bellingham, he vaulted over to the gate of the Barcelona supporters’ section, taunting them as trash thrown from the crowd rained over him. Madrid held on, gaining the tiniest of advantages in the El Clásico win count: 107 to their rivals’ 106.

As we walked out of Camp Nou, which will hold a whopping 105,000 spectators when its renovation is complete, I thought about the sort of sporting events that tend to grace bucket lists: Super Bowls and World Cup Finals and World Series games. So often the point is the spectacle of a season or tournament ending—the big trophy, the championship ring, the confetti and fireworks. El Clásico is different. There’s no trophy at the end, no ultimate resolution. Like the ideological divide for which it’s become a proxy, El Clásico is in a constant state of ebb and flow. Each time Barcelona and Real Madrid take the pitch, there’s no decisive victory so much as another brick laid in the foundation of football’s greatest rivalry. These clubs have come to blows 265 times. But as long as there are football stadiums in Barcelona and Madrid, El Clásico will endure as a conduit for the enduring rancor between the country's two biggest cities.

#6770. These 5 Brands Are Making the Holiday Pajama Sets I Want Most—I've Rounded Up the Best Ones

I'd happily make these my everyday uniform if I could!!

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Sure, decorating my house, lighting a fresh pine-scented candle, and listening to Christmas music all day, every day get me in the holiday spirit, but what really does it for me? A pair of matching holiday pajamas. As someone who wears a two-piece set to bed pretty much every single night, I love swapping in new prints and colors to fit the time of year. There’s just something about a festive set that really completes the cozy vibe!

That said, I’m not the type of person who’ll settle for a basic plaid set and call it a day. With brands dropping holiday PJs in everything from cool patterns to out-of-the-box color combos, you'll find plenty of unique options to choose from. Ahead, I rounded up five brands with seriously cute designs that'll give your nighttime wardrobe a seasonal refresh. They also make great gifts for loved ones or the perfect picks for your next matching-pajama party with friends and family!

For as long as I can remember, Old Navy has been one of the go-tos for holiday pajama sets. The brand always comes through with cute designs at affordable prices—something that feels increasingly rare in this economy! Its iconic flannel sets come in all kinds of styles, from classic plaid and gingerbread prints to lively options featuring elves, stripes, and mistletoe. Even better? Tons of this season’s styles are currently 60% off, so I’d run, not walk!

Known for its fun, quirky designs, Roller Rabbit has perfected the art of making PJs that feel anything but basic (the monkeys!) while still being incredibly cozy. Its holiday collection is no exception, with colorful prints, funky patterns, and plenty of personality. If you're a maximalist or you just love a bold pajama set, this is where to get them! I know they’re on the pricier side, but I promise they’re worth the splurge! (Ahem, these tend to sell out pretty quickly, so I’d add them to your cart ASAP if you have your eye on a pair!)

You know and love SKIMS for its buttery-soft loungewear and impressive shapewear, and I’m happy to report that its pajama selection is just as good. Right now, the holiday sets are especially gorgeous! I love how the brand sticks to the classics with familiar silhouettes, like cami sets, while giving them a festive update. Personally, I’ll be buying the bright pink plaid set!

From my teenage years to now, Victoria's Secret has always been at the top of my list for bras, underwear, loungewear, and, of course, incredibly cute pajama sets. I remember feeling so grown-up whenever I'd get a new pair from the brand, and honestly, that hasn't changed! Its 2026 holiday collection is just as good as ever, with on-trend designs that feel a little more dressed-up than your everyday PJs. Choose from cute short sets and long flannel styles for those who love something extra cozy, to silky satin sets and lightweight Henley styles for the girls who tend to run hot. There's something for every kind of sleeper!

When I think of the silkiest, most luxe pajamas I’ve ever worn, Eberjey instantly comes to mind. They’re exactly what you’d imagine sleeping in a five-star hotel would feel like: silky to the touch, featherlight, and soft as a cloud. And the holiday styles are just as dreamy! Available in the brand’s beloved TENCEL™ Modal and flannel sets, there’s a range of festive yet chic designs to choose from, including polka dots, bows, holly berries, and more.
