#6768. The 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards Celebrated Fashion’s Next Generation—and Its Icons

Rachel Scott, Ralph Lauren, and Colleen Allen were among the night’s top honorees.

Often called the Oscars of American fashion, the CFDA Fashion Awards lived up to the billing last night, drawing a starry crowd to the American Museum of Natural History. The ceremony, now in its 45th year, recognized the designers and creatives shaping the direction of American fashion, from established names to independent newcomers.

Before guests headed inside the museum halls, they stepped onto the red carpet to channel the evening’s dress code, “American design excellence,” where many of the evening’s nominees and honorees were well-represented. ELLE cover star Mona Tougaard wore a punchy primary-color look by Zane Li of LII, who was nominated in the American Emerging Designer of the Year category. Demi Moore and Lupita Nyong’o chose to rework American wardrobe classics in custom GapStudio. And Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, Rosé, and Anja Rubik glimmered in gilded Saint Laurent looks from Anthony Vaccarello’s final collection for the brand. (Vaccarello was honored with the International Designer of the Year Award.)

Then, Thom Browne, the CFDA’s chairman of the board of directors, started the ceremony with powerful opening remarks: “American fashion is at the center of the world and at the center of the spirit of our time,” he said. “It’s never been more important to tell important stories.”

Browne handed the reins off to host Keke Palmer, who delivered a major fashion moment in 1970s Bob Mackie previously worn by Raquel Welch, to begin awarding the evening’s most anticipated prizes. Rachel Scott was crowned American Womenswear Designer of the Year, her second time earning the prize, while Ralph Lauren, set to celebrate 60 years in business in 2027, won American Menswear Designer of the Year.

In her speech, Scott issued a call to action that was especially poignant ahead of the midterm elections. “In a world where independent and marginalized voices are systematically quieted, I feel extremely lucky and very, very responsible,” she said. “And we have a lot of work to do, starting tomorrow morning.”

Colleen Allen, beloved by the New York fashion scene for her bewitchingly feminine but powerful designs, won the coveted Google Shopping American Emerging Designer of the Year Award, while Ana Khouri took home Accessory Designer of the Year for her sculptural jewelry and gravity-defying ear cuffs.

Also included in the programming were a series of special honors, including Tory Burch’s Positive Change Award, Peter Marino’s Fashion Icon Award, and Inez and Vinoodh’s Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award.

#6767. How to Style White Jeans for Fall

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

These outfits prove white denim has no off-season

White jeans are now a year-round staple, no longer relegated to the summer months between Memorial Day and Labor Day. From work-ready looks anchored by tailored denim to relaxed ensembles made for weekend getaways, these white-denim outfits do it all. This fall, take inspiration from a few of our favorite street-style looks. The lineup includes everything from straight-leg and relaxed fits to low-rise baggy silhouettes, in a range of soft hues like off-white and ecru. When paired with capsule wardrobe classics, such as a white T-shirt, a brightly colored button-down shirt, or a barn jacket, the results are stylish and equally easy to pull off.

Below, discover ten white jeans outfits that prove how cool they can look throughout the fall/winter months.

There’s a reason winter whites are a perennial favorite. Matching white jeans with your outerwear creates a clean, fresh monochromatic look. For a subtle sliver of color, layer an icy blue cardigan underneath, then add classic black pumps, and finish with sculptural gold earrings.

A simple way to wear white jeans during the fall is pairing them with a ladylike jacket in brown check print. The cropped silhouette offers a flattering counterpoint to relaxed denim, while black accessories—a roomy shoulder bag and ballet flats—lend a refined touch. Consider this an easy fall workwear formula you can wear on repeat.

If you’re a minimalist, try playing with contrasting textures to make your white jeans feel even more seasonally appropriate. Style them with a roomy black suede funnel-neck jacket, pointed-toe boots, and an unexpected accessory, like this elegant tassel bag.

The best fall outfits start with great basics: White straight-leg jeans, a white T-shirt, and a lightweight trench, which are all part of a well-rounded capsule wardrobe. Give these classics a hint of surprise by tying a pop of red knit around your shoulders and slipping into mules for an unexpected detail. They’re ideal for peak fall days, when it’s not too hot or too cold, and you can get away with a little peep-toe.

A striped long-sleeve T-shirt lends a touch of nautical charm to white jeans. Go for an oversized option in red to play up the relaxed, off-duty vibe. Black shoes—whether boots, loafers, or sleek sneakers—anchor the look, while a leather bucket bag and aviator frames complete the outfit.

Barn jackets remain a major trend for fall 2026. Make a case for wearing pastels well into the cooler months with a pale pink version and white jeans, offset by a black sweater, loafers, and a brown suede bag. Whether for a casual day spent running errands in the city or a weekend away, this combination strikes the perfect balance.

White jeans don’t always have to be worn in casual settings only. Make yours feel more elegant with a tuxedo-style blazer, silk camisole, and smoking slippers. A structured top-handle bag adds a polished finishing touch, taking the look effortlessly from desk to dinner.

Dip your toes into the season’s brightest color trends by putting a bright button-down shirt with otherwise simple styling pieces, such as a white T-shirt and straight-leg jeans. A leather belt and high-vamp shoes provide pared-back elegance.

French girls know how to layer the je ne sais quoi way, and denim is often the base. White jeans get a Parisian twist when paired with not one but three fall jackets—after all, temperatures are always unpredictable. A chore coat, plaid blazer, and windbreaker jacket can all be part of your layering essentials.

Nothing is more classically cool than wearing black and white during fall/winter. Bring your baggy white jeans into the winter months with a black turtleneck cardigan and sleek textural accessories—an embossed belt, suede flats, and a rich leather bag. Use this look as a base, then add a leather jacket or a tailored wool coat for extra warmth when needed.

#6766. 31 Best Gifts for Mom in 2026, According to GQ Editors

There's an art to giving a good gift to someone who's been a mother to you, whether that's your actual mom, grandmother, or the person who's always looked out for you. And it has precious little to do with how much you spend. They say what goes around comes around, and when the occasion comes to buy her something special, there's not better time to return a little of the favor. To that end, we've rounded up the best gifts for mom, from modest indulgences to proper splurges, all chosen with an eye toward good taste, a little surprise, and the small triumph of getting it just right.

Still stumped? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

I have an AYR sweater in this very fabric, and I've been wearing the hell out of it lately. It's extraordinarily soft, with a bouncy, bouclé-like texture that you really have to feel to appreciate. The High has all that going for it, plus a cropped fit and a prim, high-set collar.

We're firm believers that a good tuxedo is one you'd wear any old day. Which is why we're digging this casual cotton tuxedo shirt from Gap's collaboration with Victoria Beckham. It's awfully chic, and a reason for her to get "dressed up" with nowhere special to go.

Breda's Jane Time Charm is a clever little thing. Made from gold-plated stainless steel, the miniature timepiece can be worn as a necklace or clipped to a keychain, but I think it makes for a pretty decoration on a lapel.

Timex's Cavatina Mini looks like something you'd stumble upon at an estate sale, with its petite 17mm case and old-school script logo. The design nods to the brand's '60s-era women's watches, though this one's fresh out of the box.

Thistles is an IYKYK eyewear label whose fashionable milieu stretches from Em Rata to Kim Gordon and any mom worth her vintage Prada. There are plenty of excellent frames to choose from, but the square-shaped Suede is a safe bet.

Coach has a bona fide can't-miss gift on its hands with the Brooklyn, a slouchy, do-it-all carryall. It comes in a range of sizes, but we're partial to the 34, a generously proportioned everyday bag with room for just about everything.

Cashmere is the safest bet you can make at Quince, so it's nice to see the brand putting it to work as the lining of these leather gloves. And at that price, there isn't much to complain about.

If she's made it this far in life without a pair of UGGs, the Zora ballet flat might be the one that finally wins her over. And if she's already living that UGG life, well, she's gonna need these.

A fresher, more spirited take on the original Coco, Coco Mademoiselle pairs sparkling orange and jasmine with rose and patchouli. For a mom with a taste for the classics, but an appreciation for modern flair, this one'll hit.

We recommended Therabody's Depuffing Wand last year, and we're running it back because it's just so dang good at what it does. Hot and cold treatments in one wonderfully unfussy little device make it a welcome addition to her skincare routine.

I like giving silk pillowcases because they're a beauty treatment and a bedroom upgrade in one. Clementine's smooth silk helps reduce friction against hair, minimizing tangles and breakage, while leaving fewer sleep creases.

Dyson's new travel-size Supersonic brings the brand's high-powered drying technology to a more portable package. It's compact enough to tuck into a carry-on without sacrificing the elite airflow of the original, and it's compatible with all the same attachments.

Laneige's Lip Sleeping Mask is a cult favorite, and chances are she already knows it, maybe even swears by it. But the new gingerbread flavor for the season? A stroke of seasonal madness, and a nice little stocking stuffer to boot.

Aesop is about as close to a sure thing as gifting gets. Its new Solias Hand Serum has a light, floral, citrusy, and herbaceous aroma, with a nourishing formula to help keep Mom's hands in fighting shape through winter.

No. 04 Bois de Balincourt has long drawn comparisons to Le Labo's Santal 33, only at a considerably friendlier price and without the burdern of its own ubiquity. Warm sandalwood and cedar, with earthy vetiver and a little spice—a perfect year-round candle.

I'm a coffee drinker through and through, but I'd consider switching allegiances to tea if it meant getting to use this teapot from Balmuda. Just looking at the thing feels therapeutic.

For farmers' market queens, this tote really does tick all the boxes: heavy-duty cotton canvas, six exterior pockets, a clever strap for securing, say, a bouquet of dahlihas, and a structured design that stands upright on its own.

This insulated Dutch oven tote from Staub and Clare V. is just the thing for the potluck monarch arriving with a cassoulet in tow. A highly specific gifting proposition, admittedly, but an excellent one nonetheless.

#6765. How Her Love of Vintage Changed Writer Keli Goff’s Life

Her collection, which has given new life to some of the great Black designers, is now a museum show.

When Keli Goff began purchasing vintage, it was a way to put together stylish looks for her new job within her budget. But over the years, as her interest grew, collecting became a way of connecting to the stories of Black designers unrecognized during their lifetimes. Goff, a writer who has been on the staff of shows including Being Mary Jane and And Just Like That, now owns work from major fashion figures like Patrick Kelly, Isaia Rankin, Stephen Burrows, and Ann Lowe, together making up one of the biggest private collections of work by Black designers. This month, the Houston Museum of African American Culture presents “Collecting in Color: Highlights from the Keli Goff Collection,” which was curated by John Guess and Danielle Finnerman. It’s the first major exhibition focused on her collection, and some of the pieces will be donated to the Bard Graduate Center’s Study Collection.

Goff’s interest in fashion design has intersected with her writing career in interesting ways. The estate of legendary costume designer Edith Head chose Goff to adapt her story for a biopic. “It’s all so surreal. I obviously have admired Edith’s work as long as I can remember, so my collection bringing this project into my life is a dream come true,” she says. Last year, Goff completed studying to become an art appraiser. She now consults in the art and auction sphere in addition to writing.

“People have been fascinated by my collection,” Goff says. “It’s a bit rare to see, frankly, collectors in this space like me. I mean like me in all sorts of ways, not just as an African American woman, but an African American woman who’s not from a privileged background. It’s important to me that I’m not the last one like me in these spaces.”

Goff spoke to ELLE about the joy of working with a museum in her Texas hometown, the old movies that inspired her love of vintage, and the designers she wishes everyone knew.

It really started by watching old movies with my mom and watching her dress up [when I was] a little girl. When I show friends old photos of her, people are always thinking, “Oh, she looks like a movie star or very Diana Ross-esque.” We would watch old movies, especially Imitation of Life and things from that era, the real glamour, the golden age of Hollywood. She would always say, “Look at the dresses, look at the dresses,” and I would. I really fell in love with old movies, which I do believe is part of how I ended up becoming a writer.

But also, I really fell in love with vintage clothes. I moved to New York and didn’t have a lot of money, and vintage was not trendy and didn’t cost thousands of dollars like it can be today. For one of my earliest jobs, I had to go to fancy events, but I had no money. I bought a couple of pieces from the ’60s at a flea market. I remember being at this event, and all these women who obviously had a lot more money to spend on clothes, asking, “Who’s this by? What boutique did you buy this at?” And I was like, “Oh, I got it at a flea market on Avenue B.” I think they thought I was joking.

I wrote a piece for The Daily Beast several years ago about the most influential Black designers in history. It was one of the most memorable pieces I’ve written. I don’t think at the time I was aware of how profoundly it impacted me, but I learned how many seminal Black American designers died of AIDS in a really short window of time. Willi Smith, one of the first Black designers to achieve major crossover commercial success in department stores, died. And so did Isaia Rankin and then Patrick Kelly. What I took away is that so much history was lost, but I also think about how different the future of American fashion might be today because these were really trailblazing and hugely influential.

They weren’t just influential Black American designers, but hugely influential American designers. Isaia Rankin basically had invented athleisure wear. It was his idea that you should be able to go from a coffee shop to a gym to the club. [He made] one of the first pieces by a Black designer I acquired online. I’ll never forget that the person selling it said, “This belonged to my aunt. Apparently, this guy used to be somebody,” which I just think is the saddest thing. He had this profound impact and then had been largely forgotten.

During the pandemic, when everyone worked from home with too much time on their hands and easy access to shop online, I ended up acquiring quite a bit, in part because a lot of the brick-and-mortar stores, particularly in Europe, were really struggling. They were so reliant on tourist foot traffic, and so a lot of them started selling online [for the first time]. And so there were a number of French boutiques I started acquiring pieces from, including some Patrick Kelly pieces that still have the original store tags from the 1980s, which I won’t remove. Those I won’t wear. The rest of them I wear when they fit. As life goes, they don’t always fit forever.

I’ve become friendly with Patrick Kelly’s widower, Bjorn Amelan, who’s a lovely, wonderful man and the keeper of Patrick’s legacy. It is important to me, when possible, to try to maintain relationships with the people I view as keepers of the legacies because I see my collection as serving the legacy of the designers. The pieces don’t belong to me. They belong to our wider community because they’re a part of our lived history.

The really cool thing is how many people I’ve met along this journey who have not only become cheerleaders but actually reach out to me about pieces. Writer Jill Kargman has become a friend and she gifted me a vintage Stephen Burrows dress. She said, “It belongs in your collection,” which is just the coolest thing ever.

I’m from Houston, and we have the Houston Museum of African American Culture here. We’re living in a really interesting time where people are having conversations about the politics of diversity, but one of the things that’s cool about fashion is that people of different political persuasions were like, “I think this collection’s really cool. I read an article about your collection, I ended up ordering a book about Elizabeth Keckley, or I ended up going down a rabbit hole about Ann Lowe.” At this moment, to be able to do an exhibition like this in my hometown felt particularly poignant.

Melanie Lawson has been a legendary anchor in Houston for decades. She was asked what she’s going to do in retirement, and she said that her husband, John Guess Jr., was the CEO of the Houston Museum of African American Culture. I sent him a note about how much Melanie inspired me and then mentioned my collection.

It was just kismet. They’ve actually never done a fashion exhibition. It was a real gamble. But what I so appreciated is that they had the same vision that, in a time in which our world is so divided, it’s really beautiful when you can find pieces of art that people can come together around.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#6763. Demi Moore Takes Denim-on-Denim Dressing to the Next Level in a GapStudio Dress at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards

A very American look for an American fashion ceremony

From hot-pink Matières Fécales ballgowns to iridescent Gucci dresses bursting with feathers and completely see-through chainmail Dolce & Gabbana slips, Demi Moore has never been afraid to take risks on the red carpet. So, when the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) hosted the 2026 Fashion Awards in New York City on Monday night (colloquially referred to as “the Oscars of American fashion”), it was no surprise to see Moore turning heads yet again.

With her look, the Oscar nominee took denim dressing to the next level, in a layered GapStudio dress designed by one of the night’s honorees: Zac Posen.

Since February 2024, Posen has acted as the creative director and executive vice president of Gap Inc., and the American brand for which he serves at the helm was recognized with the Innovation Award last night.

Posen’s experimental approach to the classic American brand was on full display when Moore arrived in a dress that looked like it was made out of nearly ten different pairs of blue jeans.

Composed of a dark-wash denim, the halter-style design featured a split-hem skirt that pooled on the ground, while the form-fitting bodice was made of stacks and stacks of material that emulated the waistbands of jeans. A line of buttons dotted the center, while up top, a final layer folded over to create a subtle sweetheart neckline.

For another denim touch, Moore carried a flap bag that even came equipped with a jean-fabric handle, designed by the brand’s executive director of accessories, Reed Krakoff. Finally, she completed the fit with tan suede pumps that peeked out from under the skirt of her dress, and a set of diamond earrings from Hassanzadeh.

Over the years, we’ve seen plenty of stars pull off denim-on-denim fits, but never with something quite like this.

#6761. Jamaica Revisited: A New Expression of Caribbean Luxury

Sandals Resorts elevates its robust amenities across the properties of its home island.

There are places in the sun that are just a little more special than the rest. Jamaica is one of them, with powder-sand shores lined with luxury resorts; a dense, verdant interior laced with waterfalls and coffee farms; waters that range from the lightest turquoise to the darkest navy; and a distinctive cuisine layered with spice. The beaches are spectacular and the natural wonders such as the crystalline YS Falls and the winding Martha Brae River are just that—full of awe and adventure.

The Taíno name for Jamaica is Xaymaca, which translates to “the land of wood and water”—and few descriptions capture the island more distinctly. For Sandals Resorts, that ethos has inspired a homegrown luxury. Born in Jamaica more than four decades ago, the brand remains deeply rooted in the island’s familial spirit, personality, food, and topography, even as its properties continue to evolve beyond their birthplace. The result is an immersive travel experience shaped by beaches, lush mountains, local flavors, deep culture, and the people who make Jamaica an unforgettable destination.

From the energy of Montego Bay and Ocho Rios to the sweeping coastline of Negril and the more tranquil pockets of the South Coast, the seven Sandals resorts across Jamaica each offer distinct ways to settle into the island. Across the collection properties, accommodations function as private retreats within a bigger resort experience. Swim-Up Suites allow guests to slide directly from the terrace into the water. Private pools create an aquatic world unto themselves. And on the Caribbean Sea, the Overwater Butler Villas turn a quiet resting place above the water into a pampered vacation lifestyle.

This year, a trio of properties are entering significantly new chapters following gorgeous reimaginings. The iconic comebacks promise renewed accommodations, including new Swim-Up suites, and new dining options. Cocooned by nature thanks to its setting beside a 500-acre preserve, Sandals Jamaica South Coast reopens November 18, with Overwater Butler Villas and the brand’s first Two Queen Junior Suites—perfect for friend-group travel. One month later, December 18 sees the return of Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, introducing a redesigned pool, Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay features newly refreshed accommodations, which are luxurious cocoons. Some days the hardest decision you make might be whether to head for the beach, dine at your favorite restaurant, or remain in your robe exactly where you are.

At Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, the resort where the brand first began, renewed ocean-view suites promise an impressive vantage point to view the gorgeous ocean. The new Bay Roc Rum Club embraces the music and rum culture that’s part of the fabric of Jamaica and the Caribbean.

Nearby, the former Sandals Jamaica Royal Caribbean emerges as Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with a unique resort experience centered around the sea and water. The new SkyPool Suites will feature a private plunge pool with an infinity edge that’s cantilevered from a large open air terrace, allowing guests to swim while enjoying uninterrupted views of the white sand and aqua waters below.

Further south, the secluded Sandals Jamaica South Coast offers ultra-luxury villas, including detached overwater villas arranged in a heart shape over the calm lagoon. Each comes equipped with see-through glass floor panels, outdoor overwater hammocks, and private boat dock access for the ultimate ocean-to-door service.

Jamaican food rarely arrives without presence. Scotch bonnets bring the heat, pimento adds the spice, and jerk carries the intensity of wood and smoke long before the plate lands on the table. That sense of heritage is part of the experience at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with Suppa, a new restaurant inspired by the island ritual of Sunday dinner. The menu celebrates familiar Jamaican flavors in savory dishes, stews, and curries served in a casual, supper-style setting made for sharing plates around the table. The adjoining Keynote Rum Bar features a soundtrack of the island’s legends in a laid-back lounge drenched in warm leather and rich tones, plus an extensive Caribbean rum selection.

The waterfront Buccan at Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay brings a different kind of fire. This open air space is where meats, seafood, and veggies are cooked over an open hearth and served at family-style tables set by the ocean. The well-received concept first debuted at the lush and secluded Sandals Saint Vincent, nestled in its own private cove, and is now arriving in Jamaica.

Visiting Sandals Jamaica South Coast, every beach day can start with Jamaica’s renowned Blue Mountain coffee and island pastries at BLŪM before afternoons stretch into hours at The Jerk Shack, enjoying must-have Jamaican jerk chicken, jerk pork, fish in foil, and other heritage-style comfort snacks. At the newly arrived Butch’s Island Chop House, excellent steak dinners and perfectly chilled martinis are on the menu.

Arguably one of the greatest luxuries while on a getaway is not having to weigh every decision. Sandals’ all-inclusive model is built around freedom. Not only are meals, snacks, and drinks included, but so are many of the resort experiences that turn a beach trip into an adventure, such as snorkeling, paddleboarding, kayaking, and daily diving for certified scuba divers, as well as classes to become PADI certified. Back on land, guests can move from the beach to an active day at the tennis and pickleball courts. For the golf lover, a day at Sandals Ochi, Sandals Dunn’s River, and Sandals Royal Plantation in Jamaica also include complimentary greens fees at Upton Estate Golf & Country Club in the green hills above Ocho Rios.

All-inclusive leaves room for every traveler to have their own version of the Caribbean holiday. One guest may spend the morning beneath the surface of the sea and the afternoon learning pickleball, then indulging in fresh sushi and sashimi. Another may decide the day’s only pursuit should be moving from a suite to a lounge chair, then being served jerk chicken or just-out-the-oven pizza beachside.

For all of Jamaica’s waterfalls, rivers, lagoons, beaches, and mountains, the element travelers often cherish most is a feeling of welcome. The ease of a conversation with the butler, the waiter who remembers your daily coffee order, the laugh with the bartender that extends a quick interaction into a memory, the recommendation to try a local dish, visit a secluded beach or a local shop or market that might have otherwise been missed is waiting in Jamaica.

That kind of Jamaican hospitality at Sandals cannot be engineered by simply refreshing a pool or designed into a new suite. It comes from people knowing how to welcome guests to their home. At Sandals Resorts, the flavor, the memorable landscapes, and the contagious Jamaican warmth makes visitors feel less like they simply arrived at a destination—and more like they’ll be welcomed back again and again.Book your Jamaican getaway today at sandals.com.

#6760. What Writing a Book About JFK Jr. Taught Me About Personal Style

John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better than pretty much anybody else. That’s a big part of why he was one of the most photographed men on the planet in the 1990s, and why he remains a menswear moodboard staple today, nearly 30 years after his untimely death. Still, no matter how hard you try, and no matter how closely you hew to the source material, all attempts to replicate JFK Jr.’s style are destined to leave you looking like a runner-up in a Washington Square Park lookalike contest.

Ask anyone who encountered John-John in his prime—which, in my experience, is virtually everyone who lived in Manhattan in the 1990s—and the first thing they’ll mention is his magnetism, his charm, and the fact that, against all odds, he was actually better-looking in person. I know this because, having recently written a book about JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve spent a good part of the last year poring over photos, reading biographies, speaking to people who knew him, and otherwise immersing myself in his world. Among the conclusions I’ve come to is that you probably won’t look as cool as JFK Jr. did wearing rollerblades, but there are a few style moves you can borrow from his playbook without resorting to full Kennedy cosplay.

JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was built on four pillars: tailoring, preppy basics, workwear, and sportswear. But it was the idiosyncratic way he combined them (i.e., a backward baseball cap with a suit, a polo neck sweater under a tweed blazer, hiking boots with tailored trousers) that resulted in some of his most memorable looks. Surprisingly, while the combination of straight-leg jeans, a button-up dress shirt, and a blazer has become shorthand for JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve never seen any evidence of him wearing it. In fact, he seldom wore jeans at all (some speculate his mother thought they looked shabby, while others told me that jeans didn’t complement his active lifestyle). That said, plenty of other ’90s style icons, from Ralph Lauren to Jerry Seinfeld, rocked this particular look, and it’s a pretty easy one to pull off. As with everything about JFK Jr.’s style, it’s not about lifting these combinations wholesale, but understanding the precise balance of contrast that makes them work.

One of the most consistent elements of JFK Jr.’s style was his love of discordant accessories, from his collection of flat caps to his ever-present wallet chain to his Oakley Eye Jacket shades. Some of these were practical—he was so prone to misplacing his wallet and keys that he needed to chain them to his pants—but others reflected his love of color (funky knit caps), his enthusiasm for skiing (fleece headbands), and his passion for travel (various hats picked up on trips to India and Thailand). Some accessories will suit you better than others, but if you have a personal connection to it, all the better. And most importantly, limit yourself to one standout add-on per outfit.

Speaking of accessories: JFK Jr. was a dedicated scarf guy, and he’d pair one with everything from joggers and sneakers to his best navy blue suit. Rather than draping a scarf loosely around his neck, he tended to tie it in either a dressy overhand or classic Parisian knot, both of which lend a more formal look. He also loved wearing a thick scarf as outerwear, throwing it over a sweatshirt on a chilly day instead of a coat, often paired with a knit cap. For best results, don’t pick a scarf that matches the rest of your outfit too closely.

Among the most surprising things I discovered about JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was his watch collection. I wasn’t able to uncover any evidence of him wearing the long-lost Rolex Daytona given to him by Aristotle Onassis (a watch that, if ever found, would give Paul Newman a run for his money), but I did identify an unusually wide range of other pieces in his collection, from a Victorinox Swiss Army field watch to a Swatch chronograph to a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is of a piece with everything else we know about JFK Jr.: he wasn’t bound by any single style, brand, or price point, and got just as much enjoyment out of a cheap quartz watch as a luxury mechanical one.

As a rich kid raised on the Upper East Side, JFK Jr.’s closet included plenty of blazers, chinos, and polos. He was a gym rat who loved playing sports, so he also had a lot of sweats, tees, and sneakers. He was a downtown socialite, so he owned a lot of nice suits and tuxes, too. He also had an enviable collection of graphic tees from NYC institutions like the Russian & Turkish Baths in the East Village and the New York Athletic Club, as well as some commemorating events like the 1984 NYC Fresh Festival, a seminal moment in hip-hop history. What stands out to me—and what I believe makes his style so distinctive—is that JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was an authentic reflection of who he was, where he came from, and what he loved. This might be the most important style lesson any of us can learn from him: Great personal style is less about clothes than wearing them in a way that expresses your individuality.

#6759. Mariah Carey Answers Vogue’s Holiday Questions

Now that Halloween has come and gone, we can officially put spooky season to rest—and the festive holiday season has come in to fill the void. And who better to ring in this cheery time of year than with Mariah Carey—the undisputed queen of Christmas? (Because, as she would say: “It’s tiiiime!”)

Consider her defrosted: This week, Carey was announced as the new star of Gucci’s 2026 holiday campaign, and last night the singer attended the Italian label’s private store event in New York City to kick off the festive party season.

In the new campaign video, Carey arrives at a holiday party decked out in full Demna-era Gucci—mix-and-mingling with guests, set to the tune of—what else?—her enduring hit “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Last night, Carey kept the celebrations going by handing out (Gucci!) gifts to all of the party attendees. A full choir even sang renditions of some of her best Christmas hits.

Pre-soirée, however, Vogue couldn’t resist the chance to catch a private moment with Carey and ask her some of our burning questions. From her festive styling tips to her party hosting no-nos, read on for the superstar’s hottest holiday takes.

Mariah Carey: It was so fun shooting the campaign. I had a lot of favorite moments—mainly the one with the dog. Did you see the dog? So cute. That was festive.

I love everything about this time of year. It’s just … something that I can’t explain. I’ve been in love with Christmas my whole life, and now when we celebrate and we do all of the things, it opens up a whole other moment of festivity.

What are my traditions in the morning? I’m not a morning person, that’s the thing. I wait till mid-afternoon, and then we start with the opening of the gifts and all the things. It’s fun and festive.

I do—but they will take a long time to explain. We see Santa every year. We go on a sleigh ride together with him. We drink hot chocolate.

I do cook during the holidays. It’s one of my favorite things to do, and I don’t cook earlier in the year. I wait ’til Christmas Eve, or the day before Christmas Eve, and I make linguini with white clam sauce—the way my dad used to make it. Everybody has that. I also make a red sauce. It’s one of my favorite things. And then I’ll just eat that for the next few days.

Eggnog. Come on! You put whatever brown liquor you have, and then just throw it into the eggnog, and it’s eggnog.

Well, I’m wearing these Gucci boots, which I love. They don’t hurt—that’s number one—and I think they’re very chic, darling. And this Gucci dress is a sleek, black, wonderful moment.

I don’t usually have a holiday bash, because I’m just doing my own thing. Is that not good? I’m not big on hosting. I’d rather go to something [where] someone’s a really good hostess or host, and then I can just join in on the fun.

I’m going to have Marilyn Monroe. Tupac. And then I’m just going to set up a table for my dogs, and make them really happy. The dogs get a seat at the table. They have to be there.

I love the song today, yesterday—whenever. It’s just something that I wrote. I wasn’t trying to write the biggest holiday song [ever]. I was just there writing my little song that ended up lasting. So it’s been a great experience.

It’s too much work to go from Halloween straight into Christmas, and then think of a New Year's resolution. I don’t know. We’ll have to wait and see what else happens between now and New Year’s.

#6757. Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Awards season brought love into Andrew Garfield’s life. On Feb. 21, 2025, People reported that Garfield has been “quietly” dating A Complete Unknown’s Monica Barbaro after the two were seen together in London.

A source told People that “they’ve been really low-key and have been spending time together quietly.” The actors’ reps did not respond to People’s request for comment.

In October 2024, Garfield told Esquire that he protects his love life, so don’t expect him to comment on any dating rumors. “I have never, and I won’t ever, speak about or confirm or deny anything about my personal life with anyone, ever,” he said.

Garfield, 43, was last romantically linked to spiritual adviser Dr. Kate Tomas; she confirmed their breakup on Oct. 11, 2024.

Barbaro, meanwhile, is a 36-year-old rising star who hasn’t spoken much about her love life either. She has touched on some offscreen relationships though, telling L’Officiel Australia in July 2023 that she has “a lovely community of friends. I love to host at my place and have everyone over for a Sunday morning, wear your PJs and just come, hang out and watch whatever, sports game or chat, catch up....Luckily, after abandoning my friends so much and leaving town, they’re still willing to come over and hang out.”

And in February 2025, she told Hollywood Authentic that attending events during awards season can really “change an actor’s life.”

When she went to the 2023 Oscars with the Top Gun: Maverick cast, “I just kept thinking: ‘Embrace it. See it. Feel it,’” she said.

“One of the coolest things about being in that conversation is getting to have that sense of community in a space that can be quite intimidating professionally,” she continued. “It was just so exciting to be there, and to watch people make speeches and honor their fellow nominees, and really truthfully do so. It’s not fake. That was so cool.”

Here, the complete (public) history of Barbaro and Garfield’s pretty private romance so far.

On January 4, Barbaro and Garfield were photographed with Eddie Redmayne and W magazine’s editor-at-large Lynn Hirschberg at the outlet’s Best Performances party in Los Angeles. Garfield had an arm around Barbaro in the photo:

On February 20, footage of Barbaro and Garfield sitting together at a performance of Jonathan Bailey’s Richard II in London circulated on social media. It sparked dating rumors that were confirmed a day later by People.

A source said the two actors had been dating quietly but did not specify when their relationship began. “They’ve been really low-key and have been spending time together quietly,” the insider said.

Neither commented on dating reports when they came out. Garfield does not have social media, while Barbaro has remained silent on the topic on Instagram.

On March 2, Barbaro and Garfield attended the Oscars but arrived separately. Fans noticed they walked down the red carpet at the same time, fueling speculation they may have traveled there together.

The couple was not photographed interacting at the ceremony, nor did they pose together at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party that they both attended. An eyewitness told Entertainment Tonight that they hung out inside there, though.

They were later photographed leaving the Vanity Fair Oscar Party and arriving at Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s Oscar party.

A source there told Entertainment Tonight that Garfield and Barbaro were glued to each other the entire time. They were seen “kissing and dancing the whole night,” the insider said.⁠

On March 16, gossip Instagram account DeuxMoi posted photos of Garfield and Barbaro shopping at a grocery store in Malibu. Garfield wore a red baseball cap, white T-shirt, and wide-legged denim jeans. Barbaro was in a white tank under a green cardigan and a blue cap. They took turns pushing a cart full of household items.

In early April, Garfield and Barbaro were spotted on vacation in Kyoto, Japan. A TikTok user shared footage of the couple holding hands and matching in gray as they walked around the city. At one point, Barbaro held on to Garfield’s arm in a sweet show of PDA.

On May 3, the couple was seen backstage at John Proctor Is the Villain on Broadway. The production shared photos of the two actors posing with the cast, writing in the caption, “new students at helen county high: thanks for joining us andrew garfield, monica barbaro, and bonnie milligan!!”

The pair was first seen at the Mark Hotel, according to Just Jared, before attending the popular new show. In the pics, they’re both wearing blue baseball caps and black jackets.

On July 6, Barbaro and Garfield enjoyed watching the match between Sonay Kartal and Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova on day seven of the 2025 Wimbledon Championships in London. The couple was engrossed in the game and one another, pausing to share some sweet PDA in between points.

They arrived in matching white Ralph Lauren looks, with Barbaro in a summer dress and heels and Garfield in white pants, a button-down, and a white cardigan around his shoulders.

On August 29, Barbaro and Garfield were photographed holding hands while at the Venice Film Festival. Garfield was wearing a pale blue button-down shirt with navy pants and sneakers. Barbaro had on a dark green leather jacket, black pants, and black flats. They both made appearances on the red carpet but did not walk together.

The couple signaled they’re still going strong in the new year during a Las Vegas date night. Barbaro and Garfield went to see Penn and Teller’s magic show and posed backstage with them. Garfield notably debuted blond hair.

“Great to have #andrewgarfield and @monicabarbaro at the show @riovegas over the weekend!” Penn and Teller wrote on January 12.

Garfield and Barbaro were photographed kissing while having dinner at Rome’s Pierluigi restaurant on June 27, marking their first major sighting in months. They were later seen walking back to their hotel together.

On July 4, they shared another kiss at Wimbledon.

On August 3, Garfield joined Barbaro in New York City following the premiere of her romantic comedy One Night Only. The couple was photographed arriving at an after-party together at The Crane Club.

For the evening, Garfield wore a deep green suit over a coordinating top, finishing the look with white sneakers. Barbaro opted for a black minidress with a plunging neckline, pointed black pumps, and a matching clutch.

Barbaro reflected on how her perspective on relationships has evolved in an interview with InStyle. “I feel like if you’re hard-up avoidant about love, it’s because, deep down, you’re actually super romantic, and you’re just afraid of getting hurt,” she said. “I dip my toe in all ideologies around romance, but mostly I’m a romantic.”

She continued, “I’m also kind of a workaholic, so I’ve never given my life over to it, which, as a woman, I’m quite proud of. But there’s also the other side of that coin, which is: You can get to a point in your life where you wake up and you look around and you’re sort of like, Oh, have I been self-protecting by [adopting] so much autonomy and independence?”

“I’m definitely shifting some of that perspective now,” she added.

The actress also spoke briefly about working with Garfield on Artificial, praising him as both a scene partner and an actor. “I mean, he’s one of the best actors of his generation, our generation,” she said. “I just learned a lot from his approach to the material and to developing character, and I felt very fortunate to get to witness that in real time.”

In his Who What Wear interview published on September 9, Garfield spoke briefly about his partner, who is also his co-star in Artificial. “I think Monica is a supremely talented actor,” he said. “I think what she did as Joan Baez [in A Complete Unknown]—what she accessed in that project—is nothing short of transformational, extraordinary, and deeply mysterious. I think she is truly incredible. I could wax lyrical more, but I’ll leave it there.”

On October 11, Garfield and Barbaro attended a screening of their upcoming film, Artificial, at the BFI London Film Festival. The couple posed together on the red carpet.

For the occasion, Barbaro wore a shimmering, pale blue Dior dress with thin straps and a softly flared skirt. She styled her brunette hair in loose waves. Garfield opted for an olive-colored blazer over a coordinating shirt, paired with dark trousers and wire-frame glasses.

On November 2, Garfield and Barbaro took in the Los Angeles Lakers’ game against the Miami Heat at Crypto.com Arena. They were photographed sitting courtside together, with Garfield wearing a burgundy top and khakis, while Barbaro chose a white button-down and jeans.

#6755. 14 Best Work Jackets for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a great work jacket has become every guy's fastest route to semi-rugged heartthrob style.

Honestly, they make looking good almost too easy. First, they inject your fits with casual, weekend tough-guy energy. (This, to be clear, is a plus.) Second, they flatter you in all the right places, framing your shoulders and neatening up your waistline whether you’re pairing them with jeans or the kinds of wide, puddling trousers we've long been yapping about.

Better still, you don’t have to spend a fortune. The classics from Dickies and Carhartt are as dependable as ever, and even the independent designer options are within reach of your budget—this is a cotton-forward option, after all. Here are 14 of our favorites, all of which will only look better after a few years (and a few scuffs) of real wear.

The Carhartt Detroit work jacket is the classic for a reason. It’s been around for more than 70 years—not quite as old as blue jeans or cowboy boots, but easily in the upper echelon of American fashion’s great exports. So much so that today, luxury brands are riffing on it, even selling pre-distressed, washed-down versions at triple the price. (And yes, this is also the work jacket that Austin Butler told us he wears.)

Cut to the waist, and built from thick, stiff canvas with three perfectly placed front pockets, the Detroit is an Eisenhower-style silhouette (during WWII, the then-Army General overhauled U.S. military dress and introduced the cropped, boxy jacket to American forces). Its insulated blanket lining and corduroy collar also make it one of the few true year-round, toasty work jackets out there. Simply put, this is a real piece of clothing for real life. (Though if it's not fancy enough for you, there’s always the street-ready, slimmer, unlined Carhartt WIP version.)

Just like Dickies' iconic 874 work pants, the brand's insulated Eisenhower jacket (there he is again) is a hard-wearing, warm, wallet-friendly piece of gear that fits incredibly well. Nearly as old as the Detroit Jacket above, it doesn’t always get the same respect. But maybe that's just because it flies a little more under the radar, with its logo patch tucked discreetly near the hem. Decades in, it remains a low-key, low-cost icon—less shouty than its Carhartt cousin, but every bit as authentic.

Wallace & Barnes, J.Crew's workwear line, is back with tough fabrics, heritage details, and a big hit of #menswear-era nostalgia—and this wool-lined work jacket shows exactly why folks missed it so much. It has all of the heartthrob-coded details you probably had in mind when you decided to look for a jacket like this: Corduroy collar, zippered chest pocket, slightly cropped fit. But it isn't just good-looking. It also has a wool-blend blanket lining, for superior warmth to help you enjoy it even if the depths of winter. And that, if cost-per-wear logic still applies, makes it more than worth its slightly higher price point.

Welcome to the world of truly warm fabrics, and actually glove-friendly pockets. Filson’s been mastering cold-weather gear since your great-great-grandfather was in short pants, and this work jacket continues that legacy. Based on the brand’s original 1914 Cruiser, it’s cut from 24-ounce Mackinaw wool — a tightly woven twill that truly blocks wind, sheds rain, and stays warm even when wet. Without being mean, it’s built to outlast even you. Pricey? Sure. But it’s the kind of thing your kids will remember you by (and fight for) someday.

Buck Mason’s archive is full to bursting with vintage pieces from decades past, which explains why its collections are filled with absolute bangers these days. Here the brand has taken a mid-century work jacket and remade it, tweaking the fit to make it a touch more relaxed, and using a soft Italian doeskin cotton fabric that’s more plush than anything a worksite would have issued back in the day. There's even more to love in the details: Shoulder pleats for easy movement, real horn buttons on the chest pockets, and a dressy point collar.

For Lo-heads, Polo Ralph Lauren's hard-wearing zipper jackets are the stuff of legend. And while you might have grown up with an inherited cotton example from your dad, in the last decade of so, Polo has been pushing its ‘Bi-Swing’ polyester and/or nylon takes instead. That's fine, but some of us aren't so willing to trade in the soft, rugged comfort of a full-cotton jacket. That's where the rarer Bayport Poplin jacket comes in. A work jacket with no delusions, it’s not stealing the working man’s valor — it knows exactly what it is. It’s Ralph Lauren, and it knows you’re working hard at hardly working. But it's also strong enough to handle whatever activities you throw at it, leisure or otherwise.

Sure, Copenhagen's Mfpen has its silhouettes dialed, but don't overlook its fabrications. Here, it’s a dense wool-blend with a multi-tonal yarn construction. Textured, substantive, perfect.

While most waxed cotton jackets lean more country estate than work site, Tom Beckbe's high-quality range include a few closer, more modern fits. Perfect for those looking for a work jacket that's also waterproof.

A designer-adjacent example for the fashion crowd, this piece from South Korea's FrizmWORKS doesn't just look good, it feels good too, thanks to that soft leather collar that's just buttery once it's flipped up.

Stan Ray is part of what you might call the big three of American workwear, alongside Dickies and Carhartt). The Texas-born brand’s aptly named Roughneck Jacket delivers exactly what you’d expect. It’s tough, practical, and built for wear. Ribbed cuffs keep the cold out, while the washed-out hue delivers a perfectly broken-in look from day one.

This jacket from New York's Corridor—made from a hefty cotton-blend twill—is a more colorful take on the work jacket, and bound to give any fall fit a lift.

Just as the Polo jacket above is an RL icon, so is this faithfully-recreated nautical deck jacket from Ralph's RRL line. It's restocked every fall, it sells out every fall.

A key feature of all work jackets is their shorter length, but for those of us who want to make sure ours hits right at the belt, look no further than Abercrombie’s entry.

A leading Parisian purveyor of vintage garms, BRUT has recently moved into making its own stuff, all rooted in the archival vintage styles they obsess over. The results are, how you say, on point.

These days, work jackets seem to have an undeniable stranglehold on the imagination of guys who spend all day staring at their keyboards. (There’s a political element to this, of course. Whether or not you act in solidarity with your fellow laborers under capitalism, a work jacket allows you to look the part of the everyman.) But also, they’re just a great jacket for busy lives! There’s a generally accommodating cut that doesn’t restrict your movement, plenty of pockets, and hardy materials that can easily handle a snag, or sudden shower.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6754. This Eccentric Village Pub Hotel on Loch Lomond Is Scotland’s Most Charming New Stay

Even if you have never set foot in Scotland, there is a good chance you already know the chorus to “The Bonnie Banks o’ Loch Lomond.” The wistful 18th-century folk ballad—all about taking the high road or the low road back to the country’s largest and arguably most romantic expanse of water—has cropped up everywhere from The Simpsons to, well, every Scottish wedding on earth.

But for the millions of travelers who actually make the pilgrimage up the A82 highway from Glasgow each year, the experience of those famous shores is often reduced to a fleeting blur of slate-blue water through a car window as they head deeper into the Highlands. Even for those who do pull over in Luss—an almost absurdly pretty conservation village of climbing rose-covered sandstone cottages and slate roofs on the loch’s western shore—it has historically been for a quick stroll down the pier (and maybe an ice cream) before getting right back on the road.

Yet when I arrived in Luss on a gloriously sunny weekend in late summer, the village was in peak form, filled with hikers in boots and day-trippers clutching coffees and ambling down the winding lanes toward the glittering water. And as I pulled up to the newly reopened Loch Lomond Arms, I spotted a steady stream of curious locals popping their heads through its antler-crowned yellow door. Set inside a 17th-century former coaching inn at the heart of this tiny community of just 120 residents, the property has long been a beloved local watering hole. And now, following a whirlwind six-month transformation, it’s been reborn as one of Scotland’s most characterful new stays.

The mastermind behind this reinvention is Patrick Colquhoun—son of the current chief of Clan Colquhoun (pronounced ka-hoon, for the uninitiated), the family that has held the surrounding 45,000-acre Luss Estate for more than 800 years—who enlisted the celebrated British interior designer Russell Sage to help breathe new life into the building. Sage is no stranger to high-end Scottish hospitality, having previously conjured the maximalist wonderland of The Fife Arms in Braemar, the whimsical, art-stuffed Victorian hotel backed by mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth.

Here, though, the brief was intentionally more modest. “I said right from the outset, it’s a coaching inn and it’s a pub—we’re not trying to be a five-star hotel,” Sage tells me. Colquhoun felt similarly, noting that while Scotland has seen plenty of big-budget luxury openings over the past decade, he wanted “an inn where the design, the food, and the welcome are taken as seriously as they would be in a grand hotel, but where you can still find yourself mixing with local residents.”

That sense of laid-back, unpretentious warmth was evident the moment I crossed the threshold. There is no formal reception desk; instead, I was greeted like an old pal by a member of the affable, mostly local team decked out in butterscotch yellow waistcoats, and ushered into the Map Room, a snug where pink velvet chairs and sturdy antique tables sit beneath a ceiling papered entirely in vintage hand-drawn charts inherited from Colquhoun’s grandfather. After a marathon journey involving three connecting flights to reach Glasgow—and coming off the back of a particularly hectic week that had left me feeling a little under the weather—the lack of fuss was firmly appreciated. Better still was what awaited upstairs when I was led to my bedroom: a golden dram of Scotch whisky and a plate of crumbly cheese straws laid out on a side table. I snacked on a straw and opened my window, plunking myself down onto the super-king four-poster bed to let the loch-side air work its magic. (By which I mean: I fell into a coma-like stupor.)

After rousing myself for a wander around, I discovered there are no room numbers at the Loch Lomond Arms. Instead, each of the 15 bedrooms (which start at a remarkably reasonable rate, given the pedigree) is named after an eccentric figure or episode from the Colquhoun family history, brought to life after Sage and his team were let loose on eight centuries of archives, attics, and outbuildings. “Fifteen rooms turns out to be about the right number,” Colquhoun jokes. “If we had 30 we might have run out of colorful relatives!”

I was ensconced in The Wallabies, an ocean-blue suite layered with tartan and curiosities that looks out over the rooftops of the village. Its name pays tribute to Patrick’s great-aunt, Fiona Colquhoun—later the Countess of Arran—who in the 1940s famously packed a mob of red-necked wallabies into the back of her E-Type Jaguar and released them onto the nearby island of Inchconnachan, where a wild colony still hops around to this day. (In a delightful touch, if I wanted my sheets changed, I simply had to leave the stuffed toy wallaby provided on the bed.)

On a subsequent tour of the property, every corner of the inn seemed to burst with history. Rather than purchasing new furniture, Sage’s team stripped, restored, and hand-painted heirloom pieces pulled straight from the family’s cupboards and drawers. “The idea of getting people engaged with a place through telling its stories is really important to me,” Sage explained. You can see it in the hallway’s stuffed lion, a nod to Patrick’s great-grandfather Sir Iain, who casually took a pet lion cub with him to the trenches during World War I (and was later court-martialed for keeping a written account of the 1914 Christmas truce). Or in Nova Scotia Love Potion, a russet-walled room tucked into the eaves with cabinetry hand-painted by artist Lizzie Bentley, dedicated to a 16th-century ancestor dubbed “the last witch in Scotland” after he concocted an illicit elixir to seduce his sister-in-law. Yes, really.

Most delightful of all, perhaps, is the room dedicated to the aforementioned Countess of Arran’s later years, when she walked a pet badger around Luss on a leash—and, at the age of 62, piloted a powerboat at 102 miles per hour to earn the moniker “the fastest granny on the water” in the British tabloids. “We had 800 years of history sitting in the family archives and a building in the village that seemed a perfect opportunity to bring the stories to life,” Patrick notes. There are QR codes subtly etched on panels on the doors that tell those stories, which could easily be the basis for a particularly unhinged Wes Anderson film—if he decided to make one set around a Scottish loch, that is. (Get writing, Wes.)

Those ancestral tales spill out of the bedrooms and into the surrounding landscape, with guest excursions designed around the very figures whose portraits line the walls. While my lingering travel fatigue meant I reluctantly had to skip a speedboat trip across the loch to Inchconnachan aboard the Beau Jangles—for this, you’ll channel the free-wheeling spirit of Lady Arran by roaring between the loch's wooded islands and dropping anchor for a glass of champagne—I did manage to head out on an exhilarating 4x4 safari into the dramatic hill ground rising behind the village. Bumping along rugged tracks, we passed through sweeping glens and areas of active peatland and native woodland restoration—part of a centuries-old commitment to conservation that makes the wild, cinematic beauty of the Highlands feel newly alive.

Honestly, though, if you need a proper recharge, there’s no shame in spending the bulk of your stay simply hunkered down inside the inn. (I say this partly to justify the fact that is what I mostly did.) What truly elevates the Loch Lomond Arms from a handsome design project into a soul-restoring getaway is its staff, most of whom hail from the local area. I spent a lovely afternoon being guided around the town by the church beadle John Taylor, whose genuinely fascinating insights into local history—I was particularly dazzled by a Viking gravestone dating back to the 11th century in the churchyard—proved that Luss has been drawing raucous overseas tourists for well over a millennium. (John even came decked out in a kilt and a sporran for our wander, an impressive display of local dedication given the afternoon heat.) And that local spirit was especially apparent on the food and beverage front, overseen by the endlessly knowledgeable Matt, who guided me through an early-evening tasting in the Map Room as a fire crackled in the hearth; I regularly spotted him throughout my stay whizzing around pouring rare Scottish malts, alongside small-batch spirits from the village’s own Luss Distillery, for other guests.

Then, there’s the food in the inn’s bustling pub and dining room, The Stag & Two Hounds, where the walls are wrapped in bespoke Trossachs-inspired wallpaper by Dundee artist Freya Cumming and the kitchen leans heavily on produce reared, caught, or foraged on the estate. My dinner began with crisp pork and apple croquettes—delivering all the hearty comfort of a Sunday roast in just a few sweet-and-savory bites—followed by silky slivers of Scottish salmon, cured in-house, of course. The real showstopper, however, was a killer steak and Lomond ale pie: tender estate beef slow-braised in dark and malty local beer beneath a lid of buttery pastry. (And for those planning a visit soon, there’s even more to look forward to on the culinary front: alongside the sun-dappled outdoor tables of The Gathering, the team is gearing up to unveil The Treasury, an intimate, candlelit fine-dining room hidden behind a curtain that will showcase the very best of the estate’s larder atop priceless family heirlooms.)

By the time I packed my bags to head back to Glasgow Airport—feeling entirely, miraculously restored after 48 hours of Highland hospitality—the Loch Lomond Arms had done exactly what it set out to do. And, it turns out, this is just the beginning of an ambitious new chapter for Luss Estates, which also offers a collection of charming historic cottages for rent around the village and has plans to bring the same design-led, high-craft ethos to future projects across the land. To paraphrase that famous old ballad: the banks of Loch Lomond just got a wee bit more bonnie.

#6752. Dior and Harper’s Bazaar Host a Screening of the New Richard Avedon Documentary in Los Angeles

With Emma Watson, Gia Coppola, and more in attendance

From a Paris Fashion Week toast to a New York City launch party, Dior and Harper’s Bazaar have been honoring the legacy of fashion photographer Richard Avedon these past few weeks. This series of intimate events has been tied to the launch of a new coffee-table book titled Richard Avedon: The Harper’s Bazaar Years, as well as a documentary film, Avedon. Now, the festivities have traveled to Los Angeles.

Avedon, who passed away in 2004 at the age of 81, was one of the most influential fashion photographers of the 20th century. In 1944, at just 21 years old, he started his career at Harper’s Bazaar under the guidance of then-editor-in-chief Carmel Snow, and he spent the next two-plus decades defining the creative vision of the publication.

Richard Avedon: The Harper’s Bazaar Years (available now) explores this artistic period by compiling rarely seen photographs, a never-before-published account from Avedon himself, a foreword by editor-in-chief Samira Nasr, and an essay by Bazaar contributing editor Derek C. Blasberg. The new documentary, meanwhile, offers a look through the Avedon archives from a different lens. It was directed by Academy Award–winning filmmaker Ron Howard (Apollo 13, A Beautiful Mind, The Da Vinci Code).

Focusing on the film, Dior and Blasberg hosted a private screening of Avedon at the William Morris Endeavor headquarters in L.A. Guests such as Emma Watson, Gia Coppola, Lauren Hutton, Devon Lee Carlson, and more gathered to watch the film before heading to the House of Dior in Beverly Hills for a cocktail reception.

Ahead, we offer an intimate look inside the event.

#6751. All About Brittany Snow’s Fiancé, Hunter Moreno

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In October 2024, The Hunting Wives actress Brittany Snow was seen with a mystery man in New York City. He was identified as cinematographer Hunter Moreno, and the pair looked very cozy, sharing a kiss while walking Snow’s dog. The actress was wearing a Yankees cap, a long black coat, and wide-legged pants for the outing with a pair of sunglasses. Moreno was in a baseball cap, jeans, and a big white hoodie.

A year earlier, Snow divorced ex-husband Tyler Stanaland, known for his role on Selling the OC, a spinoff of the popular Netflix reality show, Selling Sunset.

The former couple announced their split in September 2022 in a joint statement on Instagram that is now deleted, saying, “This decision was made with love and mutual respect for one another. We have realized we need to take some time and make sure we are each living our most fulfilling and authentic lives. We started this journey as best friends and our relationship will continue to be a priority not only for us but for our dog Charlie.”

Fast-forward to November 2025, reports surfaced that Snow and Moreno had gotten engaged. Snow has since posted tributes to him on Instagram, though she hasn’t discussed their relationship status herself.

Here’s what there is to know about Moreno and his relationship with Snow so far.

Moreno is a creative director, cinematographer, and photographer who has worked with celebrities like Selena Gomez, Cara Delevingne, Reneé Rapp, Machine Gun Kelly, Miley Cyrus, and brands like Vogue, Inkd Magazine, and Madewell. He started his career in Los Angeles, filming YouTube videos for growing influencers.

He seems to have been working on directing more music videos in 2024, and was nominated for a directing award at the People’s Choice Country Awards.

He also briefly dated Tana Mongeau in 2017.

Moreno is the co-founder and creative director of Make Sure Your Friends Are OK, or MSYFAO. The organization sells merchandise and then donates a portion of the profits to mental health charities. In an episode of Recovering From Reality with Alexis Haines, he says he was inspired by his own struggles with mental health issues.

Mental health is an important issue to Snow as well, who co-wrote a book titled September Letters about issues around mental well-being, partnering with the Mental Health Coalition.

In January 2025, Snow tagged Moreno in a series of photos taken of her for a Netflix press event, crediting him for photographing her. She wrote, “I was asked to hang out a little bit with my friends at @nightagentnetflix. I got to be an agent and run around the streets of Bangkok. Weirdly, I did not wear this dress. 🤍* press for season 2 *”

As of July 2025, the two still follow each other on Instagram, and Moreno has liked almost all her recent Instagrams. She also regularly likes his posts.

Yes. On March 28, 2026, Snow quietly tucked a photo of herself with Moreno into an Instagram carousel:

She shared a birthday tribute to him on Oct. 20, 2026. “Happy birthday to my favorite person on the planet,” she wrote. “I must have done something right to deserve someone like you. Everyone who knows you, knows you are sunshine in human form. This was the first picture we ever took together (we didn’t know it was being taken) and I’ve never stopped hugging you & laughing with you since. It’s my favorite place to be. I love u @huntermoreno.”

During her November 2026 appearance on Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard, Snow touched on her relationship with Moreno when discussing why she is thankful for her divorce from Tyler Stanaland. “I am so grateful that I went through that because the person that I am and the partner I’m with now, it’s just so different,” she said. “I can’t believe I’m grateful for my divorce. I was 37 and I was living in an Airbnb, just staring at my dog being like, ‘I don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s just you and me, kiddo, and we’re going to try to rebuild this.’”

“And I really appreciated so many women, friends of mine that were like, ‘That happened to me,’” she added. “And, you know, I would go on Reddit and look up stories from women going through things in their later 30s and finding people later in life. We have to make it what we make of it.”

On Nov. 10, 2025, a video surfaced on social media of Snow and Claire Danes talking on the red carpet of The Beast in Me’s premiere. At one point, Danes smiled and asked Snow, “You’re engaged? When did that happen?”

One day later, TMZ reported that Moreno did indeed pop the question, though Snow has not discussed their status herself.
